articles.title_orig: China’s nuclear buildup is ‘hot and heavy,’ Trump says a day after meeting with Xi
articles.title_zh: China’s nuclear buildup is ‘hot and heavy,’ Trump says a day after meeting with Xi
articles.content_orig:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Beijing is building nuclear weapons at a “hot and heavy” pace, President Donald Trump said Friday, a day after he met Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin and the three countries agreed to talks on preventing nuclear proliferation.
While Russia and the U.S. lead the world by each possessing thousands of nuclear weapons, China is rapidly expanding its nuclear arsenal. In its annual review of China’s military buildup, the Pentagon said China’s stockpile of nuclear warheads remained in the low 600s through 2024, but the country was on track to have more than 1,000 warheads by 2030.
“They’ll catch us within 10 years,” Trump said of China’s nuclear buildup during a news conference at the White House. “They’re going at it hot and heavy, but they have a lot.”
Trump’s public remarks were his first since his controversial summit with Xi and Putin , leaders of countries long considered U.S. rivals, in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen on Thursday. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who spoke to reporters alongside Trump on Friday, said it was imperative for the three nuclear powers to talk.
“These three countries possess the overwhelming majority of nuclear weapons on this planet,” Rubio said. “The idea that these three leaders should not engage on a regular basis is not just absurd, it’s dangerous.”
After the trilateral meeting, the leaders issued a joint statement , saying they “affirmed that a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought” and “will conduct a dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing the proliferation of nuclear weapons.”
Prior to the meeting, observers had doubted if China would agree to nuclear talks. With a much smaller nuclear arsenal, Beijing had resisted joining nuclear arms control talks with the U.S. and Russia.

articles.title_orig: How Carney’s Shift Toward China Could Become Leverage in Stalled U.S. Trade Talks
articles.title_zh: How Carney’s Shift Toward China Could Become Leverage in Stalled U.S. Trade Talks
articles.content_orig:
Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney shakes hands with China's President Xi Jinping at the APEC summit on Nov. 19, 2026.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney is placing particular focus on renewing relations with China as he aims to deepen international trade ties and diversify from U.S. reliance amid a three month-long trade war with the U.S.
When asked what cards Canada holds in its ongoing talks with Washington, Carney, who recently announced a new partnership with the E.U. , pointed to the country's budding relationships elsewhere.
“Our cards are that everyone else in the world wants to deal with us,” he said Wednesday during a remote interview with the New York Times from Shenzhen, China, where he was among the world leaders attending the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit . "If the U.S. doesn't want to do the deal, we're busy.” His remarks came in the wake of President Donald Trump's claim that the U.S. holds “all the cards” after trade talks collapsed in August, leading to both sides enforcing heavy retaliatory tariffs .
Carney and Trump had a meeting on the sidelines of APEC, but aside from a commitment to “continue” negotiations and stay in close contact, no progress was made. However, Carney painted his meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping in a much more positive light. Ahead of the summit, Carney and Xi announced a Canada-China trade pact , which provided additional tariff relief on Canadian food and agricultural exports into China, and in return saw Canada agree to extend tariff exemptions for certain Chinese steel and aluminum products by two years.
“Carney, who is promoting a “Canada Strong” platform as he aims to build economic resilience at home, touted the expansion of the trade arrangement with China as something that will deliver “greater certainty and prosperity for all Canadians.” He also praised the negotiation process with China, saying: “They’re very professional. They move forward in a very linear fashion.”
In an eight-day tour that took him from a European summit in Ireland to the Philippines, Cambodia, and finally China for the APEC gathering, Carney forged ahead with his plan to diversify Canada's economy away from its dependence on the U.S., which by far remains the country's largest trading partner .
Experts say Canada's progress in deepening its economic relationships with China could challenge Trump's insistence that Washington holds the upper hand in trade negotiations.
“Part of the Trump Administration’s [belief] is that everybody needs the U.S. more than anything else, and therefore the U.S. has maximum leverage,” says Jennifer Hillman, co-director of the Institute of International Economic Law at Georgetown University. “What this is clearly saying is that Canada can afford to be less willing to give the U.S. whatever it asks for [in negotiations], because they have other options.”
China has the world's second-largest economy , behind only the U.S., giving it the potential to become a much larger market for Canadian goods than some of the other countries Carney has sought to deepen relations with.
“China represents a very big market and the potential of a really big trading partner,” says Lori Turnbull, a professor in the Faculty of Management at Dalhousie University, noting it could be a leverage point in U.S. negotiations. “Doing a deal with a country like China is something that [the U.S.] will care about because of the size of China's economy and its competitive relationship with the U.S.”
Carney's latest push to strengthen trade ties with Beijing forms part of a months-long effort to renew Canada-China relations. In January, he met with Jinping to forge what he called a “ new strategic partnership ,” agreeing to allow in up to 49,000 Chinese electric vehicles at a tariff of 6.1%, rather than the previous 100% levy. China agreed to lower tariffs on Canadian agricultural products, including canola seeds, a major Canadian export.
The move drew criticism from Trump, who said that “China will eat Canada alive, completely devour it, including the destruction of their businesses, social fabric, and general way of life.”
While Canada's closer relationship with China could strengthen its hand in negotiations, experts also warn that it could backfire.
Turnbull points to the latest agreement to extend tariff exemptions on Chinese steel and aluminum as a potential source of tension with Washington. “Things like reducing tariffs on select steel and aluminum products coming from China is something that might make the U.S. and not just Donald Trump, but also [U.S. Trade Representative] Jamieson Greer angry,” she suggests.
Steel, aluminum, and auto tariffs were among the major points of contention when U.S.-Canada trade negotiations broke down in August, with both sides accusing each other of walking back commitments.
Carney, however, has played down concerns that Canada's growing trade relationship with China is a major issue for Trump.
“In my conversation with the President, he’s tried to understand where we are with China, where we’re going with China,” said Carney during a news conference in Shenzhen. “I shouldn’t speak for him, but in his hierarchy of issues, it’s not the top issue at all.”
Meanwhile, some Canadian officials have voiced concerns on expanding trade with China.
Ontario Premier Doug Ford warned Carney on Monday against opening the door for more Chinese-made EV vehicles in Canada, arguing the “government’s focus needs to be on protecting Canadian auto workers, not undermining them by importing even more state-subsidized cheap Chinese cars.”
Michael Chong, a lawmaker from Canada’s Conservative Party, during a press conference on Wednesday supported maintaining a dialogue with Beijing, but described Carney’s budding strategic partnership with China as a “risky gambit,” citing potential “national security” concerns.
In 2025, Ottawa identified China as one of the main perpetrators of foreign interference and espionage against Canada alongside other countries such as Russia and Iran. The Canadian government’s own analysis of Canada-China relations also points out that there are "associated risks” in broader trade cooperation in key areas, such as “prevalent and persistent intellectual property theft, and the risk of diversion of sensitive goods and technologies intended for civilian use for military purposes and applications.”
Carney said ahead of his Asia trip that he would raise concerns about foreign interference in his meeting with Xi. "The advantage of these meetings is you can raise issues directly and frankly,” he told reporters in Montreal on Nov. 10. Carney added that he would stress the importance Canada places on "the non-interference in our affairs by China and other countries.”
In a press briefing during the APEC summit, Carney emphasized that Canada's trade with China is largely focused on commodities, rather than sensitive technologies such as advanced semiconductors.
“We are exporting canola, we are exporting pork. We are exporting halibut,” Carney said , also citing liquefied natural gas and oil. “These are important industries. These are not cutting-edge semi-conductors.”
Experts point out that Canada could pursue deeper cooperation with other international partners in sectors where a closer relationship with China would be more difficult, including defense and advanced technology.
“[Canada] is not going to partner with China on defense, security, AI, and digital technology, things like that would be very difficult. [Carney] would have an impossible time trying to convince Canadians that's what we should be doing,” says Turnbull. “For those things, [Canada] would be putting [its] arms around the European Union.”

articles.title_orig: China takes centre stage at trilateral with US, Russia
articles.title_zh: China takes centre stage at trilateral with US, Russia
articles.content_orig:
Xi, Putin and Trump outline priorities that include UN reform, boosting oil supplies and ‘protection of diplomatic immunity’
China, Russia and the US say they have agreed a peace statement after an unprecedented trilateral summit, but the declaration made no mention of the wars in Ukraine and Iran caused by two of the participants.
The declaration on Thursday also outlined a set of priorities that included changing the UN, boosting oil supplies and what it said was the protection of diplomatic immunity.
The statement affirmed that “a nuclear war cannot be won and must not be fought”, but stopped short of suggesting the beginnings of a framework for denuclearisation.
The meeting between Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump has dominated the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit this week, with China, the host, promising it would be “groundbreaking”.
“We are really making history,” Trump told Xi and Putin at the start of the meeting. “No peace was ever forged by declining opportunities for engagement.”
Putin told a press conference later that the three men had had a “free discussion” and now had a “mutual understanding”.
Some had hopes that the talks, which lasted about one hour and 20 minutes, could be used to discuss reductions in arms between the world’s three largest nuclear powers. Beijing has previously rebuffed Trump’s advances to join such talks, pointing to the larger US and Russian stockpiles. On Thursday, though, Xi called for nuclear weapons to “be completely prohibited and thoroughly destroyed over time to make the world free of [them]”.
The language of the declaration around nuclear war is the same as that previously issued by the five permanent members of the UN security council, which includes France and the UK.
“The real test will be whether the three countries follow through on their stated commitment to discuss nuclear risk reduction and preventing nuclear proliferation,” said Patricia Kim, an expert on Chinese foreign policy at the Brookings Institution, a US thinktank. Even the suggestion that China would engage was significant, said Yun Sun, a senior fellow at the Stimson Center.
Analysts had said that the meeting’s primary significance was in its optics. “Overall, very little of substance seems to have been accomplished … This summit appears to have been all about the symbolism and prestige value,” said Prof William Hurst, from the University of Cambridge’s Centre for Geopolitics. Putin pushed back at the suggestion the summit had just been a photo-op. “It is a serious collaborative work,” he said.
In the declaration, the men “committed themselves to maintaining strategic stability and international security”.
First among their concerns was “promoting UN reform so that it may respond more effectively to global challenges”. Sun said this was a favourite topic of China’s and showed that Beijing was “flexing its diplomatic muscles”. She said: “It is able to set the agenda and the deliverables according to its priorities … and make other great powers accept them.”
The declaration also agreed that “the international criminal court [ICC] and other similar institutions must not abuse their jurisdiction”. Putin is subject to an ICC arrest warrant and so the clause added to the perception that he has done well from the summit. Since the 2022 invasion of Ukraine, the Russian president has been treated as an international pariah by Kyiv’s allies and he has not been to an Apec summit in years.
Hurst said: “This was no Yalta moment, but it was certainly a solid public demonstration of Russia’s (and Putin’s) continuing relevance and power. It’s yet another example of Putin playing a poor hand to maximum effect.”
Xi, his status as a global power broker now assured, began the morning by addressing Apec leaders, reiterating the themes of trade openness and innovation he has emphasised throughout the summit. However, Apec affairs appeared to take a back seat for most of the day, with business dominating the discussions. For all the camaraderie on display, relations are complex. Russia is under US sanctions over the Ukraine war, while China and the US spent much of the last year engaged in an escalating tit-for-tat trade war before Trump and Xi called a truce .
Trump and Putin earlier held a separate meeting – their first since August 2025 – where the US president called his Russian counterpart his “friend”.
European allies meeting in Berlin to show their support for Ukraine expressed indignation at the cosy optics. “Mr Putin is not our friend and ⁠will never be,” the Polish prime minister, Donald Tusk, said in a rejoinder to Trump. The Danish prime minister, Mette Frederiksen, said she found it “very incomprehensible” that a US ​president would want to sit down with Putin.
The peace declaration in Shenzhen said the three countries planned “to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products for the benefit of all nations”. That was important, said Shan Guo from Hutong Research, a Shanghai-based advisory firm, but “now let’s see if the US will lift sanctions”.
Trump and Xi then held their third bilateral of this year. Xi said the US-China relationship was “generally stable and positive”, according to state media. But he cautioned Washington over Taiwan, saying the US “must keep doing the right thing to avoid major setbacks in US-China relations”.
Another watched-for topic lacking detailed findings was that of AI. Xi said the two countries should “enhance communication and coordination to guard against security risks … and ensure that AI remains under human control at all times”.
Ultimately, the lack of breakthroughs might suit China, which has no appetite to move beyond the role of convener, said Kim. “Beijing has little interest in taking on the diplomatic risks of brokering an actual peace agreement in Ukraine or resolving the conflict with Iran. That would entangle China in conflicts it would rather avoid,” she said.

articles.title_orig: China's BYD has SUV that infringes on JLR Defender design, Dutch court rules
articles.title_zh: China's BYD has SUV that infringes on JLR Defender design, Dutch court rules
articles.content_orig:
By FREDA LEWIS-STEMPEL, SENIOR MOTORING REPORTER
Updated: 05:34 EST, 20 November 2026
One of China's newest luxury car brands has proven its off-roading might by getting its range-topping SUV to tow a jumbo jet.
Denza – the luxury technology sub-brand of BYD – used its Bao 5 boxy SUV to pull the famous airliner – which weighs a whopping 180 tons – some 1,600m down a runway.
The Bao 5 is Denza's Land Rover Defender rival, with the boxy 4x4 plug-in hybrid (PHEV) offering 56 miles of EV-only range and 537bhp and 750Nm of torque from its 1.5-litre turbocharged petrol engine.
As well as pulling the passenger jet using all four wheels, the Chinese family car also became the first production vehicle to tow a plane on two wheels and the first to tow a 747 using electric power alone.
Denza said it set out to achieve something 'hugely ambitious' that 'had never been tried before', and that 'truly challenged the capability of the advanced plug-in hybrid powertrain'.
The Bao 5 went on sale in October and costs from £69,500 – so it doesn't have BYD's bargain price tags on its side. First UK owners are taking delivery now.
To prove the Bao 5's rugged capabilities and the might of its DMO (Dual Mode Off-road) powertrain, the SUV towed the massive aircraft for three runs of Dunsfold Aerodrome in Surrey.
The first run was on all four wheels, a second on three wheels, and a final run on two wheels – which had never been attempted before.
Over the combined distance of all three runs – which allowed for stops for filming and to remove wheels – the Bao 5 towed the 747 the equivalent of four laps of a standard-size athletics track.
Denza used a standard Bao 5 for the runs: a production-specification car in Ultimate guise with minimal modifications. The DMO plug-in hybrid powertrain was used in its normal form.
A bespoke towing attachment was made to connect the Bao 5 to the aircraft, while the car's passenger seats were removed to facilitate the installation of 4,500kg of ballast when driving with two wheels, and 2,000kg when driving on three wheels.
Additionally, small stabilisers were added to each axle to balance out the removal of the two driven wheels.
The plug-in hybrid SUV pulled the plane using all four wheels, as well as two wheels, and on electric power alone
A standard Bao 5 was used for the runs with minimal modifications. The DMO PHEV powertrain was used in its normal form too
In total the Bao 5 towed the 747 for 1,600 metres - the equivalent of four laps of a standard-size athletics track
Should luxury SUVs be built for extreme feats or focus on practical everyday needs?
The Boeing 747-400 used for the runs left active service in 2020 but still retains its engines and fully furnished interior.
To make matters harder for the Bao 5 – which promises to 'conquer the unexpected' – the weather was typically British with torrential rain arriving for the final attempts.
However, eventually, the runway dried out sufficiently for the car to find enough traction to get the 747 moving.
The incredible feat comes just days after reports emerged that JLR in August had orchestrated a raid on the European offices of Denza's Chinese parent group, BYD, over accusations that its new Ti7 SUV is a dupe of its best-selling Defender SUV.
However, JLR suffered a setback last week when a judge ordered the carmaker to destroy all copies of documents seized , which were deemed not relevant to its copycat claims.
The Denza Bao 5's (left) boxy proportions are very much like those of the popular Land Rover Defender (right). But the Bao 5 as 56 miles of EV range compared to the Defender PHEV's 27 miles
Denza is the BYD brand few people will have heard of.
Founded in China in 2010, the luxury tech arm of BYD focuses on 'new energy vehicles' – EVs and advanced hybrids.
Denza's first model went on sale in China at the end of 2014, and then in 2025 B YD announced that Denza would arrive in Europe, with Britain set to be one of its first markets.
Denza promises to 'blend cutting-edge technology with sophisticated design to deliver a smarter, safer and more refined driving experience'.
Having pinpointed the boxy 4x4 market as its first move in the UK, Denza sees the Bao 5 not only as a Defender adversary, but as an 'entry ticket to the segment'.
The Bao 5 can produce 537bhp and 760nM and can do 0-62mph in 4.8 seconds
Inside the Bao 5 has a 12.3-inch driver display, a 15.6-inch infotainment screen, a wide head-up display and a passenger widescreen as well as cockpit-style buttons
The square-cut SUV has an upright stance, assertive front-end, ring-shaped headlights framing a dark grille, scalloped lower bumper and contrasting skid plate.
But while it's all business on the outside, the cabin is luxurious.
It mixes state-of-the-art tech – a 12.3-inch full-LCD driver display, 50-inch head-up display, 15.6-inch central touchscreen and 12.3-inch passenger display – with soft materials and utilitarian off-roading features.
The cockpit-style button panel and gear selector are paired with practical and durable features in angular grab-handle-style air vents.
As well as the 56 miles of electric-only mode – significantly more than the Defender PHEV's 27-mile EV range – with a full petrol tank and a battery charged to 100 per cent you get 537 miles in total without needing to stop.

articles.title_orig: Russian missiles land in Poland, as Europe held military drills nearby. NATO calls it a violation
articles.title_zh: Russian missiles land in Poland, as Europe held military drills nearby. NATO calls it a violation
articles.content_orig:
Poland's government said Russian missiles landed in the country overnight as Vladimir Putin's forces hammered Ukraine with what President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called "one of the largest attacks" since the war began. The strikes on Ukraine killed at least eight people, according to Zelenskyy.
The prime minister of Poland, a NATO member, decried the Russian weapons landing in his country as "an intentional provocation" of the U.S.-led military alliance.
"We know that what landed on Polish soil came from Russia. Therefore — ⁠and this is not just my own assessment, but ‌also that of our foreign partners, including those within NATO — it does not look like an ‌accident," Prime Minister ⁠Donald Tusk said. "It ‌appears that we ⁠are dealing with an intentional ⁠provocation."
NATO and Allied planes responded to the incident, including Polish F-16s, Swedish JAS 39 Gripens, a Dutch A330 Multi Role Tanker Transport (MRTT) aerial refueling aircraft and others. NATO and Allied ground-based air defenses were also alerted.
"Russia is trying to compensate for its military and diplomatic impotence with precisely this kind of terror," Zelenskyy wrote, adding that Putin's attempt to "redraw the world" with his Chinese and U.S. counterparts during their summit Thursday in China had been a "failure."
Russia fired more than 400 drones and 110 missiles at Ukraine overnight and early Friday, including cluster munitions, Zelenskyy said in a fiery social media post . Some of the Russian weapons hit the Austrian embassy and landed near the Netherlands embassy in Kyiv, prompting France to call for a meeting of the United Nations Security Council.
"Russia will have to answer for this," French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot wrote in a social media post.
Poland's defense minister said three Russian weapons, believed to have been two missiles and a drone, entered southeast Poland's airspace on Friday. Poland scrambled fighter jets and Patriot anti-missile systems in the country's southeast were activated, but no injuries were reported.
Drones have repeatedly entered the airspace of Poland and other NATO countries, mostly near Ukraine but not all, since Russia launched its full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022.
The Article 5 collective defense clause in NATO's founding charter states that an attack on one member is considered an attack on all 32.
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte said in a Friday social media post that he had spoken with Tusk "about the grave violations of Polish airspace overnight" and stressed that the alliance stands "in solidarity with Poland and will continue to strengthen our ability to deter and defend."
"This incident is clearly dangerous — a consequence of Russia's ongoing war against Ukraine," Rutte said. "I condemn Russia's attacks as well as its ongoing war. We continue to stand united as Allies and will continue to support Ukraine."
NATO's Supreme Allied Commander for Europe, U.S. Air Force Gen. Alexus Grynkewich, was in "close contact with Poland's chief of defense and minister of defense as Poland's investigation into the overnight airspace violations continues," his spokesperson Martin O'Donnell told CBS News on Friday.
Thousands of troops from 11 European countries that support Kyiv, members of the so-called Coalition of the Willing , are currently in Poland taking part in a major military exercise framed as training for a possible post-war mission in Ukraine.
According to Polish defense officials, two missiles thought to be Russian Kh-101s and one jet-powered drone landed between 30 and 60 miles inside Polish territory from the border with Ukraine.
"It is hard to regard it as a coincidence that the time and place of the violation of Polish airspace coincide with the Coalition of the Willing's exercises," Deputy Polish Prime Minister and Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz wrote in a social media post .
The escalation comes a day after President Trump sat with Xi and Putin —   whom he greeted warmly and called his friend — in Shenzhen, China, for a rare face-to-face meeting that seemed to achieve little .
The presidents discussed the Ukraine war, which Mr. Trump has long pushed to end through negotiations, but soon after the 90-minute meeting, Putin ruled out direct talks with Kyiv , citing a strike earlier this week by Ukrainian forces that severely damaged a highly symbolic bridge linking Russia and Ukraine's Russian-occupied Crimean Peninsula.
"We will respond to these strikes," Putin warned Thursday. "I want everyone to know this. I believe that our retaliatory actions … will be far more painful than what the Kiev regime did to the bridge."
Ukrainian forces managed to intercept 79 of the 110 missiles Russia launched overnight, Zelenskyy said, but none of the 27 ballistic missiles, which he attributed to Kyiv's lack of interceptors. He has been pleading with the Trump administration to help Ukraine replenish its missile interceptor stocks for months, saying the shortage is being paid for in civilian lives.
Russia's attack targeted Kyiv and nine other regions, leaving more than two dozen people wounded in addition to the eight confirmed to have been killed, according to Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi .
"Missiles hit critical infrastructure in the capital, including bridges," he said. "A water supply facility, office and commercial buildings were damaged."
A hospital in Kharkiv was damaged, as well as businesses in the Mykolaiv, Odesa and Chernihiv regions, and residential buildings in the regions of Dnipropetrovsk, Vinnytsia, Sumy, Chernihiv and Lviv, which is in the far west, close to Poland, Koretskyi said, adding that energy infrastructure was also hit.
Some nuclear plants were forced to reduce power generation after the attacks, according to an energy ministry official .
"The tactics of the strike this time were particularly vile," Zelenskyy said in his post on social media, noting that there had been "several groups of missiles with pauses of 20-30 minutes to complicate extinguishing the fires, clearing the rubble and recovery."
"A clear response from the world to all this is also needed," he said. "It is important that there are not only statements from partners about supporting Ukraine and Ukrainians, but also the implementation of specific agreements on air defense … We very much hope that the Pentagon will release the supply that we expect."
Charlie  D'Agata contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Anthropic shares fall a day after blockbuster IPO
articles.title_zh: Anthropic shares fall a day after blockbuster IPO
articles.content_orig:
Watch: How did Anthropic's stock market debut unfold?
Anthropic's shares have dropped back towards their initial price after a soaring first day on the stock market, as a wider tech sell-off deepens.
The fall in tech stocks continued to weigh on markets through Friday, with the S&P 500 down about 2.8% and the Dow Jones Industrial Average down more than 1% by mid-afternoon.
Both US indexes touched correction territory, a point where they are trading at 10% or more down from a recent high.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index also fell more than 4% by afternoon trading as shares in major tech companies continued to fall.
The speed at which AI investment has been growing -  with more than $1 trillion spent in the last year alone by a small handful of major tech companies - has led to ongoing concerns of a financial bubble. Questions are being raised over whether those investments will pay off, and when.
Despite a positive first day of trading, Anthropic's shares fell on Friday, dropping at one point by more than 12% to about $85, close to its initial public offering (IPO)  price of $83.
The artificial intelligence (AI) company's introduction to the Nasdaq stock exchange on Thursday was a crucial test for the industry and was largely seen as a success, with trading starting at $111.50.
The maker of the Claude chatbot raised a record $81bn in its initial public offering (IPO), but its share price moved significantly in the first day of trading.
The shares peaked at $115 on Thursday, before easing to end the day up 17% at $97.17.
Analysts said volatility was to be expected in the first days or even weeks of Anthropic's trading, as the company was the first frontier AI firm to go public so had no direct peers.
Some have also noted the similarities with Elon Musk's SpaceX, which at the time of its debut in June was the largest IPO on record. Shares in the rocket and AI company experienced large swings in its first few weeks of trading.
Most tech companies see their shares fall after hitting the stock market, often after reporting quarterly results for the first time.
But many, including Meta, Amazon and Google, have gone on to become the largest and most profitable corporations in the world.
Ed Moya, a strategist at market intelligence firm AlphaSense, said Anthropic's blockbuster IPO did not appear to have restored confidence in the broader AI market.
While AI demand was still very strong, Moya told the BBC that investors were trying to answer the question of how much were they willing to pay for that growth.
"As we've gone through the past past few weeks, it seems that there's been more risks that have surfaced," he said.
"Right now you're starting to see Wall Street is trying to shift from rewarding growth at any price, to demanding stronger cash flow and a clearer path to profitability."
Shares in some of the largest US tech companies also fell on Friday as the market sell off continued.
Nvidia shares had plunged by more than 11% by the afternoon, while Musk's firms SpaceX and Tesla had both fallen by more than 6%.
Meta was down more than 5% and Amazon was down more than 3.5%, while Apple and Alphabet experienced smaller falls.
Europe's main stock markets - which contain fewer tech stocks - also took a hit.
Germany's Dax index closed down 2.6%, France's CAC 40 was down 1.9% and the UK's FTSE 100 ended trading 1% lower.
Earlier on Friday, tech-heavy Asian markets saw steep falls.
South Korea's Kospi and Japan's Nikkei 225 indexes closed down about 5%, with shares in memory chip makers Sk Hynix, Kioxia and Tokyo Electron, and other tech firms such as Samsung Electronics, seeing losses.
Taiwan's stock market dropped about 6% on Friday, taking the weekly fall to more than 17% and what was reported to be its biggest weekly fall since 1990.

articles.title_orig: Trump on gas prices, China summit, war in Iran, and more | Full remarks
articles.title_zh: Trump on gas prices, China summit, war in Iran, and more | Full remarks
articles.content_orig:
Trump, Xi and Putin don't have much to say after their historic meeting.
President Donald Trump is headed back to Washington after a historic trilateral meeting with presidents Xi Jinping of China and Vladimir Putin of Russia -- the first-ever sitdown between the three global superpowers -- with no tangible diplomatic breakthroughs in hand.
Following their meeting, the three leaders released what was described as a symbolic four-point "peace declaration," focusing on reform at the United Nations, oil supply, nuclear risk reduction and opposition to what it called the International Criminal Court's "jurisdiction abuse."
The symbolic peace declaration made no mention of Russia's war with Ukraine, which is in its fifth year, or the war with Iran. Both Russia and China have faced accusations by U.S. and European officials of providing satellite imagery and broader intelligence support to Iran, accusations both countries have denied.
Trump left Shenzhen without taking questions from reporters after the meeting but announced in a post on his social media platform while traveling back to Washington that he would hold a news conference at the White House on Friday.
Here are takeaways from Trump's trip:
The three leaders affirmed their commitment that nuclear war should never be fought but announced no commitments to reduce their respective nuclear arsenals.
Trump had insisted nuclear arms control be a central topic of the summit.
"As the world's three largest nuclear powers by far, the United States, Russia, and China are uniquely positioned to discuss how to reduce the number of nuclear weapons on Earth, and also to lessen the risk that those weapons will ever be used," Trump said in brief remarks ahead of the meeting. "The power is unbelievable, unthinkable."
"It's not an ​easy thing to do -- give them up," Trump said.
Trump also used the issue of nuclear proliferation to defend the U.S. war with Iran, repeating his assertion that Iran cannot obtain a nuclear weapon.
"It's also vital that we cooperate to combat the threat of nuclear proliferation in other countries around the world. That's what we're doing in Iran. We're not going to let Iran have a nuclear weapon," he said.
In a joint statement released following the meeting, the three leaders said they had an "in-depth exchange of views on the current international situation" and "committed to maintaining strategic stability and international security."
Trump, Xi, and Putin said the three countries will conduct a dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing the proliferation of nuclear weapons.
The "peace declaration" released after the meeting made no mention of Russia's war in Ukraine or the U.S.-led war in Iran.
"We are going to be discussing the war between Russia and Ukraine, and we already have. President Putin and I have had a long discussion today for quite a while. That's what pretty much what the discussion was about, and I think things are happening," Trump said.
For his part, Putin briefly commented on his escalating war in Ukraine during opening remarks.
"Our countries have numerous shared interests in the settlement of regional conflicts, including obviously the conflict in Ukraine. We discussed this yesterday with the Chairman of the People's Republic of China and today at the initiative of the U.S. president, we devoted significant attention to this during our bilateral meeting," the Russian president said, speaking through a translator.
The leaders also declared they plan to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products "for the benefit of all nations" while also reaffirming the importance of the stable flow of energy.
The oil market has been roiled in the nine months of the U.S.'s war with Iran, with the critical waterway through which a fifth of the world's oil supplies has transited under constant threat. Ukrainian attacks on Russian energy facilities have further exacerbated global energy flows.
There were no signs upon conclusion of their meeting that Trump secured any agreements from Xi or Putin to help solve the Iran conflict.
Trump also highlighted that the three would discuss the International Criminal Court, the international body that works to uphold international law and prosecute war crimes. The Trump administration has targeted the ICC and its judges with sanctions and has sharply criticized the body.
"In another area of potential cooperation between us, I'll be suggesting ways to protect our nation's sovereignty from rogue globalist organizations such as the International Criminal Court, which has gotten out of control, which I believe we all agree has really strayed far from beyond its jurisdiction," Trump said in his opening remarks.
As part of the peace declaration, the three heads of state "recognized that the principle of state consent and respect for immunities of State officials are of paramount importance, and concurred that the International Criminal Court and other similar bodies must not abuse their jurisdiction."
ABC News has reached out to the ICC for comment.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia stock extends $2.5 trillion rout as SEC probe reportedly investigates its accounting
articles.title_zh: Nvidia stock extends $2.5 trillion rout as SEC probe reportedly investigates its accounting
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Nvidia's worst week on record keeps getting worse. Now the government is asking questions about its books.
Nvidia ( NVDA ) stock is down about 10% Friday, on track for its worst day since the DeepSeek rout in January 2025 and its seventh straight loss. The drop comes as Reuters reported that the Securities and Exchange Commission's probe of the chipmaker is examining potential accounting issues.
The Wall Street Journal reported Tuesday that the probe includes an examination of whether Nvidia's disclosures misled investors. Nvidia didn't respond to Bloomberg's request for comment on that report, and the SEC declined to comment.
The selling is setting records. Nvidia is shedding about $400 billion in market value Friday and is on track to lose more than $750 billion this week. That would top the $573 billion it lost last week, the biggest one-week drop for any company on record, according to Dow Jones Market Data.
Since its Oct. 6 record, Nvidia has lost more than $2.5 trillion in market value, which The Kobeissi Letter calls the biggest 45-day loss for any stock in history. The world's most valuable company six weeks ago now ranks fourth in the US, behind Apple ( AAPL ), Microsoft ( MSFT ) and Alphabet ( GOOGL ).
Nvidia's latest quarterly report raised a few questions. The company said its 10-Q, the detailed quarterly filing, would come "in the coming weeks" instead of the same evening as usual, and the release mentioned an ongoing investigation by an independent board committee.
Nvidia booked about $104 billion of revenue through its Singapore unit in 2025, roughly half its sales, the Financial Times reported. The Journal said the disclosure questions include Singapore-based Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer US officials suspect of rerouting its chips to China.
Nvidia's customers are also taking longer to pay, with bills outstanding at 64 days of sales, the most since 2022. It's not clear which of these, if any, the SEC is focused on.
Washington wants answers fast. "I think we need answers in the next 10 days from the board and from the outside counsel," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Tuesday, after Jensen Huang's exit as CEO.
The sell-off is spreading across chip stocks and the broader market .
Baird's Ted Mortonson, a technology desk sector strategist, saw more scrutiny coming even before Friday's report.
"Every single deal that Nvidia has done on circular finance is going to be put under the microscope," he said on Yahoo Finance's live show Thursday.

articles.title_orig: Rights groups urge sanctions after top UN court finds Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya
articles.title_zh: Rights groups urge sanctions after top UN court finds Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya
articles.content_orig:
Myanmar committed genocide against the country’s long-persecuted Rohingya minority, the United Nations’ top court found Thursday, an unprecedented ruling that survivors of the atrocities have waited almost a decade to hear.
The historic judgement marks the first time the International Court of Justice (ICJ), also known as the World Court, has held a state accountable for genocide in its 80-year history — and the ruling will have repercussions far beyond Myanmar.
The court’s decision — by nine votes to six — also comes at a time when the broader idea of international justice has come under fire from the Trump administration.
For the Rohingya, the ICJ’s judgment is a “turning point.”
“It is the difference between being told our history was a tragedy, and being told our history was a crime that must be answered for,” said Murshid Alam, who was just 12 years old when he was driven from his home in Myanmar’s Rakhine state.
The ICJ’s rulings are final and binding, but the court — which hears disputes between states — doesn’t have the power to enforce its decisions. Its orders, however, are sent to the UN Security Council, which could decide to implement the court’s ruling through a resolution.
Between 2016 and 2017, the military in Buddhist-majority Myanmar targeted villages and towns home to Rohingya communities, looting, burning and slaughtering their inhabitants, and expelling hundreds of thousands from the country.
CNN reporting at the time documented harrowing stories from Rohingya who saw their family members raped or killed by soldiers, and in some case their Buddhist neighbors joining in the massacres . Photos showed streams of terrified people fleeing burning villages on foot or piling into overcrowded boats as they sought to reach neighboring Bangladesh and safety.
This case against Myanmar was brought in 2019 by The Gambia, a country thousands of miles from where the killings took place, in a world-first. The United States and Canada previously declared the atrocities as genocide.
Years after more than 700,000 Rohingya fled a brutal military crackdown in Myanmar, the world’s highest court has ruled the country responsible for genocide. The verdict marks a historic moment for survivors. But CNN’s Hanako Montgomery reports many remain stranded in Bangladesh with little hope of returning home.
After seven years of weighing evidence and hearing witness testimony, the ICJ found that the scale and nature of Myanmar’s atrocities were “characteristic of an intent to destroy a substantial part of the group,” presiding judge Iwasawa Yuji said during a nearly three-hour reading.
“The court is of the view that the only reasonable inference that can explain Myanmar’s actions is an intention to destroy” the Rohingya population in northern Rakhine state.
In its judgment, the court established the military “engaged in indiscriminate killings” and gave particular weight to the “widespread acts of sexual violence, and extreme acts of violence against children” as well as security forces’ attacks on “Rohingya as they sought to flee in large numbers to Bangladesh.”
Myanmar had denied its “clearance operations” were intended to destroy the Rohingya population, and said the military was conducting legitimate counterterrorism operations against a Rohingya insurgent group. The court rejected that defense, saying the Myanmar military did not distinguish between militants and civilians.
A spokesperson for Myanmar’s military-backed government dismissed the ICJ’s ruling on Friday, saying it was “unfair” and “not a decision made unanimously.”
“Not all 15 judges agreed with the decision,” the spokesperson said.
Murshid Alam was a child when he was forced out of his home in Myanmar’s Rakhine state by a hail of gunfire. In the chaos of the escape, he was shot in his ear — a “terrifying experience,” he told CNN. The wound has healed, but the “secondary trauma of losing my home and seeing my community destroyed” has not.
Alam was one of more than 740,000 Rohingya people who fled to Bangladesh to escape the massacres. The sprawling refugee camps that he came of age in have since become the world’s largest, hosting more than 1.2 million people.
“Our generation has grown up in displacement. We have known nothing but statelessness,” said Alam, 22, who now works to educate and advocate for young people in the Cox’s Bazar camps as founder of the Rohingya Youth Union.
The genocide ruling, he said, “tells us that the world sees our suffering and refuses to let it be erased.”
UN human rights chief Volker Türk told CNN the judgment was “historic” and particularly striking for the way it examined “the decades of discrimination and marginalization of the Rohingya.”
Following The Gambia’s successful application to bring the case, the ICJ allowed South Africa to bring a case against Israel over its war with Hamas in Gaza that has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians. Israel denies the genocide charge.
That has led to concerns among some the court could come into collision with the Trump administration – already on a campaign to “ dismantle ” another institution, the International Criminal Court. Last month, its UN ambassador Mike Waltz accused the ICJ of trying to lower the threshold for a genocide verdict in the Myanmar case that he claimed could potentially be “weaponized” against American soldiers.
A US State Department spokesperson told CNN in a statement Thursday they “are studying the decision to fully assess its implications.”
“The proper interpretation of the Genocide Convention is of paramount importance, as is preventing politicization of the ICJ,” the spokesperson added.
The ICJ ordered Myanmar to make reparations to the Rohingya, including to “allow and facilitate the safe, voluntary, and dignified return to their place of residence and reunification of families,” and return all property lost or damaged. It also ordered Myanmar to ensure their future protection from discrimination and persecution.
It is unlikely Myanmar will adhere. The head of the Myanmar military during the massacres, Min Aung Hlaing is now the country’s leader after he overthrew the elected government – and has dismissed the Rohingya identity as “imaginary.” His military-backed government has shown little interest in allowing Rohingya to return.
What they would return to is another question. In the Rohingya homeland of Rakhine state, the military-backed government is not in control. An ethnic armed group called the Arakan Army controls the vast majority of the state, including areas that border Bangladesh, and has been accused of widespread abuses against civilians in its areas.
The world’s deadliest sea route keeps getting busier
Meanwhile, the military has ramped up airstrikes across the state as part of its grinding civil war, dropping bombs on civilian markets and hospitals, in response to territorial losses.
Rohingya now living in the camps cannot work and face dire conditions, including trafficking, exploitation, meagre food rations, and a lack of basic education.
Alam, in the Bangladesh refugee camp, hoped the ruling could pave the way for a return to the home he fled as a young boy.
“The Rohingya do not want to live in refugee camps forever. We want to return to our homeland in Rakhine state with our rights, our citizenship, and our dignity fully restored,” he said.

articles.title_orig: 10 years on, Britain reopens the Brexit fight — this time embracing the E.U.
articles.title_zh: 10 years on, Britain reopens the Brexit fight — this time embracing the E.U.
articles.content_orig:
President of European Council says EU ‘remains open to have the closest possible relationship’ with the UK
The British prime minister Andy Burnham said his deal with the European Union will add up to £17bn a year to the British economy as he paved the way for even closer ties to Brussels. Burnham said it was a “good day for Britain and a good day for Europe”, as he met EU chiefs in Brussels to announce a package covering food and agriculture exports, emissions trading, and a youth experience scheme which could open the doors for 100,000 young Europeans to temporarily work in the UK, with Britons able to do the same on the continent.
Burnham ‌said Friday’s deal was “probably the limit” of what could be done before the next national election due by mid-2029 , but he envisaged an informal conversation in about a year ‌with the EU about what could be achieved next.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said she welcomed Burnham’s willingness to have a broad debate about future relations with the EU. “We are open for brainstorming, and we welcome this brainstorming, so count on us,” she said.
At the summit, postponed from July after the resignation of Burnham’s predecessor Keir Starmer, ‌the two sides addressed some of the Brexit losses with a package of agreements. The most significant allows cross-border trade in animals, plants and related products, such as sausages or seeds, without the certificates and controls currently required. Britain has estimated this could add up to £5.1bn per year to its economy.
A further agreement will link the emissions trading systems of Britain and the EU, which would exempt British and EU goods, such as steel, from each other’s border carbon levies. Each side is also set to allow 100,000 young people a year in to work or study for three years.
However, one potential dampener emerged as the 27-nation bloc and London jostled over linking ultimate implementation of the new deals to Britain agreeing to cut university fees for EU students. Britain ⁠prefers to offer only “significantly reduced” fees, and the aim is to resolve the issue within six months.
Retailers and manufacturers have welcomed Andy Burnham’s new trade deal with the European Union as a “big win” but warned they need “clear and early” guidance from government to aid the transition, Press Association reported. The chief executive of the British Retail Consortium (BRC) called the SPS deal a “big win” for UK retailers but warned that businesses need “at least 18 months” to transition to the new arrangements.
Nigel Farage, the veteran anti-EU campaigner and leader of the Reform UK party, said the deal “was about the first steps, incrementally, to taking us back into membership of the European Union,” and again predicted an early election next year. Farage told reporters he would campaign to preserve Brexit. “I am ready for this fight,” he said.
Meanwhile, Denmark’s foreign minister on Friday said Moscow’s defence attache in Copenhagen would be expelled after Russia was suspected of being behind an attempted assassination of a Ukrainian rapper. “We have just summoned the Russian ambassador to the ministry of foreign affairs and notified him of the government’s decision to expel the Russian defence attache from Denmark” within seven days, Lars Lokke Rasmussen told a news conference.
Students and young workers have taken to the streets in more than 20 European countries in coordinated protests over the surging cost of living and housing, deteriorating learning conditions and rising military spending. Activists from more than 50 groups in countries including Belgium, France, Germany, Greece, Italy, Portugal , Spain and the UK held rallies on Friday, lighting flares, burning cardboard models of tanks and waving placards, many reading “fight for our future”.
You can read more in our full story:

“We are saying this very clearly: we have exposed you”, he said.
He also added Denmark was mulling suspending Schengen visas to Russians.
The UK prime minister called the newly agreed post-Brexit reset deal a “win-win” for the UK and the EU, although the level of tuition fees EU students will pay to study at UK universities remains unresolved.
The prime minister met Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission president, and António Costa, the European Council president, at the EU-UK summit in Brussels.
Reform UK leader Nigel Farage claimed that Andy Burnham’s reset agreements with the EU “was in direct contradiction of the Labour manifesto upon which they were elected in 2024”.
He also said Burnham’s actions “went completely against the pledge that he made to the voters of Makerfield just a few months ago”.
The Reform leader later added: “Burnham’s whole rationale is 73% of the people want to be closer to Europe .
“Well, if you ask me do I want better relations with our European neighbours? Do I think we could have a better trade deal than we’ve got at the moment? I am part of that 73%.
“But what he completely misunderstands is that is not an open ticket to rejoin a significant chunk of the single market today.”
Students and young workers have taken to the streets in more than 20 European countries in coordinated protests over the surging cost of living and housing, deteriorating learning conditions and rising military spending.
Activists from more than 50 groups in countries including Belgium, France, Germany, Greece, Italy, Portugal , Spain and the UK held rallies on Friday, lighting flares, burning cardboard models of tanks and waving placards, many reading “fight for our future”.
Calling it Europe’s biggest coordinated youth protest of recent years, the Youth Strike coalition said demonstrations were planned in about 400 cities under the slogan “fight for our future, not their wars”.
It made five broad demands, including an end to militarisation and conscription; structural investment in education and welfare; solidarity with Palestine; climate and social justice, and a “radical transformation of the system we live in”.
An Italian organiser, Alessandro di Miceli, said the Europe-wide protests were “to claim our right to a better and dignified future”. Specific demands differed from country to country, he said, but were all “deeply connected between each other”.
A Portuguese organiser, Leonor Chicó, said: “As young people, we know that we must organise and fight for our future, because no one else will do it for us.” Governments “show us every day that the needs of our generation are not their priority”, she said.
Shabbir Lakha from the UK-based Stop The War coalition said the mobilisation was “a crucial step towards building a lasting international movement capable of bringing together young people, students and workers around common demands”.
After weeks of demonstrations across several countries sparked by long-running French school protests , governments are struggling to respond to growing calls for affordable housing, functioning public services and greater social equality.

He said: “There is a clear democratic mandate for what has been done today. It’s in the Labour manifesto… There will be nothing beyond the significance of this in this parliament.”

articles.content_orig:
Mr. Trump called Stephen Miller, his new chief of staff and longtime aide, up to the lectern. Miller claimed the president over the last two years has achieved "more than any president has achieved by far in American history."
"No president has done what he has done over the last two years," Miller said. "What you're going to see over the next two years — as astonishing as that has been — under his leadership, the next two years are going to be the greatest two years in American history."
After Miller left the podium, Mr. Trump asked, "Do you want to run for president?"
He later praised Miller as "a talent" and said he has "a big heart."
"A lot of people think he doesn't," Mr. Trump said.
The president said he has not lost confidence in Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, despite a rift between Lutnick and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and others in the administration about how to handle chips going to China. Republicans on Capitol Hill have been calling for Lutnick to testify and answer their questions.
"I have not lost confidence," the president said, calling Lutnick a "different" kind of guy, perhaps not like Bessent, whom the president said is out of "central casting." The president called Lutnick a "natural" businessman.
"It's different folks, right?" Mr. Trump said.
The president said he received a phone call from Texas Democratic Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa, claiming she wants to have a "strong border."
"I received a phone call from the new governor, governor-elect of Texas," Mr. Trump said. "She was really nice. It was a very productive call. And she wants to have a strong border. And I think we'll be able to work something out."
Hinojosa defeated Republican Gov. Greg Abbott by about seven points.
Asked about reports that Iran is developing plans to detonate a dirty bomb in Washington, D.C., the president said he's heard that "rumor" but his administration won't let it happen.
"There is a rumor that they're building a dirty bomb," the president said, insisting the U.S. knows what the Iranians are doing.
"We know a lot about what's happening in Iran. We know everything they say. We know who they are, where they are. We'll find out about it. We will not allow that," he said.
Mr. Trump said he plans to veto Democratic-led legislation over the next two years unless Democrats work with him on his priorities.
"They're going to send things my way, and I'm going to veto them. And then they're going to send more things, and I'm going to veto them," he said.
Mr. Trump said he would eventually give Democrats an ultimatum: "I'm going to say, I'm going to veto unless you want to do this and this and this."
"If they want to get things done, I want to get things done too," he said, adding that he's open to working with Democrats on healthcare and other legislation.
The president would not say whether he has spoken yet with House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, who is expected to become House speaker early next year. But he called the New York Democrat "a smart guy."
"He's a streetwise guy," he said.
Mr. Trump said corporate system outages across the country are all separate issues, company by company.
"They're all separate events," he said.
The president said thousands of companies are upgrading their systems right now. "And when they upgrade, bad things happen," he said.
"I have a very good understanding of what we're talking about," the president said of AI and company systems. The president insisted the companies will fix it all soon.
The director of national intelligence suggested this week that the outages resulted from software patches and upgrades. The FAA groundstop, however, likely resulted from a hardware issue.
The president called the air traffic control system "ancient."
Mr. Trump said he wants Nvidia's former CEO Jensen Huang leading the company again, calling him "one of the truly most brilliant minds in the world."
"I would love to see him back," he said, adding that Huang should "be given a second chance."
"I'd like to see Jensen make a big apology and go back because he created something with Blackwell," he said, referring to the company's most advanced AI chip.
"You can't copy the chip because it's so advanced and so complex that it can't be copied. And Jensen did that, and I think there are very few people in that company that can do that."
Mr. Trump said Huang's work has put the U.S. 10 years ahead of other countries when it comes to AI chips.
"I think the company, if they were smart, they [would] take that brilliant man, accept an apology and let him go back to work," Mr. Trump said.
The president said having a good relationship with Putin and Russia gives the U.S. additional strength, appearing to express sympathy for Putin over the war that the Russian president began and continues to wage in Ukraine.
Mr. Trump said Putin was "very nice" about what he described as the fake Russia "hoax," referring to allegations that his 2016 presidential campaign colluded with Moscow.
"I consider him to be somebody that I have a very good relationship," the president said. "And it's actually very good. He's got lots of nuclear — he's second to us in nuclear weapons, it's very good. I think it, I think it gives us a lot of additional strength. And he's having a hard time right now because he's in a war that should have lasted one day and it's lasted for five years."
After Putin left the meetings in China, Russia launched more attacks on Ukraine, despite Mr. Trump saying Russia wants to end the war.
"You're very lucky to have somebody that has a relationship with the heads of the most powerful countries," he said.
Mr. Trump denied that he was upset with Vance over a statement he put out after the election that blamed GOP losses on the conflict.
As the question was being asked, Rubio caught Vance's eye and shook his head.
"I didn't say I was unhappy with it. I thought the statement was fine," Mr. Trump said. "It was a very accurate statement."
But he said he would "absolutely" do it again, adding that the war drove up fuel prices "far less than I thought."
In a post on X the day after Election Day, Vance said many Trump voters backed Democrats this election because of the Iran war, cost of living and inflation and the U.S. relationship with Israel.
"The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night," Vance wrote. "If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that's at least honest. But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there."
Speaking after the president, Vance also praised the bipartisan bill to overhaul permitting as "amazing," saying it will "allow the United States to build like we've never built before."
"That means more homes, more factories, more power plants," Vance said, connecting the Senate-passed legislation to Mr. Trump's trip abroad. "But that doesn't matter unless you create more incentives in the global economy for people to invest in the United States of America."
"So what we saw last week was two really big wins for the American people: the trade deals, but also the major piece of legislation," Vance said. "It's going to pay dividends for the American people."
Mr. Trump said the relationship between him, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin is "fantastic."
The president said he was unaware it was the first trilateral meeting of the U.S., China and Russian heads of state until the press reported it.
"First ever trilateral," he said. "I never knew that. You reported it. And I said, 'if they report it, it must make sense.'"
"It was great, great electricity," he added. "Unbelievable. And the relationship is fantastic between the three of us."
They discussed the "responsibility" that comes with being the world's three largest nuclear powers, he said.

Friday, November 20 @ 1:40 PM ET: A Microsoft spokesperson shared an official statement discussing the upcoming changes. That statement has been added to this piece in its own section.
Users of one of Microsoft’s best free apps will have to add “find a new to do list app” to their list of tasks. But they shouldn’t do so on Microsoft To Do, since all versions of the app are now destined for retirement.
Microsoft To Do will be retired on June 30, 2027 . While the apps will shut down on that date, the underlying To Do service, APIs, and related synchronization support will retire later on separate timelines. Microsoft detailed its plans in a support document . The writing was on the wall that Microsoft To Do was not a priority at Microsoft. The software felt like abandonware, rarely receiving updates or new features. Not that a task tracking app should require many updates, but the Microsoft To Do webpage still uses an icon from Windows 10.
Just a few months ago our Ben Wilson pleaded with Microsoft to keep Microsoft To Do around . His worry that the app would be moved to the Microsoft Graveyard became a reality quickly. Microsoft has focused on Planner recently, and that will be the path forward for business and education users who want to sync tasks across devices and platforms. Planner is not available for personal users.
Even those who switch to Planner will have extra work to do, since tasks will not migrate from Microsoft To Do to Planner.
Microsoft To Do was made by the Wunderlist team after Microsoft acquired that popular application. Wunderlist had a passionate user base and Microsoft To Do earned praise for its swift performance and cross-device syncing. Microsoft eventually shut down Wunderlist and pushed users to Microsoft To Do when the latter was ready for mainstream use.
Microsoft To Do has served as a natural extension to the Microsoft 365 ecosystem for years. Its integration with Outlook felt like magic when it was new. With Microsoft To Do set for retirement, users will have to look for alternatives. I’d recommend Todoist or TickTick as replacements for Microsoft To Do. Google Keep and Apple Reminders are also strong candidates depending on the platforms you use. It’s frustrating to see Microsoft To Do placed on a path to retirement. It’s a useful app that performs well on the web, Windows 11, iOS, and Android. I’d argue it was the pinnacle of Microsoft’s cross-platform app strategy.
After publication, Microsoft shared the following statement regarding Microsoft To Do's retirement. The company reiterated that Planner is the future for work and school users, while personal users will be able to export their data.
“We're bringing task management experiences together across Microsoft 365 to make it easier for customers to manage individual tasks and team plans. As part of this transition, Microsoft To Do apps will retire on June 30, 2027 , with work and school experiences coming together in Microsoft Planner . Existing integrations across Microsoft 365, including Outlook and Teams, will also be updated to work with Planner. We recognize this change will affect customers differently, particularly those using personal Microsoft accounts , and we're committed to helping them prepare. Customers will be able to export their To Do data before retirement , and we'll share additional guidance to support the transition." – Howard Crow, Director of Product, Agents and AI , Microsoft (emphasis added).
In short, personal users are not being given a replacement. They are being given an export button.

articles.title_orig: Ukraine strikes Kerch Bridge as Putin ally declares ‘no one needs Europe’
articles.title_zh: Ukraine strikes Kerch Bridge as Putin ally declares ‘no one needs Europe’
articles.content_orig:
Topic: Unrest, Conflict and War
When drones and missiles collapsed a bridge connecting Russia to the Crimean Peninsula, Ukraine's military declared: "The symbol of the occupation has cracked."
Hours later, at a summit held a continent away, an angry-looking Vladimir Putin immediately vowed to end any prospect of peace with Ukraine.
"There will be no agreements. We will respond," he said on the sidelines of the APEC summit in the Chinese city of Shenzhen .
But one expert says the bridge's destruction is a "huge blow to Putin's credibility as Russian leader" in a war his country appears to be losing.
The Crimean Bridge, which was constructed in 2016 after Russian forces occupied the Ukrainian peninsula in defiance of international law. ( Reuters: Alexey Pavlishak )
Ukraine's Crimean Peninsula extends south from the country's mainland into the Black Sea.
It has been occupied by Russian forces in defiance of international law since 2014.
Access is via two main roads to the north and the Crimean Bridge, from Crimea's east coast to the Russian mainland further east.
The northern roads lead into Russian-occupied Ukrainian territory that frequently comes under attack from the Ukrainian military.
The 19-kilometre Crimean Bridge, with separate road and rail links running over the Kerch Strait to connect the peninsula to Russia's Krasnodar region, provides the only other road and rail traffic.
It is also a vital road and rail artery connecting the Black Sea with the Azov Sea to the bridge's north.
Russia has relied on the bridge to maintain access to Crimea throughout the current war.
Instructions: Use left and right arrow keys to control image transition
On Tuesday, local time, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced his military had performed what he described as a wartime masterstroke strike weeks in the making.
He said Ukrainian forces knocked out defence systems, radars, electronic warfare equipment and other designated targets before launching a final attack using long-range drones on the bridge's road section.
At the same time, Neptune missiles targeted the railway, before precision-guided Flamingo missiles were also fired at the bridge.
The bridge is Europe's longest and a source of pride among some Russians. ( Reuters: Supplied/Vantor )
Videos later shared by Mr Zelenskyy and the Ukrainian military appeared to show key moments from the attack, with one of the bridge's arches fallen while part of its deck was in the water.
Crimea's Russian-installed governor, Sergei Aksyonov, confirmed the attack halted traffic but said the rail track had been restored. He did not reveal the extent of damage to the bridge.
Malcolm Davis, a senior defence analyst with the Australian Strategic Policy Institute, said the bridge's collapse reinforces a message Ukraine has declared since 2014: "Crimea does not belong to Russia."
"By cutting off access … It signifies to the world that Putin does not control Crimea, that Crimea is part of Ukraine, and reinforces the fact that Russia is certainly not winning this war," he told the ABC.
"It is certainly a major setback to Putin … That's a huge blow to Putin's credibility as Russian leader."
The Crimean Bridge is Europe's longest, and a source of considerable pride for Russia.
Construction began in 2016, despite strong objections from Ukraine, and was completed in little over two years.
Putin drove across it at its formal opening on May 15, 2018, but for Ukrainians, the bridge remains the most visible and persistent reminder of the Kremlin's claim over the Crimean Peninsula.
Vladimir Putin formally opened the bridge in 2018. ( Reuters: Alexander Nemenov/Pool )
This week's strikes were also not the first launched by Ukraine in opposition to the Russian occupation.
In October 2022, Moscow said a truck bomb had been used to target the bridge, temporarily halting road and rail traffic.
Two months later, Putin walked over the repaired road.
Vladimir Putin walked on the bridge's newly repaired roadway after it came under attack by Ukrainian forces in 2022. ( Reuters: Supplied/Sputnik/Mikhail Metzel )
The following year, it came under fire again in attacks by two maritime drones that killed two people, according to Russia's Investigative Committee.
Dr Davis said the latest strikes could be the most significant yet.
"What happens is that the Russian forces on Crimea ultimately start losing effectiveness in the coming weeks," he said.
"[It] makes it easier for the Ukrainians, if they wanted to, to try and recapture Crimea in the future."
In China, Mr Putin claimed the Crimean Bridge had been used exclusively for civilian purposes, rather than to ship military equipment and petrol to Russia's frontline troops.
In the wake of the attack, Russian-installed authorities in Crimea said a ferry service to the Russian mainland would start on Friday, local time, to maintain deliveries of food, medicine and fuel for the peninsula's nearly 2.5 million inhabitants.
Marat Khusnullin, a Russian government vice-premier, told state TV he believed it would take about a week to establish how long repairs would take.
But Inger Kroon, a structural engineering specialist, told Reuters the task of replacing the roughly 227-metre road span and its arch could take more than a year.
The attack came as both Russia and Ukraine were awaiting confirmation of a date for another round of US-mediated peace talks, aimed at ending the war between the two nations.
And while US President Donald Trump said he planned to discuss the war during his highly anticipated meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Mr Putin in China, no concrete decision on peace came from the talks.
Dr Davis said he did not believe Russia was ever seriously committed to peace negotiations, and expected Mr Putin to "retaliate with massive attacks" against Ukraine.
"This is a bad defeat for the Russians," he said.
"But the war will continue. There's no sign of this coming to an end any time soon."

articles.title_orig: Celebrate the year with every Pokémon from Community Days in 2026!
articles.title_zh: Celebrate the year with every Pokémon from Community Days in 2026!
articles.content_orig:
Hello Trainers! Welcome! Hope everyone had a great weekend with the GO Wild Area Global . Well the revelry continues with the currently running Dynamax Trails Event and the upcoming Pawniard Community Day. Trainers who evolve Bisharp between 2:00 p.m. to 9:00 p.m. local time that day will get a Kingambit that knows Kowtow Cleave , an exclusive Dark type Charged Attack. Trainers may be wondering about how Kowtow Cleave performs in PvE, where Kingambit fits in the raid meta and whether it is worth evolving a Bisharp during the event. Well, let’s find out!
Kingambit is the final evolution of the Pawniard line and is a Dark and Steel type Pokémon. It has fairly balanced stats. Unlike many Dark attackers that hit hard but faint quickly, Kingambit can stay in a raid for a longer time. Its dual typing also gives it several useful resistances which includes triple resistance to Psychic and double resistance to Poison . It is however, double weak to Fighting attacks.
With Snarl and Foul Play as its moveset, Kingambit was already a respectable Dark attacker. With strong bulk and Snarl generating energy quickly, Kingambit could use Charged Attacks often and deal respectable damage to opposing raid bosses. But with Kowtow Cleave, Kingambit goes from respectable and into the must-have category. Using our DPS Comparer Tool , let us compare Kingambit’s performance against Top Dark Attackers :
The best raid moveset for Kingambit is now Snarl paired with Kowtow Cleave . As evident above, this combination gives Kingambit the strongest overall Dark type performance, making it the currently the best non-shadow non-Mega Dark raid attacker. Kingambit goes past long time Dark staples like Tyranitar, Hydreigon and even Darkrai. Even if we include Ghost attackers in Kingambit’s overall performance, it still retains its position among non-mega attackers, which is a solid achievement.
As a Steel attacker, Metal Claw and Iron Head is Kingambit’s preferred moveset. However, Kingambit’s performance as a Steel attacker is less impressive than its Dark type performance. If your main goal is top meta performance, Dark is the realm where Kingambit should be.
Absolutely! Trainers, do not miss out on this opportunity and definitely evolve your Bisharp for a Kingambit that knows Kowtow Cleave. Kingambit may not be the very best Dark attacker but it still holds its own as a dependable option, especially for newer Trainers, or for those who or on a budget and may not have a deep roster of mega and shadow Dark type attackers. Kingambit is most useful against Psychic raid bosses. Not only does it deal super-effective damage, but it also triple resists Psychic attacks. This lets Kingambit stay in the fight for longer duration and make a rather meaningful contribution.
That is it Trainers! We are at the end. Kowtow Cleave gives Kingambit an exclusive Dark type attack and makes the Pawniard Community Day worth participating in. It improves Kingambit’s raid performance and gives the Pokémon a more distinct identity in PvE. If you are looking to add some depth to your Dark raid team, Kingambit is a good investment. It is relatively easy to obtain during Community Day and can become a useful member of your team.
When Kingambit draws its blade, raid bosses begin to fade!
Let us know Trainers! How did your Wild Area weekend went? Is Pawniard→Kingambit your favorite cross generational evolution line? If not, then which one is?
And as always, stay safe! Happy Community Day! May everyone get a SHUNDO!
