articles.title_orig: Anthropic staffer claims solution to mathematics’ Riemann hypothesis
articles.title_zh: Anthropic staffer claims solution to mathematics’ Riemann hypothesis
articles.content_orig:
Anthropic mathematician claims to prove Riemann hypothesis, most famous problem in all of math
An AI-generated solution of the 167-year-old problem, long considered far out of reach to human mathematicians, would cap off the technology’s year-long conquest of math in spectacular fashion
By Joseph Howlett edited by Claire Cameron
vectorfusionart via Shutterstock
Levent Alpöge, a mathematician and employee at artificial intelligence company Anthropic, claimed on Friday to have proven the most famous problem in all of mathematics using an LLM.
“I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis,” Alpöge wrote in a statement posted on his website.
The Riemann hypothesis was first proposed in 1859 by the mathematician Bernhard Riemann. It claims that the locations of the prime numbers along the number line, which appear random at first blush, are actually determined by an intricate, meaningful order.
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing . By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
The conjecture has since become the North Star for the entire field of number theory, and is the most famous open problem in math. It’s one of the few open problems on which the Clay Mathematics Institute has placed a million-dollar bounty. Progress toward solving the Riemann hypothesis was so rare that most top experts spent little of their time actually working on it, because there was no obvious path to proving Riemann’s guess. The first chink in the problem’s armor appeared in October, when one of the proofs in OpenAI’s massive dump of math results made significant progress on making sense of the primes.
Now the long struggle appears over. Alpöge posted his Claude proof coded in the programming language Lean, which verifies the mathematical correctness of each argument. Issues can arise in Lean, but it shouldn’t take long for experts to verify whether the hypothesis is properly coded, and if the proof is correct.
If that happens, it will cap off a year in which AI’s mathematical capabilities ascended from unreliable college student to a superhuman force, leaving no part of the discipline undisrupted. The announcement comes just a day after Anthropic's record-breaking debut on the stock market.
Alpöge says his proof confirms the “Generalized Riemann Hypothesis,” a gargantuan expansion on Riemann’s initial guess that undergirds the entire mathematical universe with untold hidden structure. There is no superlative strong enough for how this would transform mathematics, instantly unlocking a deluge of truths contingent upon the ambitious conjecture.
“If the proof is correct and understood, this completes a dictionary between different branches of math where the connections were only partial,” says Hector Pasten, a mathematician at the Pontifical Catholic University of Chile. “Something like a Rosetta Stone.”
The work could open whole new areas of research. "If true, even from a first high level scan of the summary of the proposed argument, it is very plausible to me that the new ideas in the proof will open up brand new avenues of thinking in number theory and have an immense impact beside the obviously extremely influential result in itself," says mathematician Carlo Pagano, a professor at Concordia University and a visiting researcher at Google DeepMind.
Alpöge’s statement is elegiac—recognizing the sense of grief many mathematicians are feeling—but also optimistic. “It is natural to feel that this is an end, in my case a loss of a principal guiding light,” he wrote, “but what I saw during the course of progress so amazed me that I believe it is one dawn across science of something far greater.”
The Anthropic mathematician has been the subject of headlines since he tweeted a Claude-generated solution to the famous Jacobian conjecture in July, kicking off math’s unprecedented summer. He was central to September’s Navier-Stokes controversy involving OpenAI, when NYU mathematician Tristan Buckmaster implied that the company had stolen his and Alpöge’s work.
The Riemann result, if correct, will echo far beyond mathematics. It doesn’t have any immediate real-world applications—it won’t upend global banking or make the internet run faster. But after a year of watching LLMs surpass one math benchmark after another, there is no more staggering achievement it could possibly reach. A machine may have just solved a problem that the smartest people on the planet all agreed they were nowhere close to figuring out. As MIT mathematician Andrew Sutherland once put it to me: “An AI that can prove the Riemann hypothesis is not one I’d want to meet. If that happens, mathematicians having jobs will be the least of our problems.”
“This is indeed an historic moment,” Sutherland told me today after he had independently compiled Alpöge’s result in Lean. “The world has changed… I know there will be a wide range of reactions in our community, but to me this is a human triumph, and a day for celebration.” It’s worth celebrating, Sutherland says, the human work behind the development of Lean and LLMs—and, for that matter, the millennia of mathematical achievements upon which today’s advance rests. But processing the earthshaking reality of what has occurred “is going to take some time.” “There is much work to be done to understand the mathematical details of the proof,” he says. “And I can’t wait to dig into them. But perhaps the single most important step in the proof was building a machine that can think.”
This is a breaking news story and will be updated.

articles.title_orig: When Nazis were held accountable for war crimes
articles.title_zh: When Nazis were held accountable for war crimes
articles.content_orig:
Holocaust historian Bill Tinglin, on Thursday during a panel discussion in Bethage on the Nuremberg trials, said a lesson learned from the tribunals is people must be held accountable, even if "they have uniforms or they’re doing things that they said they were led by their government to do." Credit: Debbie Egan-Chin
One by one, the accused Nazi war criminals who hadn't died by suicide or other means lined up in a Nuremberg, Germany, courtroom 81 years ago Friday to face what had previously seemed almost beyond belief: justice.
The start of the Nuremberg Trials on Nov. 20, 1945 , their legacy of successfully bringing the powerful to justice for committing atrocities in the name of hate, and ways to make sure something like the Holocaust is never repeated, were the topics of a panel discussion Thursday at the Museum of American Armor in Bethpage .
"We must hold people accountable [even if] they have uniforms or they’re doing things that they said they were led by their government to do," said Dr. Bill Tinglin, a Holocaust historian who sat on the panel. "That’s how the Nuremberg [defendants] were held accountable."
Several dozen people turned out for the event, which was organized by the Garden City-based law firm Rosenberg, Calica, Birney, Liebman & Ross. In addition to Tinglin, the panel included Mindy Perlmutter, the executive director of the Jewish Community Relations Council , Gloria Sesso, who chairs the Long Island Council for Social Studies, retired U.S. Army Col. Jason Halloren and Joshua Liebman, a partner with the host law firm.
Time has not erased the antisemitism that fueled the rise of Adolf Hitler and the Nazi defendants at Nuremberg, according to the panel speakers.
The Anti-Defamation League put the number of antisemitic incidents nationwide in 2024 and 2025 combined at roughly 16,000.
"My grandfather would be forced to say that things are starting to look frighteningly familiar, when compared to the streets of Vienna before the Holocaust," said museum spokesperson Gary Lewi in an email to Newsday after the discussion, citing "today’s events that are happening out there with swastikas on synagogues."
A recent example occurred in Lawrence. On Nov. 10, the Nassau County Police Department arrested and charged a Brooklyn man after he allegedly drew a swastika on a Jewish community center in the village.
Sesso, the social studies education expert, said a major outcome of the Nuremberg trials was the documentation of the crimes of the Holocaust, allowing its history to be taught accurately.
Halloren, the retired Army officer, who is the Museum of American Armor’s senior trustee, said the trials set an international legal foundation "for holding people accountable."
"All the things that led up to [atrocities like the Holocaust] — the creating a perception that a certain population ... is evil — to allow that to go on is criminal in nature," Halloren said.
Sam Kmack covers the Town of Islip for Newsday. He is a graduate of the University of Southern California and previously worked as a city watchdog reporter in the Phoenix metro area, as well as an investigative journalist at the Arizona Center for Investigative Reporting.

articles.title_orig: Google says it’s going to shut off Google Assistant on smart speakers next year
articles.title_zh: Google says it’s going to shut off Google Assistant on smart speakers next year
articles.content_orig:
Google is making some big changes to its smart home offerings, including killing the Nest app.﻿
Google is making some big changes to its smart home offerings, including killing the Nest app.﻿
Google is announcing some significant changes to its smart home software. Starting next year, the company will shut down the Nest app in favor of the Google Home app and retire Google Assistant on its smart home devices.
The Nest app shutdown takes place on January 25th, 2027, meaning you’ll have to manage your Nest products, including Nest thermostats, cameras, and Nest Protect alarms, from the Google Home app instead. If you get the Google Home app set up, Google will move over your Nest devices, including cameras and video history, to the Home app on that January 25th date. The company will also automatically transfer Nest Aware (1st Gen) subscriptions to Google Home Premium. Google says it will begin deleting Nest account data on March 25th, 2027.
The changes for Google Assistant will take place later: On August 2nd, 2027, the Gemini for Home voice assistant will replace Google Assistant on smart speakers and smart displays, the company says. Google argues that Gemini for Home allows users to ask more complex questions and speak naturally instead of needing to use dedicated commands or specific language.
Gemini for Home was announced last year , so it’s not exactly a shock that Google is going to move on from Google Assistant in the smart home (especially when the company also killed Google Assistant on phones earlier this year ). The company says it plans to share more updates about the changes ahead of the August 2027 transition.

articles.title_orig: A visual tour of ‘Grand Theft Auto VI’s’ stunningly realized Miami
articles.title_zh: A visual tour of ‘Grand Theft Auto VI’s’ stunningly realized Miami
articles.content_orig:
CEDAR KEY, Fla. (WCJB) - The developers of “Grand Theft Auto VI” used the iconic seaside City of Cedar Key in North Central Florida as inspiration for one of the game’s locations.
GTA 6 brings players back to the fictional U.S. state of Leonida and Vice City, Rockstar Games’ fictional version of Miami and South Florida. Game designers used real-world locations in Florida as inspiration.
Dock Street and other iconic parts of Cedar Key are recreated in the game’s Watson Bay. Resident Michael Presley Bobbitt recorded a walk-through of the location, pointing out real-world locations.
“This is such a cool, unique place. Who would have ever thought that a fishing village of 700 people would be on the global stage? Come and check it out, friends,” Bobbitt said.
Leaders with the Cedar Key Chamber of Commerce said they hope the game could drive tourism to the island.
“If you live here, you’re connected with every one of those buildings, so it was fun to pick out what’s changed since it was shot, but I will say getting Cedar Key on the map that way is a whole new audience for us, so we kind of love it,” said Tara Barney, a chamber of commerce board member.
A landmark resembling the Ocala Drive-In Theater also appears in the game. A flea market is connected to the business in the game, just like its counterpart in real life.
The Ocala Drive-In Theater is one of only four left in the state.
The owner addressed rumors last month, as previously reported, that his family business was closing down. He said they may sell at some point in the future, but the business is still open.

articles.title_orig: Reward for Missing Climber Raises Safety Worries
articles.title_zh: Reward for Missing Climber Raises Safety Worries
articles.content_orig:
The Chinese embassy in Japan has warned its citizens against off-season ascents of Mount Fuji amid concerns that the hefty reward offered by a missing hiker's family could encourage more reckless climbing.
Chen Jie, 25, vanished on 8 November on the mountain. His family is offering 500,000 yuan ($75,000; £57,300) to anyone who finds him alive, and 100,000 yuan to anyone who recovers his body, say Chinese and Japanese media reports.
Strong winds and blizzards pose serious risks during the closed season, especially as shelter and first-aid centres are not operational, the embassy said on Tuesday.
Mount Fuji's official climbing season runs from around early July to early September.
Earlier this year, authorities of Yamanashi province, where the northern part of Mount Fuji sits, had said that people who attempt to climb Mount Fuji during off-peak seasons and then require rescue by helicopter will have to pay for the service from next year on.
Authorities will also require those looking to scale Fuji during the off-season to submit detailed climbing plans.
"We hope that these measures will cause people to rethink what climbing Mount Fuji during the winter is like," Kotaro Nagasaki, the prefecture governor, said at the time.
On Wednesday, Nagasaki told reporters that attempts to find the missing climber could lead to "secondary disasters"
According to Japanese news outlet the Mainichi Shimbun, Nagasaki appeared to appeal to Chen's family, saying: "I understand that your family is important, but please refrain from doing anything that could endanger others."
Some social media users in Japan have similarly expressed fears would entice people to venture into the mountains ill-prepared and lead to more accidents,
Yamanashi police said Chen had set out on his hike on 8 November with two friends, who turned back after they realised the mountain was closed and that they weren't suitably equipped for the conditions of the trails.
Chen pressed on alone from the fifth station of the Yoshida Trail, which sits at around 2,300m (7545ft) above sea level.
A friend last heard from Chen at 10:30 that day, when he sent a video message saying: "I'm going up the mountain... There's no one in sight."
The highest point of Mount Fuji, which is Japan's tallest peak, stands at 3,776m.
Local authorities launched a search for Chen on 10 November, but it had to be halted several times because of poor weather.
Chen's father reportedly arrived in Japan on 13 November. It is not clear when he posted the reward offer.

articles.title_orig: S&P 500 Is Set for Longest Losing Run Since 2020: Markets Wrap
articles.title_zh: S&P 500 Is Set for Longest Losing Run Since 2020: Markets Wrap
articles.content_orig:
Stocks were slammed on Friday, closing out a brutal week for markets as the much-hyped Anthropic IPO caused investors to take profits on the artificial intelligence-led rally rather than revive it. The Nasdaq Composite turned negative for the year, and the S&P 500 entered correction territory alongside the Dow Jones Industrial Average .
The tech-heavy Nasdaq shed 4.3% and was down 1.7% year to date. The broad market S&P 500 traded down 2.9%, while the blue-chip Dow fell 573 points, or 1.2%. Both the S&P 500 and Dow were more than 10% below their closing records.
Anthropic lost 10%, giving back most of its 17% jump in its Nasdaq debut Thursday and pressuring the broader AI trade. Chipmakers Advanced Micro Devices and Nvidia slid 12% and more than 11%, respectively. Nvidia saw selling pressure increase after Reuters reported that the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission is exploring possible accounting issues at the company. Micron Technology dropped more than 13%.
Those declines in tech built on the losses seen in Thursday's horrid session, where the major averages each losing more than 2%, and the Dow closing below the key 50,000 level for the first time since June.
"This is not just a valuation-driven correction. It's becoming broader," said Massimo Santicchia, head of U.S. equities at Procyon. "Right now, it's definitely risk-off."
The losses are alarming investors who were hopeful that Nvidia's earnings and Anthropic's IPO would revive enthusiasm for the AI trade. Now, the market looks to be on the cusp of a true capitulation after getting roiled in recent weeks with a series of negative headlines. Signs of moderation in the capital expenditures splurge, Democratic wins in the 2026 midterms and Jensen Huang's ouster at Nvidia all raised questions about the future of the AI buildout.
On top of that, the potential for more interest rate hikes from the Federal Reserve is spooking traders as well.
Investors hid out in defensive areas of the market, with retailers such as Walmart and Costco as well as others like Johnson & Johnson and Procter & Gamble seeing gains. Walmart gained 2%, while Costco, Johnson & Johnson and Procter & Gamble each rose more than 1%.
"The stock market is going through an AI repricing, reflecting an environment of slowing data center buildouts, reduced funding sources for AI-related projects and a slower trajectory of technology-related earnings growth," said Richard Saperstein, chief investment officer at Treasury Partners.
For the week, the Dow has fallen 7%, putting it on pace for its worst weekly performance since April 2025 in the wake of President Donald Trump's sweeping tariffs announcement . The S&P 500 has decreased almost 8%, while the Nasdaq is down about 9%, with both also headed for their largest one-week pullbacks in more than a year.
Anthropic was the most-traded single stock by Vanguard's self-directed retail traders on Thursday, underscoring the buzz among mom-and-pop investors around the artificial intelligence leader's historic IPO.
Just about 0.2% of Vanguard's self-directed investors bought Anthropic on Thursday, which was its first day on the public market. These investors bought a median of 20 shares or roughly $1,950.
Vanguard said about around out of every 10 Anthropic buyers were men. By comparison, men account for 55% of Vanguard's investor base.
To be sure, Vanguard said a higher percentage of its base traded SpaceX during its public market debut session in June.
Anthropic jumped 17% in trading on Thursday after it went public. But the stock has dropped nearly 10% in afternoon trading Friday, which is its first full day on the market.
BTIG's chief market technician Jonathan Krinsky in an appearance on CNBC's " The Exchange " Friday pointed to technicals that make him think the sell-off isn't over just yet.
He specifically noted Apple , the largest stock by market cap, which is only down by 3% from its 2026 highs earlier this month. "When the S&P has been down at least 8% or more, when it's made its final bottom, the median drawdown for Apple has been 23%," he said. "It would be historically unprecedented to see a final bottom on the S&P with Apple where it is right now."
He added that 50% of the S&P 500's stocks are above their 50-day moving average, a level that is higher than a number closer to below 40% — or even 20% — when durable bottoms hit.
Krinsky did note, though, that relief for semiconductors may be coming, as the group is retreating to levels that it last traded at in early April when the group started to surge higher . The iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) in late trading Friday was at levels it last closed below on April 9.
Anthropic debuted with a 17% advance on Thursday, starting off on the wrong foot as its performance came up short when compared with the day-one gains from other notable IPOs since last year.
The day-one moves of Circle , Figma , Cerebras and SpaceX all outdid Anthropic's, with Figma seeing the biggest jump at 250% .
Anthropic shares gave back much of that advance on Friday, falling more than 12% in afternoon trading.
President Donald Trump said on Friday that he wants to stop U.S. companies from building data centers in other countries.
"We're going to fight very hard for the data centers," Trump said at a White House press conference. He added that companies would face tremendous penalties for building data centers abroad. "We want them to build it here."
He added that he is concerned about U.S. companies building in China instead. "We're not allowing that to happen," he said.
— Kevin Breuninger and Davis Giangiulio
The VIX volatility index , a gauge of how much the S&P 500 might move in the next 30 days based on options trading, rose another 13% intraday Friday to 32.27, after jumping as much as 16% Thursday, according to FactSet data.
The VIX, a gauge of skittishness on Wall Street, has now risen for six of the past seven days. The index hasn't closed above 30 since late March.
Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook expressed caution about the dangers posed by inflation, saying Friday that if the central bank doesn't act now it risks having to do more later.
"Inflation has been above target for more than five and a half years, and every additional day poses greater risk that price- and wage-setters will adjust their inflation expectations upward," Cook said in remarks delivered in Chile.
"Furthermore, waiting longer to implement rate increases risks getting behind the curve," she added. "If we fall behind, additional and larger rate increases may be required later to catch up, which could increase stress on our financial system and have unnecessarily damaging effects on American households."
Cook was one of only two FOMC members who voted against the pause. Markets strongly expect the committee to approve a quarter percentage point hike at the Dec. 8-9 meeting.
The tech selling intensified in late-morning trading, with the sector down more than 5% on the day. That decline pushed its week-to-date losses to 10.5% as of 11:57 a.m. ET. That would be tech's biggest one-week drop since April 4, 2025, when the Trump administration announced massive tariffs on imported products.
The Nasdaq Composite dropped Friday, turning negative for 2026, as even Anthropic's IPO and Nvidia's earnings failed to revive the artificial intelligence trade. The tech-heavy index was last lower by 2.6% for the trading session, falling slightly on the year.
Bitcoin slid more than 4% with the broader market, falling below the $60,000 level for the first time since July.
The flagship cryptocurrency was last trading at $59,554.95 and is now heading for a retest its July low of $57,737.35.
Ether fell 6% to $1,650.79, its lowest level since July 2.
The outlook for consumers improved in November as expectations for inflation eased, according to a University of Michigan survey Friday.

articles.title_orig: At APEC Summit, U.S., China and Russia Vow to Increase Oil Supply Amid Global Energy Transition
articles.title_zh: At APEC Summit, U.S., China and Russia Vow to Increase Oil Supply Amid Global Energy Transition
articles.content_orig:
The United States, China and Russia have pledged to increase petrol supplies as the wars in Iran – started by Israel and the US – and Ukraine – started by Russia – continue to upend global energy markets.
Following their trilateral summit in Shenzhen, China, on Thursday, US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russia’s President Vladimir Putin said in a joint statement that they “plan to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products for the benefit of all nations”.
The three leaders also “reaffirmed the importance of stable energy flows”.
But analysts are sceptical about how this will actually work amid the US having little to no spare refining capacity, Russia being constrained by continued Ukrainian attacks on its energy infrastructure and China’s crude oil imports disrupted by the US and Israel’s war on Iran.
“The trilateral statement should be treated as political noise rather than the first step to boosting global fuel supplies,” Hamad Hussain, a senior climate and commodities economist at Capital Economics, told Al Jazeera.
“The announcement sounds like it is designed to placate consumers and constituencies. Previous efforts to increase supply [like the US-Russian diesel deal] went nowhere,” Frederic Schneider, a nonresident senior fellow at the Middle East Council on Global Affairs, told Al Jazeera.
So is what the three leaders said impossible?
China and the US are the world’s biggest oil refiners by capacity, followed by Russia and India.
China has roughly 18.5 to 18.83 million barrels per day (bpd) of oil refining capacity. But refining in the country is dependent on its crude oil imports, which have been badly disrupted by the continuing US-Iran conflict in the Strait of Hormuz, through which Gulf oil exporters normally ship crude oil – much of it to Asia.
According to a November report by the US Energy Information Administration (EIA), crude oil refinery imports in China fell by 2.1 million bpd in the second quarter of 2026 and by an additional 0.8 million barrels bpd in the third quarter of the year.
As of January 1 this year, the US had an operable crude oil distillation capacity of about 18.16 million bpd. Production has increased since the war began, and is already running at near full capacity.
According to an October EIA report, “the US refinery fleet has run at higher-than-normal rates this year, with refinery utilisation averaging more than 95 percent of capacity between May and September, the highest for those months since 1998”.
Russia has roughly 6.5 million bpd of oil refining capacity, according to the International Energy Agency.
But Ukrainian drone strikes on its energy infrastructure have severely impacted its refining capacity. “In June, Russian refinery throughput fell to 3.8 million barrels per day, its lowest level in more than 20 years and roughly 30 percent below a year earlier,” a September International Energy Agency report noted.
Meanwhile, India has an oil refining capacity of about 5.36 million bpd, according to government figures. But New Delhi is also heavily dependent on crude oil imports, and this has been affected by blockades in the Strait of Hormuz.
According to the EIA, US refineries are currently running at close to maximum capacity.
This has been driven largely by “tight global supplies for distillate fuel oil, leading to high international demand for US distillate fuel oil exports”, a November EIA report states. Distillate fuel oil is refined petroleum which includes diesel fuels and light fuel oils.
Hussain said that while it may be profitable to refine more oil amid higher oil prices this year, the issue is that Washington “does not have spare capacity” to do so.
The Trump administration says it is determined to boost global fuel supply and US Energy Secretary Chris Wright has said his department is “talking about reopening every refinery we can” to do so.
According to a November 19 Reuters report, US refiner Valero Energy agreed to buy the century-old LyondellBasell Industries refinery near Houston, Texas, in October and restore a portion of the facility, adding 165,000 bpd of processing capacity by the end of 2027.
The plan would reverse years of refinery closures in the US and add about 1 percent to overall US refining capacity of 18 million bpd, Reuters reported. But analysts say the total price tag of acquiring and recommissioning this refinery could reach $1bn.
Since last year, long-range Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian oil refineries have resulted in serious fuel shortages across the country.
According to the IEA, in the first eight months of 2026, a Russian refinery was hit on average once every three days.
Reuters has reported that drone attacks have slashed Russian oil refineries’ combined crude processing volumes by 45 percent since late October and several regions have also begun limiting fuel.
On Friday, Reuters also reported that the Russia-installed governor of Crimea’s Sevastopol region, Mikhail Razvozhayev, said petrol sales there were being limited to one full car tank and 20 litres (5.3 gallons) in jerrycans at a number of pumping stations from Thursday.
He said the measures were being introduced to prevent people from filling canisters with hundreds of litres at a time, causing queues and preventing others from refilling.
The Siberian city of Tomsk also capped sales of petrol and diesel to 30 and 50 litres, respectively, from last week, according to local authorities.
On Thursday, the city of Penza, 770km (480 miles) southeast of Moscow, restricted petrol sales to 50 litres while limiting diesel to 200 litres per vehicle. At least half a dozen other regions introduced restrictions earlier this month.
With Ukrainian attacks continuing and Russia limiting fuel, refining more is currently a challenge for the country.
According to a November EIA report, Russia is also a major fuel exporter, especially of diesel. So any issues with its refining and decline in its exports will have a global impact.
While Trump and Putin agreed on a deal in October to allow some Russian diesel exports, none of the shipped fuel has reached customers, as traders have refused to take it .
The EIA noted that Russia’s loss of refinery operations has also “reduced refining activity in Asia and the Middle East, contributing to diesel prices increasing to the highest nominal levels on record in September”.
The conflict in the Strait of Hormuz strained crude oil imports to China earlier this year, but these have largely recovered.
While Beijing does not officially disclose the volumes of crude flowing into or out of its strategic and commercial stockpiles, Reuters reported that the world’s largest crude importer saw arrivals of 9.88 million bpd in October, up 9.4 percent from September’s 9.03 million bpd and the most since March, just after the war began.
Before the Iran war began on February 28, China was purchasing an average of 10.5 million barrels of crude per day by sea, according to sea-borne commodity data group Vortexa .
China also began stockpiling crude oil in October as imports recovered.
According to Hussain, “China does have some spare refinery capacity it could utilise”.
“But given that petrol and diesel inventories appear to be low in China, any increase in refined output may be used to replenish reserves rather than for export, which would keep global fuel supply constrained,” he said.
“In any case, the return of refined output from the Middle East will be key to lowering global fuel prices,” he added.

articles.title_orig: Trump, Xi and Putin Seek to Project Power at Their First Summit
articles.title_zh: Trump, Xi and Putin Seek to Project Power at Their First Summit
articles.content_orig:
It was the first-ever meeting of the leaders of the world’s three biggest nuclear powers—one that host Xi Jinping opened by hailing its “pioneering significance.”
Exactly what was achieved when Xi met with Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump at Kylin Villa in northwestern Shenzhen on Thursday, however, has onlookers scratching their heads. Xi started by invoking the responsibility of Great Powers toward world peace; Putin delved into historic “shared interests;” while Trump immediately lashed out at “rogue globalist organisations,” such as the International Criminal Court (ICC).
The ICC “has gotten out of control,” Trump told his companions seated around a round wooden table, and has “really strayed far beyond its jurisdiction.”
It was almost as if this historic trilateral , held on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit, didn’t have any fixed agenda. It hadn’t. When the confab was first proposed, Putin wanted to talk about Ukraine, though U.S. officials pushed back. Trump instead suggested nuclear arms and Iran, but Beijing wasn’t keen. Finally, China’s Foreign Ministry settled on “safeguarding world peace and promoting strategic stability in major-power relations.”
It was therefore an occasion rich with platitudes but not a lot else. “In this global village, major countries shoulder special responsibilities,” said Xi, who also called for the destruction of all nuclear weapons. “Positive interaction among major powers is not an optional question, but a compulsory one.”
Still, the meeting served its purpose. Trump gained a chance to project influence after chastening midterms and the unfolding Nvidia saga that forced the resignation of his close friend Jensen Huang as CEO. Xi got to flaunt himself as the consummate statesman, while Putin took a baby step out from the diplomatic cold. But it was also a distinctly unsettling sight for the U.S. President to be sitting beside two of America’s most consequential adversaries, whose governments declared in 2022 that their friendship with each other had “no limits.”
Before the three-way meeting, Trump met separately with Putin and then Xi. His roughly 40 minutes with the Russian President began on a hopeful note: “Wonderful things can come out of this—or at least start,” Trump said. During an hour of talks with Xi, Trump returned to a more familiar concern. “I’ll be asking you to do some more for our farmers,” he said. He also suggested that Washington and Beijing could work together to end Russia’s war in Ukraine.
That prospect mattered to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, who said Wednesday that the war could end in a single meeting if the U.S. and China used their economic leverage against Moscow. Instead, Trump launched a broadside against the ICC, which has issued an arrest warrant against Putin for war crimes, urging his autocratic counterparts to cooperate on “ways to protect our nations’ sovereignty.”
Trump also said it was “vital that we cooperate to combat the threat of nuclear proliferation in other countries around the world,” before segueing into a justification of his war in Iran : “That’s what we’re doing in Iran. We’re not going to let Iran have a nuclear weapon.”
Of course, this was always going to be an occasion that would put style over substance. On Wednesday, Xi surprised onlookers by greeting a clearly delighted Trump on the tarmac at Shenzhen Baoan Airport. Their handshake turned into a brief hug, before five People’s Liberation Army J-10C fighter jets flew overhead, billowing red, yellow, and blue smoke.
In personally meeting Trump as he deplaned Air Force One, Xi reciprocated the welcome he received from the U.S. President at Joint Base Andrews in September. The gesture was a first by a top Chinese leader since Mao Zedong met Nikita Khrushchev at Beijing’s airport in 1959.
Putin had to suffice with being greeted by Xi’s chief of staff, Cai Qi, upon his earlier arrival in the wee hours of Wednesday morning. But Xi spent much of that afternoon in talks with his embattled Russian counterpart, who used his speech to assembled CEOs to lambast Western sanctions, crowing that the U.S. and Europe had “punished themselves” with punitive measures, which Russia had successfully sidestepped anyway.
Upon emerging from his two-hour bilateral with Putin, Xi called on both countries to “lead and advance … the democratization of international relations.” Putin, in turn, boasted that economic coercion was “a thing of the past.” Later in the evening, Putin and Trump shook hands before the gala dinner as Xi looked on smiling.
“Beijing’s top priority would be to create a more stable external environment for China’s development, particularly by making relations with Washington more predictable while maintaining steady cooperation with Moscow,” says Sun Chenghao, a fellow with Tsinghua University’s Centre for International Security and Strategy.
Still, the summit threatened to be overshadowed by the Nvidia scandal, with company founder Huang admitting an affair with a woman accused of illicitly funneling chips to China and whom U.S. intelligence agencies reportedly suspect may be a Chinese spy. On Nov. 16, the U.S. Commerce Department issued an interim rule aimed at stopping Chinese firms from accessing advanced U.S. chips through data centers abroad.
Trump told Fox News that he and Xi “spoke the whole evening” during Wednesday’s gala dinner but only “briefly” discussed Nvidia. Trump also claimed he was unaware of the espionage allegations, which China vehemently denies. “I haven’t heard that she was a spy,” Trump said. “She was a businesswoman who bought chips, and who knows if they were bought right or wrong.”
Trump also appeared to shoot down any hopes of regulation governing AI: “We oppose any form of globalist regulation or anything to control or stifle [AI], and we won’t allow that to happen,” he said.
Still, the historic trilateral did succeed in visibly placing China at the center of Great Power diplomacy. Hosting the leaders alongside APEC supports Beijing’s claim that global influence is shifting eastward, with China as a stabilizing power, particularly amid unpredictable U.S. policy.
“The optics might actually play well for China,” says Chong Ja Ian, a professor of international relations at the National University of Singapore. “It certainly would fit the sort of image that Beijing and Xi would like to create for themselves.”
But while APEC was created in 1989 to ease trade and investment across the region, today’s world has been gripped by rising protectionism. The Trump Administration has levied tariffs on 60 trading partners that together account for 99.4% of U.S. imports, according to the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative. Moreover, Europe is increasingly chary about cheap Chinese exports that Brussels says are fueled by subsidies and industrial overcapacity.
Xi used his Wednesday address to business leaders to promise a more open Chinese market and present the world’s second-largest economy as a source of opportunity. “History tells us that opening doors brings progress while closing doors leaves one behind,” he said.
Yet the image of three elderly leaders debating global problems behind closed doors sits uneasily beside Xi’s call for a more multipolar world. Pro-Kremlin media was especially keen to frame the meeting as Yalta 2.0 after the historic powwow between Roosevelt, Stalin, and Churchill toward the end of World War II.
But it is Ukraine’s plucky defiance of Putin's invasion that underscores how today’s Middle Powers have more agency. At the World Economic Forum in Davos in January, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney urged third countries to work together on trade, security and technology in order to shape the rules and resist economic coercion. “Middle powers must act together because if you are not at the table, you are on the menu,” Carney said.

articles.title_orig: This VIX Signal Is Bullish For The S&P 500.
articles.title_zh: This VIX Signal Is Bullish For The S&P 500.
articles.content_orig:
There's a bull market... in fear.
Faced with a barrage of headlines from nationwide tech outages to Nvidia earnings and Anthropic's initial public offering, traders on Tuesday piled into protective put options on the S&P 500 Index at a rate that suggests fear beyond just an AI-specific correction. The Cboe Volatility Index (VIX) surged nearly 5 points to a high of 27.7 at the worst of Tuesday's selling and the ratio of put to call volumes on the SPDR S&P 500 ETF (SPY) hit 1.5, the highest since the first week of April, according to Barchart data. The 'VIX' was last still hovering above 26. With the VIX climbing four days in a row, the volatility gauge hasn't traded under 16 since Oct. 16, arguably trending higher as the S&P 500 slips below this month's lows, trading under 7,300 for the lowest price for the benchmark equity gauge since June. Cboe's three-month volatility gauge, VIX3M, briefly touched the highest since April.
While Nvidia earnings are contributing to the uncertainty – the stock's options currently imply more than a 7% move after its report, the biggest in almost two years – volatility in the S&P 500 jumped more than in the Nasdaq 100 Tuesday, pointing to a more widespread fear among investors. "SPX vol is expanding faster than NDX vol, as SPX vol is coming from a lower base," Eric Metz, CIO, SpiderRock Advisors for BlackRock, said via email. "Today, the market is pricing acute near-term stress in large-caps broadly, but tech-specific fear is still notable. Even within the technology cohort, Tuesday's laggards took on a different tone. Software stocks declined the most ahead of Anthropic's IPO, with options volume on the iShares Expanded Tech-Software Sector ETF (IGV) surging to almost four times the 30-day average, according to Cboe LiveVol data. Salesforce was hardest hit, with put contracts outpacing calls on twice the average options volume. "There's a lot of reasons to be risk-off," said Noel Smith, co-CIO of Kai Asset Management. "This is a market-wide phenomenon today that's not just AI stocks." To be sure, bulls weren't totally absent from the session, with the Nasdaq 100 Index holding its November low and VIX still under its Nov. 5 high of 28.4. "While vol is now at a relatively elevated level, we have not seen much fear in the options market," said VolSignals' Matthew Nadel, citing fixed-strike volatility in S&P 500 options, which measures volatility changes across specific options strikes. "We have seen a pretty decent move higher in SPX fixed strike vol, however the move up in vol has been mostly orderly."

articles.title_orig: Friend zone: rejected by US voters, Trump enjoys autocrats’ warm embrace
articles.title_zh: Friend zone: rejected by US voters, Trump enjoys autocrats’ warm embrace
articles.content_orig:
The US president rated his summit with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin as 12 out of 10 but China and Russia had the most to celebrate
H e got by with a little help from his friends. Rebuked by millions of voters in a still resilient democracy, Donald Trump travelled to Asia this week and found comfort in the company of autocrats who still flatter him.
The US president, reduced to lame-duck status at home by a humiliating midterm election defeat, returned to the global stage in a meeting with two strongmen in Shenzhen, China, that critics described as a new low for America’s claim to moral authority.
“ Who is he? ” Trump asked rhetorically, pointing as he walked towards the Russian leader, Vladimir Putin. “He’s my friend.” Separately he told the Chinese president, Xi Jinping: “You’re my friend, and we have a very special relationship.”
Trump, Xi and Putin convened at the Kylin Villa in Shenzhen, China, for the first-ever trilateral summit among the leaders of the US, China and Russia, the world’s three biggest nuclear powers. The official product of their 70-minute closed-door meeting was a four-point document titled the “Declaration Toward Peace” that made no mention of the wars in Iran or Ukraine.
But the defining image was of the trio sitting around a huge circular wooden table. At its hollow centre sat an immaculate arrangement of pink flowers, an ancient Chinese motif meant to evoke harmony. To US-based critics, however, the optics sent a different signal.
Steve Schmidt , a former adviser to George W Bush and John McCain, said: “The image of the grotesque large round table with a war criminal dictator, a stable dictator and an irrational, delusional wannabe dictator is an image of deep shame and weakness for the United States.
“It’s a repudiation of American values, American honour, common sense and the national security interests of the country, and a betrayal of America’s allies all across the world.”
Beijing understood how to satisfy the Trump ego. When Air Force One landed in Shenzhen for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit, Xi made the unusual move of greeting Trump personally on the tarmac. An honour guard stood at attention, crowds waved miniature US and Chinese flags, schoolchildren shook pompoms and Xi drew Trump into a warm embrace.
Trump took the bait with delight. For him, victory was not measured in negotiating concessions but in the lavish banquet and the seat reserved for him at the head table. “That’s a big win for us,” he said in a TV interview. “It’s a big win for China too. We get along.” Trump was even treated to a performance of YMCA, the signature song of his campaign rallies.
In their first meeting since failed negotiations in Alaska last year, Trump held one-on-one talks with Putin that touched on Ukraine but secured no immediate commitments. The meeting occurred against a backdrop of Trump recently rejecting new sanctions on Russia.
In a bilateral meeting with Xi, Trump raised the US-led war in Iran, emphasising a joint interest in fully reopening the strait of Hormuz and preventing Iran from acquiring nuclear weapons. Xi focused on US-China trade stability and asserted China’s sovereign position on Taiwan, treating it as an unalterable domestic issue.
In one ominous remark, Trump told Xi: “I think as long as you and I are in charge of things, we’ll never have a problem.” He later told NBC News that the pair had also agreed that artificial intelligence needed some form of safety “guardrails” but offered few details.
The main event was the trilateral summit, with observers watching body language closely for any clues about the dynamics among Xi, relishing his role as host, Putin, whose war in Ukraine is faltering, and Trump, ostensibly the most powerful of the three but politically wounded at home. To many, it offered little more than a glorified photo op.
Brett Bruen , the president of the public affairs agency Global Situation Room and the former global engagement director of the Barack Obama White House, said: “Brand Trump has been badly sullied by a historic defeat at the hands of American voters. However, this isn’t going to improve his standing internationally and certainly not domestically.
“If anything, it put on display his desperation. It put on display his isolation internationally from the very people that he’s going to need to be able to secure trade deals or peace deals. Once again he’s returning from China with the luggage hold empty of any diplomatic accomplishments.”
The formal output of the summit was a study in profound omissions and authoritarian wishlists. The text made no mention of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, nor of the spiralling US military conflict with Iran.
Instead, the trio agreed on four broad points: pledging dialogue to reduce nuclear risks, committing to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum, calling for “reforms” to the United Nations and declaring that state sovereignty and the immunity of state officials must be respected while warning that the international criminal court (ICC) must not abuse its jurisdiction.
Putin currently faces an active ICC arrest warrant for war crimes in Ukraine, while the Trump administration has sanctioned ICC officials to shield itself and its ally Israel from judicial scrutiny.
Ned Price , a former deputy to the US representative to the UN, said: “The joint statement was notable, not because Russia and China said it, but because the United States also co-signed.
“The United Nations they want is not a United Nations that’s more effective but rather a United Nations that is less effective at upholding the rules of the road, the very principles that have been at the centre of the UN system since its founding: the idea that big countries can’t bully small countries, that borders can’t be redrawn by force.”
The talks have done little to dispel the impression that Trump regards Congress, the media and elections as pesky encumbrances while gazing with awe and some envy at Xi and Putin. As the Shenzhen summit concluded, European leaders and Nato officials convened urgently in Berlin to reinforce their support for Ukraine and resist any high-level partitioning of European security.
The summit was a propaganda win for Putin, who went from international pariah status to equal billing with the world’s two biggest economies. It was also a victory for Xi. Without making any concessions on Taiwan, trade tariffs or its industrial lifeline to Moscow, China positioned itself as the arbiter of 21st-century diplomacy.
“Xi was able to burnish China’s diplomatic sway and give Putin and Trump something that each leader respectively coveted,” said Ali Wyne , senior research and advocacy adviser for US-China relations at the International Crisis Group. “He gave Putin the opportunity to demonstrate that despite Russia’s wartime losses, despite western sanctions, Russia remains a great power.
“He gave Trump the opportunity to demonstrate, at least in Trump’s own mind, that despite these bruising midterm elections, Trump is a singularly visionary and consequential peacemaker, thereby appealing to Trump’s ego.”
While neither Beijing nor Moscow harbours any illusions about Trump’s volatile temperament, both recognise the ticking clock on his second term and know they are likely to outlast him.
Wyne added: “Both of them recognise that it is next to impossible that any of President Trump’s successors will view them in comparable terms as friends, adopt conciliatory dispositions, and on certain issues come close to aligning US positions with those of China and Russia.”
Although he was caught on camera apparently nodding off, Trump departed China appearing politically rejuvenated after his encounters with his two “friends”. He hailed the visit as “Highly Consequential” on social media and said later: “On a scale of zero to 10, I think it was a 12.”

articles.title_orig: Teenage Engineering’s first CD player puts the spinning disc on display
articles.title_zh: Teenage Engineering’s first CD player puts the spinning disc on display
articles.content_orig:
The EP/BC–1 can wirelessly stream audio to Bluetooth headphones or multiple devices using Auracast.
The EP/BC–1 can wirelessly stream audio to Bluetooth headphones or multiple devices using Auracast.
Teenage Engineering announced what it describes as “a modern take on a classic CD player” with its new EP/BC–1 featuring a slab-like design that leaves the spinning disc exposed instead of hiding it under a lid or inside a slide-out tray. The company says the EP/BC–1 is the first entry in its new broadcast series of products and was designed to bring “physical audio formats into a modern context, evolved from a shared obligation within the company to preserve the formats they grew up with.”
The EP/BC-1 is available now through Teenage Engineering’s online store for $299. The CD player joins the company’s existing EP–series of audio devices and has the same dimensions as its KO II synthesizer that launched in 2023 so it can be paired with, and connected to, other Teenage Engineering gear including the recently-announced EP-35 battery-powered amp .
Although it’s designed to play a nearly 45 year old medium, the EP/BC-1 features modern conveniences like variable speed playback, cue markers, a jog wheel for forward and reverse search, and built-in beat detection. There’s a very retro-looking series of digital displays showing track, index, time information, and audio levels, and around the edges you’ll find both digital and analog audio connections including a headphone jack and a USB 2.0 port.
If you want to go completely wireless the CD player has a rechargeable battery and supports both Bluetooth connections to headphones and Auracast streaming to multiple devices that support it. The EP/BC-1 is compatible with standard CDs as well as discs full of MP3 files, and when using the former it can rip tracks to 44.1 Hz/16-bit WAV files. If you want MP3s or other formats, you’ll need to convert them yourself.

articles.title_orig: Britain Announces Brexit Reset Deal at E.U. Summit: What to Know
articles.title_zh: Britain Announces Brexit Reset Deal at E.U. Summit: What to Know
articles.content_orig:
BRUSSELS — Britain and the European Union agreed Friday to remove barriers to trade and expand travel opportunities for young people as they pledged to rebuild their strained ties with an “ambitious and dynamic” relationship. But they left big decisions about softening or reversing Brexit for another day.
In a joint statement after a summit in Brussels, the U.K. and EU confirmed agreements that will scrap border checks on plant and animal products, cut carbon taxes on some exports by linking their emissions trading schemes and let 100,000 young adults from each side live and work in the other’s countries for up to three years.
Other areas remain a work in progress , with the two sides giving themselves six months to reach an agreement on the level of university fees for EU students in the U.K. and vice versa.
Friday’s summit was part of efforts to forge a closer relationship, a decade after Britain voted to leave the EU and six years after the divorce became final.
Supporters of Brexit argued that leaving the EU’s vast free-trade area and web of rules would let Britain take back control of its borders, laws and economy, and strike new trade deals around the world. Critics say Brexit has left Britain weaker and more isolated, and new deals with countries including Australia and Japan have not made up for the economic hit from erecting barriers between Britain and its closest and biggest economic partners.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the deal is “a turning point” in EU-U.K. relations, and U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham called it a “historic moment.”
“This is a good day for Britain, and this is a good day for Europe,” he said.
This was only the second EU-U.K. summit since Britain became the first country to leave the world’s biggest trading bloc. Months — likely years — of negotiations lie ahead on everything from electricity markets to manufacturing rules.
Burnham said the summit was a step toward undoing a decade of damage caused by the divorce.
He said the two sides are “rebuilding the bridges that were broken all of those years ago” and “building a much more constructive relationship with our nearest neighbors and our largest market.”
Burnham has said all options should be on the table for future relations, including rejoining the now 27-nation bloc. But he’s stressed that reversing Brexit is just one possible outcome , and far from imminent. It would need the backing not just of British voters, but the unanimous support of a mistrustful EU. Still, he has broken a long political code of silence on the option of rejoining.
“We remain open to have the closest possible relationship,” European Council President António Costa said. But he also recalled the obligations of EU membership, including single-market principles on the free movement of goods, services, people and capital.
Burnham pitched the package of agreements approved Friday as a way of “cutting costs, keeping prices down in the supermarkets and creating opportunities for young people .” He said the deals could bring in 17 billion pounds ($22 billion) a year and add 0.5% to Britain’s economic output.
British retailers welcomed the deal to remove checks on food and agricultural products, which will make it cheaper and easier for U.K. businesses to export to Europe.
“Getting our spaghetti bolognese from Lincolnshire onto a shelf in Dublin takes hundreds of extra miles, mountains of paperwork, a vet’s signature and even the Latin name of a cow,” said Alex Freudmann, managing director of food at Marks and Spencer.
Freudmann said Friday’s announcement “is a major step forward.”
But nothing in U.K.-EU relations is ever quick or simple. EU negotiators want European students to pay domestic fees if they study in Britain rather than the higher fees for foreign students, something the U.K. has resisted.
An EU official said negotiations had not been easy but they sensed good will to resolve the issue. The official was designated to brief reporters about the summit but only on condition that they not be named.
Talks are also continuing on Britain’s desire to be included in the bloc’s “made in Europe” rules, which favor European manufacturers for public projects over rivals from China or elsewhere.
To get the deals, the U.K. must accept some EU rules and standards that it has no role in setting. Supporters of Brexit say that undermines Britain’s independence.
Nigel Farage , leader of the euroskeptic, anti-immigration party Reform UK, told reporters in Brussels that Burnham had taken “the first step, incrementally, to take us back into membership of the European Union.”
The war in Ukraine, and the U.K.’s military strength, are drawing the two sides back together, and the summit produced pledges of stronger cooperation on security and defense, as well as efforts to restrict irregular migration.
Nevertheless, feelings remain raw , and EU officials have been reluctant to encourage talk of the U.K. rejoining. They are weary from the shifting demands of seven British prime ministers over the last decade and want clarity about the country’s intentions.
Von der Leyen said that a lot has changed in their relations since the Brexit vote, including the pandemic and Russia’s war on Ukraine. She said that the EU is “totally open to do the necessary brainstorming for the wider picture, the bigger picture” of what ties could look like in the future.
Burnham said he wanted the two sides to do that brainstorming before their next summit, probably a year from now.
For now, Burnham remains bound by the pledge made by Keir Starmer, his predecessor as Labour Party leader and prime minister, not to rejoin the bloc’s tariff-free customs union or frictionless single market, or to restore free movement for EU nationals to the U.K.
He acknowledged Friday’s agreements are “the limit of what we can achieve” before a national election.
“Incremental steps … only take us so far,” he said.

articles.title_orig: European Union and UK strike a 'landmark deal' to strengthen ties after Brexit
articles.title_zh: European Union and UK strike a 'landmark deal' to strengthen ties after Brexit
articles.content_orig:
European Union top officials and UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced deals on trade and youth mobility at Friday's Brussels summit.
This might be the first step to rebuild ties, a decade after Britain voted to leave the EU.
During the delegations' meeting, Burnham said the deal was a "landmark agreement," while European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen called it a "turning point" in relations.
"This is a good day for Britain. This is a good day for Europe," Burnham said.
Speaking at the joint press conference, European Council President Antonio Costa said the bloc respected the British decision to leave the EU and would respect its choice to strengthen ties in the post-Brexit era.
He said jokingly that the EU and UK "may drive on the opposite sides of the road, but what matters is they are heading for the same direction."
Burnham said that the deals were made with young people in mind, adding: "This deal is for you. This deal really is about lifting your life chances."
He went further and said " Brexit took opportunities from young people," and that they have to "open up new opportunities" for young people.
Von der Leyen said the youth experience project would "open horizons and create friendships that will last a lifetime."
She said the trade agreement is a "two way street" and it means "more choice for the customers."
Von der Leyen also mentioned the agreement on the carbon market, saying that it would cut emissions and generate investments in cleaner industries.
She also said Britain will rejoin the Erasmus+ program, adding, "We miss them so much."
Burnham said the agreements reached Friday, however, represent the most the UK could achieve at the moment, "What we are announcing today is probably ‌the limit of what we can achieve in this ‌Parliament, given what needs ‌to be done to implement it."
In September, Burnham said he would seek a political consensus on the country's future relationship with the EU, even suggesting he could campaign to take Britain back into the bloc at the next election.
"Britain and Europe share values, interests and a global neighborhood. In a more dangerous world, we are stronger together. A closer partnership with Europe is good for working people, good for Britain and good for Europe," Burnham said as he arrived in Brussels.
The three key agreements establish ways to:
The "youth experience scheme" would allow 100,000 people under 30 from each side to reside for up to three years in each other's territory for work, study or travel without being subject to existing visa requirements.
No deal was reached on tuition fees for EU students studying in Britain, a deal-breaker for the bloc. The EU has pressed for the UK to reduce university tuition fees for EU students to the same level paid by British students
"There will be further discussions coming out of it on issues including on tuition fees," Burnham said.
Von der Leyen ‌said ⁠she was confident negotiators would reach a ​solution ​on ‌tuition fees, "We will be working ‌on that in ‌the ​next month and as we have a ​track record of finding ⁠solutions,."
On the food deal, the EU and UK have agreed to scrap certificates and border checks on food and animal products to ease post-Brexit trade. In return, Britain will align more closely with EU food safety and animal health rules.
They also agreed to link their emissions-trading systems, allowing them to recognize each other's carbon allowances and exempt traded goods from carbon border taxes.
According to the AFP news agency, London estimates the deal could boost the British economy by 3.8 billion pounds annually, and spare 6.5 billion pounds worth of steel, aluminum and other industrial exports from additional taxation.
Leaders said they will establish a "structured dialogue on migration." Their joint summit statement said this would include "engagement with third countries" and "returns to third countries," among other issues.
The two sides agreed to launch formal talks on economic security and strengthen cooperation on export controls and supply chains, among other areas.

On Monday, Burnham said it ​was the "obvious truth" that ‌Britain had lost more than it had gained from Brexit .
Polling firm YouGov runs a regular tracker on whether the UK was right or wrong to vote to quit.
Since mid-2022, a majority of people surveyed said Britain was wrong to leave. In September, the "Bregret" camp rose to 60% — the highest ever.

articles.title_orig: Iraqi forces deploy to Jurf al-Sakhar after deal with Iran-backed group
articles.title_zh: Iraqi forces deploy to Jurf al-Sakhar after deal with Iran-backed group
articles.content_orig:
Iraqi security forces have been deployed to Jurf al-Sakhar, a stronghold of the powerful Iran-aligned Kataib Hezbollah armed group.
Security forces arrived in the town, which sits in Babil province about 60km southwest of Baghdad and is also known as Jurf al-Nasr , on Friday.
The deployment, which is understood to have been driven by pressure from the United States and its Gulf allies, comes a day after a compromise deal was sealed that will see Kataib Hezbollah move to other areas of the country.
The government announced on Monday that it would take control of Jurf al-Sakhar after a probe raised suspicions that the group had stolen hundreds of millions of dollars’ worth of Iraqi oil via illicit oil refineries.
It gave the group, which is believed to have thousands of trained fighters, a deadline of Friday to leave the town. However, under Thursday’s deal, they are expected to withdraw from the area within a month.
Kataib Hezbollah, one of dozens of heavily armed pro-Iranian groups that have semi-official status in Iraq, has denied the allegations of stealing oil. Nine senior security and oil officials have been dismissed following the investigation into alleged oil smuggling in Jurf al-Sakhar.
Analysts suspect the push for withdrawal is a calculated strategy to sever the financial arteries of armed factions that refuse to integrate into Iraq’s state apparatus. Baghdad has also come under pressure from the US to reduce Iran’s influence in the country.
Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi has had to tread a fine line as he seeks to contain Kataib Hezbollah without triggering a confrontation.
Al-Zaidi said on Friday, as he addressed the government forces entering the town, that they were “not waging war”.
“Everyone present there are your brothers,” he told the troops, “the sons of this nation, and their blood is our blood.”
However, he insisted that his decision to restrict weapons to state control was final.
Under the compromise, a combined force comprising an Iraqi army brigade, a Federal Police battalion and an Energy Police regiment will provide protection for oil pipelines in the area.
Two brigades from the Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF) Commission, a collection of armed groups that are part of Iraq’s official security forces, will also participate.
Lieutenant General Ahmed Hatem Hamid said on Friday that a control headquarters had been established in Jurf al-Sakhar and that the Federal Police would control the facility, according to the Iraqi News Agency (INA).
Iraq’s Energy Police have also begun securing an oil pipeline running through Jurf al-Sakhar, INA reported.
Baghdad-based security and strategic analyst Fadel Abu Raghif told Al Jazeera that the deal for Iraqi security forces to enter Jurf al-Sakhar came after lengthy and delicate talks with Kataib Hezbollah.
The agreement followed “in-depth negotiations, and after wrangling and a tug of war that lasted about two months or so,” Abu Raghif said.
Highlighting the delicacy of the situation, Esmail Qaani, the commander of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps’ Quds Force, had visited Iraq earlier this week to help defuse tension and seal the deal.
Kataib Hezbollah helped recapture Jurf al-Sakhar from ISIL (ISIS) and has had a large presence in the town for more than a decade.
Reporting from Babil province, Al Jazeera’s Samer Al Kobeisi said the departure of Kataib Hezbollah would allow the reopening of an area that has been closed for about 12 years, according to the government.

articles.title_orig: ‘Buyers are out for blood’: With home sales at a record low, buyers are calling the shots
articles.title_zh: ‘Buyers are out for blood’: With home sales at a record low, buyers are calling the shots
articles.content_orig:
Two new reports on the housing market show activity slowing even more, after a September spike in mortgage rates sent it into a deep freeze.
Pending home sales in October dropped 4.7% month-over-month and were down 16.7% from October of last year, according to the National Association of Realtors. This is the lowest level in the index's 25-year history.
Analysts had been looking for a much smaller decline, likely because mortgage rates pulled back slightly in October, only to rise sharply again last week. The average rate on the 30-year fixed started October at 7.54% according to Mortgage News Daily and ended the month at 7.27%.
The pending count is based on signed contracts — people out shopping and signing deals during the month. It is therefore an indicator of future closed sales.
"Two consecutive months of record-low pending contracts point to very sluggish fourth-quarter home sales closings, and annual existing-home sales could be the lowest since the mid-1990s," said Lawrence Yun, NAR's chief economist in a release.
Regionally, sales were down across the nation with the sharpest drops in the South, which is usually busiest for sales and the West which is most expensive.
Another report released Wednesday showed gains in home construction in October but raised a red flag going forward. Single-family housing starts rose 4% from September, according to the U.S. Census, but were down 3.2% year over year. Building permits, an indicator of future construction, dropped 8.7% for the month and were down 12.9% from October 2025. That is the lowest level for permits since May 2020, the start of the Covid-19 pandemic.
"Builders are dealing with a litany of obstacles to selling homes, whether it's rising costs of land, labor, and materials, high financing costs, or weak buyer demand," wrote Joel Berner, senior economist at Realtor.com. "This month's data shows them slowing down activity at the top of their funnel, which will result in slower months of starts and completions later on."
The construction report follows a bleak reading on homebuilder sentiment , which fell to the lowest level in 14 years in November, on the monthly index from the National Association of Home Builders. Builders cited multiple challenges, including higher mortgage rates, higher costs for energy, materials and labor, as well as weaker consumer confidence.

Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge claims he has proved the Riemann hypothesis, one of mathematics’s most notoriously difficult problems, with the help of Claude, cracking a puzzle that has eluded some of the world’s best mathematicians for decades. If verified, it would mark yet another seismic achievement for AI in mathematics and add to the upheaval already unleashed by OpenAI’s previous, often inelegant forays into the field.
Alpöge’s solution has yet to be verified independently. Anthropic has not commented or involved itself in Alpöge’s announcement. In a document on his website , Alpöge says he texted Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei about the solution “late Sunday night” and suggests he held off publication until after the company’s IPO on Thursday .
The Riemann hypothesis is one of seven Millennium Prize problems, which are widely considered some of the most formidable open challenges in mathematics. First proposed in 1859, the Riemann hypothesis concerns the distribution of prime numbers and how zeroes of a function are involved. It’s regarded as one of the most important unsolved problems in mathematics.
A statement on Alpöge’s website says Claude was integral to developing the proof:
I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof 1 of the Riemann Hypothesis. In fact, the method easily extends much further, resolving the so-called Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, and I expect, with more time, the Extended Riemann Hypothesis too. Claude and I have also formalized the arguments without assumptions. It is natural to feel that this is an end, in my case a loss of a principal guiding light, but what I saw during the course of progress so amazed me that I believe it is one dawn across science of something far greater.
The Verge reached out to Anthropic but didn’t immediately hear back. Anthropic said it was working on the Riemann Hypothesis with Claude in August , but noted at the time: “We don’t expect that the techniques Claude used will lead to proving the Riemann hypothesis.”
Alpöge’s solution, presented in Lean, has only been published on his website and has not yet been publicly accepted by the Clay Mathematics Institute, which administers the Millennium Prize and offers a $1 million bounty for each problem solved. Under the institute’s rules , a proposed solution must be published and withstand at least two years of scrutiny before it can be considered for the prize, during which time it must have “received general acceptance in the global mathematics community.”
In the quarter-century since the prize was established, only one problem has been officially solved: The Poincaré conjecture , a topological problem concerning three-dimensional spheres. In September, OpenAI claimed to have cracked another, the Navier-Stokes problem, which concerns the flow of fluids.
OpenAI said it pursued Navier-Stokes after hearing rumors that rival researchers were closing in on a solution. Alpöge had been working on the problem with New York University mathematics professor Tristan Buckmaster. Buckmaster claimed OpenAI produced a solution for Navier-Stokes using the route he and Alpöge were working on with OpenAI’s Codex and Claude.
OpenAI spent millions of dollars and deployed 10,000 agents in the attempt. The result is widely considered credible, though it has yet to receive formal recognition. But the achievement has been marred by allegations of questionable research practices, including claims it used unpublished work from mathematicians who had shared their research with its AI tools. OpenAI has strongly denied wrongdoing, but this has done little to quell the uproar.
Though most of the spotlight has been on OpenAI’s movement in math, Alpöge said in July that he solved the Jacobean conjecture using Claude. The deluge of findings has left mathematicians scrambling to digest the material and figure out where they belong in what is rapidly becoming a profoundly different mathematical landscape.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia Stock Drops Below $150 Support After Jensen Huang Scandal: Key Levels to Watch
articles.title_zh: Nvidia Stock Drops Below $150 Support After Jensen Huang Scandal: Key Levels to Watch
articles.content_orig:
The last time Wall Street was this down on Nvidia the chipmaker's flagship product was the GeForce graphics processor for high-end PC video games, and markets were reeling from the global financial crisis.
Nvidia shares tumbled 14% on Friday, sliding for a seventh straight day as investors grew increasingly concerned about life after co-founder Jensen Huang . The stock closed lower for a seventh consecutive week, the longest such stretch since 2008.
Shares of Nvidia are down 46% over the period, pushing the company's market cap down by about $2.6 trillion. The stock is now trading at roughly 8.4 times forward earnings, while Advanced Micro Devices is valued at 29 times profit for the next 12 months.
On Friday, Reuters reported that the Securities and Exchange Commission is exploring potential accounting issues at Nvidia, pushing the stock down further.
Once the most valuable company in the world, Nvidia now has a market cap of $3 trillion, putting it fourth behind Apple , Microsoft and Alphabet .
Nvidia is reeling from the removal of Huang, who resigned on Nov. 12, after multiple reported affairs , including one with a Chinese businesswoman who was allegedly a spy.
Harvey Jones, Nvidia's newly appointed board chair, said earlier this week that Huang had resigned after "disclosure of personal behavior inconsistent with the company's code of conduct, standards and cultural norms."
But the chipmaker's losing streak started before Nvidia was thrown into crisis as investors worried over the sustainability of the AI buildout, particularly after the midterm elections, and emerging competition in AI chips from Google and AMD.
Even a better-than-expected earnings report, which included an increase to fiscal 2028 guidance, didn't stem the selling. Interim CEO Colette Kress, the company's longtime CFO, projected revenue growth next fiscal year of 75%, and said that customers aren't going anywhere.
On Tuesday's earnings call with analysts, Kress signed off by saying, "we've got this." In a company meeting the next day, executives told staff that it was moving its yearly review process, which can come with more stock, from March to December.
For investors, one major question is whether Nvidia can continue to innovate and sustain its commanding lead in the AI chip market without its visionary leader. Almost the entire company now is built around the  AI trade, a phenomenon that began taking hold just four years ago with the launch of OpenAI's ChatGPT.
Before that, Nvidia's primary business was selling graphics cards used for video games. In mid-2008, the last time the stock was this deep into a weekly losing streak, Nvidia was generating less than $1 billion per quarter. Now it pulls in more than $1 billion per day. At the time, the entire market was in freefall due to the worst financial crisis since the Great Depression.
