articles.title_orig: Donald Trump seeks Ukraine peace deal before January
articles.title_zh: Donald Trump seeks Ukraine peace deal before January
articles.content_orig:
Xi, Putin and Trump outline priorities that include UN reform, boosting oil supplies and ‘protection of diplomatic immunity’
China, Russia and the US say they have agreed a peace statement after an unprecedented trilateral summit, but the declaration made no mention of the wars in Ukraine and Iran caused by two of the participants.
The declaration on Thursday also outlined a set of priorities that included changing the UN, boosting oil supplies and what it said was the protection of diplomatic immunity.
The statement affirmed that “a nuclear war cannot be won and must not be fought”, but stopped short of suggesting the beginnings of a framework for denuclearisation.
The meeting between Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump has dominated the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit this week, with China, the host, promising it would be “groundbreaking”.
“We are really making history,” Trump told Xi and Putin at the start of the meeting. “No peace was ever forged by declining opportunities for engagement.”
Putin told a press conference later that the three men had had a “free discussion” and now had a “mutual understanding”.
Some had hopes that the talks, which lasted about one hour and 20 minutes, could be used to discuss reductions in arms between the world’s three largest nuclear powers. Beijing has previously rebuffed Trump’s advances to join such talks, pointing to the larger US and Russian stockpiles. On Thursday, though, Xi called for nuclear weapons to “be completely prohibited and thoroughly destroyed over time to make the world free of [them]”.
The language of the declaration around nuclear war is the same as that previously issued by the five permanent members of the UN security council, which includes France and the UK.
“The real test will be whether the three countries follow through on their stated commitment to discuss nuclear risk reduction and preventing nuclear proliferation,” said Patricia Kim, an expert on Chinese foreign policy at the Brookings Institution, a US thinktank. Even the suggestion that China would engage was significant, said Yun Sun, a senior fellow at the Stimson Center.
Analysts had said that the meeting’s primary significance was in its optics. “Overall, very little of substance seems to have been accomplished … This summit appears to have been all about the symbolism and prestige value,” said Prof William Hurst, from the University of Cambridge’s Centre for Geopolitics. Putin pushed back at the suggestion the summit had just been a photo-op. “It is a serious collaborative work,” he said.
In the declaration, the men “committed themselves to maintaining strategic stability and international security”.
First among their concerns was “promoting UN reform so that it may respond more effectively to global challenges”. Sun said this was a favourite topic of China’s and showed that Beijing was “flexing its diplomatic muscles”. She said: “It is able to set the agenda and the deliverables according to its priorities … and make other great powers accept them.”
The declaration also agreed that “the international criminal court [ICC] and other similar institutions must not abuse their jurisdiction”. Putin is subject to an ICC arrest warrant and so the clause added to the perception that he has done well from the summit. Since the 2022 invasion of Ukraine, the Russian president has been treated as an international pariah by Kyiv’s allies and he has not been to an Apec summit in years.
Hurst said: “This was no Yalta moment, but it was certainly a solid public demonstration of Russia’s (and Putin’s) continuing relevance and power. It’s yet another example of Putin playing a poor hand to maximum effect.”
Xi, his status as a global power broker now assured, began the morning by addressing Apec leaders, reiterating the themes of trade openness and innovation he has emphasised throughout the summit. However, Apec affairs appeared to take a back seat for most of the day, with business dominating the discussions. For all the camaraderie on display, relations are complex. Russia is under US sanctions over the Ukraine war, while China and the US spent much of the last year engaged in an escalating tit-for-tat trade war before Trump and Xi called a truce .
Trump and Putin earlier held a separate meeting – their first since August 2025 – where the US president called his Russian counterpart his “friend”.
European allies meeting in Berlin to show their support for Ukraine expressed indignation at the cosy optics. “Mr Putin is not our friend and ⁠will never be,” the Polish prime minister, Donald Tusk, said in a rejoinder to Trump. The Danish prime minister, Mette Frederiksen, said she found it “very incomprehensible” that a US ​president would want to sit down with Putin.
The peace declaration in Shenzhen said the three countries planned “to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products for the benefit of all nations”. That was important, said Shan Guo from Hutong Research, a Shanghai-based advisory firm, but “now let’s see if the US will lift sanctions”.
Trump and Xi then held their third bilateral of this year. Xi said the US-China relationship was “generally stable and positive”, according to state media. But he cautioned Washington over Taiwan, saying the US “must keep doing the right thing to avoid major setbacks in US-China relations”.
Another watched-for topic lacking detailed findings was that of AI. Xi said the two countries should “enhance communication and coordination to guard against security risks … and ensure that AI remains under human control at all times”.
Ultimately, the lack of breakthroughs might suit China, which has no appetite to move beyond the role of convener, said Kim. “Beijing has little interest in taking on the diplomatic risks of brokering an actual peace agreement in Ukraine or resolving the conflict with Iran. That would entangle China in conflicts it would rather avoid,” she said.

articles.title_orig: Bending Spoons buys Mailchimp for $3.68B
articles.title_zh: Bending Spoons buys Mailchimp for $3.68B
articles.content_orig:
Bending Spoons has bought up another distressed internet company. This time, it’s the email marketing firm Mailchimp, bought for $3.68 billion from the tax-preparation giant Intuit.
Intuit acquired the company in 2021 for roughly $12 billion, so it’s taking quite a loss — and, perhaps, Bending Spoons is getting quite a bargain. At the time of the sale to Intuit, that acquisition caused headlines because Mailchimp employees reportedly received no equity, so no share of the sale proceeds, because the founders had allegedly promised them they didn’t need it as they would never sell.
Flash forward to now, with Intuit hit hard by the Death Star to SaaS trade — aka AI — with the company’s shares worth less than half what they were a year ago. The company told Reuters that the sale will let it sharpen its focus on AI tools for small businesses, and the new cash will be used to repurchase shares.
Bending Spoons describes the transaction as an all-cash deal, although that’s not quite true: As part of the same package, Intuit is buying $368 million in newly minted shares of Bending Spoons, so the net effect is a split of 90% cash to 10% stock.
Still, the transaction is a major pickup for Bending Spoons, which has become a kind of clearinghouse for late-stage web properties, with its game plan to hold them long term. In just the last year, the company has snapped up AOL, Eventbrite, Airtable, and Miro . Previous acquisitions include older stalwarts like Evernote, Meetup, and Vimeo. In each case, Bending Spoons integrated the products into centralized engineering and revenue systems, resulting in significant cost savings while often improving the available support and product resources.
“We want to place ourselves as an operator that takes beloved brands and makes them much better,” Bending Spoons co-founder and chief product officer, Matteo Danieli, told TechCrunch in July .

articles.title_orig: Valve says it might have to raise the price of supply-limited Steam Machines
articles.title_zh: Valve says it might have to raise the price of supply-limited Steam Machines
articles.content_orig:
When the Steam Machine first started shipping in June , Valve said it was producing fewer units at a higher price than initially planned because it couldn’t secure supplies of scarce RAM and storage components at a reasonable cost. Now, as the last of the initial batch of Steam Machine reservations are finally being fulfilled, Valve says those supply and cost issues will continue into the foreseeable future and may even require a price change.
“We are continuing to build more Steam Machine units, but memory and storage costs continue to increase at unprecedented levels,” Valve wrote in a blog post on Thursday . “As a result we don’t yet know the number we are able to make, and at what price we’ll be able to offer them. The 2TB model in particular will be especially constrained.”
If Valve does have to raise the price of the Steam Machine, it will be in good company. All three major console manufacturers instituted historically atypical price increases in 2025 , with additional price hikes happening this year.
For the Steam Machine, though, Valve may be more susceptible to supply-related price shocks than its larger competitors in the gaming hardware space. Valve “likely [doesn’t] have the same kind of priority as a Nintendo, Sony, or Microsoft when it comes to suppliers,” F-Squared analyst Michael Futter told us earlier this year . And while the bigger players can still negotiate somewhat with chip suppliers, Valve’s Steam Machine is “a niche product that cannot benefit in the same way when it comes to procurement,” Niko Partners analyst Daniel Ahmad said.
While Valve has not publicly discussed total Steam Machine sales, estimates based on public Steam Top Sellers charts suggest the company was selling 12,000 to 15,000 a week back in July. By contrast, the PS5 has averaged over 300,000 weekly unit sales worldwide in its roughly six years on the market.
For now, at least, Valve says it has fulfilled an expectation it set in July that “everyone in the reservation queue will have the option to purchase by the end of this year.” The company now says there is “no waitlist remaining” for the 512GB Steam Machine model and that “purchase invites” have been sent to the remaining randomized 2TB reservation holders (who placed orders back in April). The 512GB model was even briefly back in stock on the Steam Store yesterday, even as Valve continues to pare down the waitlist for 2TB stock.
Valve says it plans to release additional updates on Steam Machine availability in January.

articles.title_orig: Trump says Iran wants a deal, Saudi Arabia and Yemen's Houthis exchange fire and other Mideast news
articles.title_zh: Trump says Iran wants a deal, Saudi Arabia and Yemen's Houthis exchange fire and other Mideast news
articles.content_orig:
"We want to make a real deal, not a fake deal," Trump said.
Talks between the U.S. and Iran remain stalled despite the two countries signing a memorandum of understanding in June, aimed at ending the war that began with joint American-Israeli strikes on the country in February. The opening strikes killed a host of top Iranian officials and commanders, among them Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.
The two sides have continued to exchange strikes, though have not returned to the intense fighting seen in the early stages of the conflict. The U.S. says it is enforcing a naval blockade of the country's Persian Gulf and Gulf of Oman ports, while Iran claims control over the strategic Strait of Hormuz and continues to claim attacks on shipping transiting the waterway.
Meanwhile, intensified fighting between Saudi-backed Yemeni forces and Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen has seen the latter repeatedly attack Saudi military, oil infrastructure and transport facilities.
See the most recent developments below.
Saudi Arabia and the Iranian-backed Houthis in Yemen continued to exchange escalating threats and strikes on Friday, according to both sides.
The Iranian-backed Houthis in Yemen threatened a Saudi power station and Red Sea ports, including Jeddah, according to statements from the Houthis.
Recently, the Houthis struck inside of Riyadh’s financial center, causing damage to the Public Investment Fund tower, the headquarters of Saudi Arabia’s sovereign wealth fund and Riyadh’s tallest skyscraper, Saudi Arabia's Civil Defense confirmed.
"We declare that the financial center in King Abdullah Economic City in Riyadh, the capital of the enemy Saudi Arabia, is a military target for our forces. Therefore, we call on all employees, workers, and citizens to stay away from it immediately," the Houthis warned in a statement.
This incident comes after the Saudi-led coalition said it hit the Houthi-held Hodeidah port and Sanaa.
The Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted and destroyed Houthi missiles and military targets in alerts Friday.
In a security alert, Maritime security firm Marisks warned that the announcements represent a "significant escalation in Houthi threats."
"The announcements represent a significant escalation in Houthi threats against Saudi maritime and energy infrastructure, reinforcing the maritime restrictions previously declared against Saudi-affiliated shipping on July 20th. The possibility of attacks against Saudi ports, energy installations and Saudi-owned, managed or affiliated vessels operating in the Red Sea remains elevated," Marisks wrote.
President Donald Trump vowed to never let Iran have a nuclear weapon, referencing George H. W. Bush, while giving a press conference at the White House Friday.
"We're not going to let them have a nuclear weapon. Iran, I say it, I'll say it now -- and I'm not George Bush -- Watch my lips. No, you don't have to watch my lips. But Iran will never have a nuclear weapon, ever," Trump said.
While accepting the nomination at the 1988 Republican National Convention, Bush famously said the phrase: "Read my lips: no new taxes."
Asked about his statement blaming Republican midterm losses on the war with Iran, Vice President JD Vance said his role is to support the president.
Asked whether the war with Iran was worth losing the majority in the Senate, Vance said, "I think the president is the one who makes the decision, and the president has said he would do it again. And my view is that, my goal is and my job is to support the president of the United States."
"The goal of keeping Iran from getting a nuclear weapon is absolutely what we need to be doing. It's the biggest state sponsor of terrorism. If they had a nuclear weapon, they would use it as leverage or God forbid, they would attack, and kill thousands, hundreds of thousands, potentially, of innocent people," Vance told reporters at a press conference at the White House.
President Donald Trump said that the war with Iran drove up fuel prices "far less" than he thought it would.
"The war drove up prices, fuel prices far less than I thought. I thought it would go up to $300 a barrel. It's almost down to $80 a barrel right now," Trump said during a press conference at the White House Friday.
Asked about a statement from Vice President JD Vance that blamed Republican midterm losses on the war with Iran, Trump denied being "unhappy" with that statement.
"I thought the statement was fine, except I would have had one other thing that if we're asked, I would have said 'Would you do it again?' And absolutely. The answer is yes, because we cannot allow Iran to have a nuclear weapon," Trump said.

articles.title_orig: What is the EU-UK youth experience scheme and when will it start?
articles.title_zh: What is the EU-UK youth experience scheme and when will it start?
articles.content_orig:
Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
Britain is set to allow 100,000 young European citizens to come to the UK every year as part of a repurposed deal being finalised with the EU, it’s been reported.
Talks between UK and EU negotiators were “going down to the wire”, No 10 said hours before Friday’s summit, at which Andy Burnham hopes to agree closer ties with Brussels.
The UK has provisionally agreed to potentially double the number of EU youngsters coming in under a youth mobility scheme , according to The Guardian .
The cap on numbers will rise from the 50,000-80,000 at present up to 100,000. It was also agreed to raise the age limit from 30 to 31.
The number of young British people allowed to go to the EU will be at least matched but could some countries, including Germany, could take unlimited numbers each year.
Both sides were on Thursday still thrashing out details of the UK’s role in shaping future European food and farming rules.
The prime minister wants a closer relationship with the European Union but has ruled out a return to the single market, customs union or freedom of movement.
His press secretary said Brexit had done more harm than good.
Mr Burnham is due within hours to sign new agreements on food and energy as well as youth mobility.
Sources said the UK was still resisting pressure from the EU on tuition fees for European students coming to Britain under the youth mobility scheme.
The prime minister’s press secretary said: “The talks with the EU are going down to the wire.
“If we secure a deal, the government will bring forward legislation to Parliament next week.
“There is a consensus in the country that change needs to happen.”
He continued: “Brexit has done more harm than good.
“The cost of living has risen, it’s harder for British people to travel and businesses to trade, and the small boats crisis has reached our shores.
“We ended up with a harder Brexit than was promised at the referendum. The hard Brexit that was negotiated has impacted people’s everyday lives, longer queues at the airport and young people missing out on the chance to live, work or study abroad.”
He said Russia posed a much more direct threat to European security.
It’s feared the agreement will prevent the UK from banning imports of foie gras – cruelly produced geese and duck livers – a move that, before the 2024 general election, Labour had pledged to do.
Abigail Penny, executive director of Animal Equality UK, said: “Force-feeding is a crime in the UK, yet we continue to allow foie gras to reach our shores.”
The charity’s hopes of a ban have been repeatedly dashed by successive governments . Campaigners had said any ban would be a Brexit benefit.
Tory leader Kemi Badenoch said Labour’s talks with Brussels would take the UK backwards on control of money, laws and borders.
Mr Burnham has raised hopes that Friday’s summit could mean “a really big win potentially” on a “Channel action plan” to tackle small boat crossings .
Asked whether Britain could still walk away from a deal, Mr Burnham said: “There would always be those circumstances because I’m in this to get the best deal for Britain, always.
“But what’s in it for us? There’s the possibility of lower food prices, and I can’t turn my back on that. Lower costs for business, cutting red tape.
“And a really big win potentially – more collaboration on immigration, a Channel action plan, which is a really big deal if we can land that tomorrow.”
He said recent polling showed 73 per cent of Britons favoured closer ties with Europe.
Asked about foie gras, a government spokesperson told The Independent : “We are negotiating a food and drink deal that will slash red tape and costly paperwork, make it easier and cheaper to export seafood, boost the British economy by up to £5 billion a year, and back British businesses and jobs.
“We are working closely with businesses to ensure a smooth transition so they can make the most of the benefits this deal unlocks.”

articles.title_orig: Poland condemns Russian 'provocation' after three airspace violations
articles.title_zh: Poland condemns Russian 'provocation' after three airspace violations
articles.content_orig:
Poland has said Russia violated its airspace three times overnight, in what Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said was a “provocation” by Moscow.
Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz told a news conference on Friday that investigations were under way at three locations – Nowy Lipowiec, roughly 60km (37 miles) from the Poland-Ukraine border, Molodycz, about 50km (31 miles) to the south, and Rudnik nad Sanem, about 50km to the west.
Kosiniak-Kamysz added that the three objects were probably two missiles and a drone.
The incursions were reported as Poland held military exercises involving the “ Coalition of the Willing “, a group of European countries coordinating help and support for Ukraine.
The potential crash site near Nowy Lipowiec is about 76km (47 miles) from where European troops were taking part in military exercises to prepare for a potential post-war mission in Ukraine, aimed at helping to stabilise the country and rebuild its military once the war ends.
“These exercises, combined with the presence of defence ministers from France, the United Kingdom, and the Baltic states – along with eight chiefs of staff, including those from our key allies – suggest that the convergence of these events is no accident,” Kosiniak-Kamysz said.
The defence minister said Poland would ask NATO for more support securing the alliance’s eastern flank.
NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte said in a post on X that the incident was “clearly dangerous” and that NATO stood in solidarity with Poland.
Tusk said Rutte would visit Warsaw on Saturday. The Polish prime minister added that there was no doubt the objects that landed in Poland were Russian.
“It seems we are dealing with an intentional provocation,” he said. “Today, it is clearer than ever before that ⁠Poland must participate in decisions and discussions regarding the future of Ukraine and security in Europe.”
British ⁠Prime Minister Andy Burnham condemned Russia’s violation of Polish airspace, calling it “utterly ⁠unacceptable”.
“Europe will not be ⁠deterred from our support for Ukraine,” he said at an EU-UK summit news conference in ‌Brussels. “We will not allow [Russian President Vladimir] Putin to divide our continent, and ‌we recognise that the front line in Ukraine is the front line for freedom and democracy everywhere.”
Drones have repeatedly strayed into the airspace of countries on NATO’s eastern flank during Russia’s war in Ukraine, fuelling tension with the Western military alliance and stoking fears that the conflict ⁠could spread.
The incident in Poland came against the backdrop of Russian attacks in Ukraine that killed eight people, injured dozens more and damaged bridges and transport infrastructure.

articles.title_orig: The Nasdaq Is In Its Third Correction of 2026. Here’s the Lesson Most Investors Are Missing.
articles.title_zh: The Nasdaq Is In Its Third Correction of 2026. Here’s the Lesson Most Investors Are Missing.
articles.content_orig:
By Matt Frankel, CFP® – Nov 20, 2026 at 11:02AM EST
10 stocks we like better ›
The stock market has had a rough November. The Nasdaq Composite closed more than 10% below its Oct. 6 record on Nov. 16, which put it back in correction territory. The tech-heavy Nasdaq-100 has fallen even further and now sits about 15% below its October high.
Corrections, typically defined as declines of 10% or more from recent highs, historically have occurred about once a year. However, this is already the Nasdaq's third correction of 2026. That might sound alarming, but the first two have a valuable lesson to teach investors.
Image source: Getty Images.
In March, the war with Iran and rising oil prices pushed the Nasdaq Composite to a close of 20,795 on March 30, down more than 13% from its previous record. By June 1, the index had climbed to a new record of 27,190, about 31% above its March low.
The second correction came in July as chip stocks sold off. The Nasdaq closed at approximately 24,443 on July 29, just over 10% below its June high. By Oct. 6, the index had hit another record just below 27,600, roughly 13% above its July low.
In both cases, investors who sold during the correction locked in losses and missed a rebound. Volatility like this is the price of admission for owning growth stocks, and a correction doesn't automatically mean the bull market is over.
In short, the best time to plan for a correction is before it happens. Make sure any money you'll need in the next few years isn't in stocks, keep your regular contributions going, and keep a list of businesses you'd love to own at lower prices. Those steps won't make a correction painless, but they make it far less likely that you'll sell at the worst possible time. A diversified portfolio also helps take some of the sting out of sell-offs like this one.
To be sure, there's no guarantee this correction ends the same way as the other two. This one is driven by fears about AI spending and leadership changes at major tech companies, as well as by the Federal Reserve, which is widely expected to raise interest rates in December. I'm confident that the Nasdaq will eventually make a new all-time high, but there's no way of knowing when the rebound will happen, how gradual or sharp it will be, or whether things will get significantly worse before they get better.
Having said all that, three corrections in a single year, with two all-time highs in between them, should remind investors that sell-offs are a normal part of the process. Each of this year's corrections has been a test of patience rather than a read on the market's long-term direction, and I expect this one to be no different.

articles.title_orig: Anti-migrant activist Daniel Thomas jailed for slashing migrant dinghy
articles.title_zh: Anti-migrant activist Daniel Thomas jailed for slashing migrant dinghy
articles.content_orig:
Anti-migrant activist Daniel Thomas has been jailed for 15 months for slashing a dinghy with a knife in the English Channel.
The 37-year-old, known to his supporters as Danny Tommo, live-streamed himself cutting the boat while a French rescue worker was on board in September.
Sentencing him after he admitted criminal damage, a judge called Thomas a "publicity seeker" whose actions were a "flagrant interference" with the work of rescue crews.
His barrister argued it was an act of "performative activism" rather than a "political crime" and said nobody had been put in danger.
Thomas founded the anti-migrant group Patriot Platform, which was behind protests in Portsmouth and Dover involving masked men in September.
He appeared at Portsmouth Crown Court by video link from HMP Winchester, and sat with his head in his hands for much of the hearing.
The court heard he had watched migrants being taken off the dinghy by the RNLI, Border Force and the French Coastguard on 22 September, before telling those on his boat to steer towards it.
He said "let's get rid of that boat" before slashing it about eight times, the court heard.
It had previously been reported that Thomas said "this is what needs to happen to everyone in these boats" in his live-stream of the incident, but the court heard on Friday that he said "this is what needs to happen to every one of these boats".
Earlier in the footage, Thomas told viewers "no violence, nothing like that" and urged them to "share this everywhere".
He gave a postcode in Gosport, which the judge said he believed was to "encourage protest".
After slashing the boat, he shouted at the rescue worker: "Get off the boat, you've got time to get off the boat," the court heard.
Joel Smith KC, prosecuting, said it was "more a matter of luck than judgement that serious consequences did not arise".
The dinghy was later destroyed by French authorities, meaning the value of the damage could not be proven.
Judge James Newton-Price KC said it was "not for me to make any judgement of the political cause," but that the attack was "intended to have an impact on a live audience".
Commenting on the Border Force, coastguard and RNLI crews, he said: "They do necessary, highly sensitive and difficult jobs, which should not be disrupted by a publicity-seeker slashing with a knife a boat they were attempting to recover."
Simon Pentol KC, defending, said the dinghy did not sink and made its way back to France without help.
The judge accepted that prison had caused hardship for Thomas's family, including his four children. He said the sentence would have been 20 months had he gone to trial, and his time on remand would count towards it.
A separate charge of failing to give police the PIN to his phone, which Thomas denied, was ordered to lie on his file.
He is due to stand trial at Westminster Magistrates' Court in June over separate alleged offences in Dover, which he denies.

articles.title_orig: ILO and China reaffirm commitment to South-South cooperation for decent work and social justice
articles.title_zh: ILO and China reaffirm commitment to South-South cooperation for decent work and social justice
articles.content_orig:
12th Joint Committee Meeting reviews progress and explores new opportunities to strengthen cooperation on employment, skills, social protection and emerging challenges in the world of work.
GENEVA (ILO News) – The International Labour Organization (ILO) and China’s Ministry of Human Resources and Social Security (MOHRSS) have reaffirmed their commitment to advancing decent work and social justice through South-South cooperation, with a focus on emerging labour-market challenges and partnerships across the Global South.
The commitment was highlighted at the 12th Joint Committee Meeting on ILO–China Cooperation, held in Geneva on 20 November 2026. The meeting reviewed progress since the previous Joint Committee Meeting in 2021 and explored opportunities to deepen cooperation.
The discussions took place against a backdrop of rapid technological change, persistent labour-market inequalities and the need to accelerate progress towards the Sustainable Development Goals.
Participants underscored the importance of translating development cooperation into practical improvements focusing on areas of longstanding cooperation including employment opportunities, skills and social protection.
Since 2021, China-supported ILO initiatives have contributed to strengthening institutional capacity, policy exchange and knowledge sharing, particularly across countries in the Asia-Pacific region.
Cooperation in skills development has supported training institutions and responses to growing demand for digital, green and industry-relevant skills. Employment initiatives have promoted high-quality and full employment, stronger public employment services, entrepreneurship and regional policy dialogue. In social protection, cooperation has supported efforts to expand coverage and improve service delivery, including through digital transformation.
Participants emphasized the importance of building on these achievements, sharing good practices and strengthening national institutions to ensure sustainable results.
Looking ahead, discussions explored how South-South cooperation could help countries navigate changes in the world of work, particularly those associated with artificial intelligence and the platform economy.
Participants considered opportunities to harness technological innovation for productivity and employment while addressing potential risks for workers and enterprises. They also highlighted the importance of connecting country-level initiatives with regional and global policy dialogue to broaden the impact of development cooperation.
The meeting further considered the role of the ILO–China partnership within wider development frameworks including the Global Development Initiative (GDI) and the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI). China’s presidency of the BRICs in 2027 will also offer an important opportunity to advance cooperation on various world of work issues.
China has been a member of the ILO since its founding and has developed a longstanding partnership with the Organization. The ILO–China cooperation framework encompasses employment promotion, skills development, social protection, occupational safety and health, and South-South cooperation. Through technical cooperation, policy dialogue and knowledge exchange, the partnership supports countries in advancing decent work and meeting the Sustainable Development Goals.

China’s crude oil imports from the Persian Gulf surged by 42.4% in October from September, to the highest level since the Iran war began, as supply via the Strait of Hormuz rebounded and Gulf producers slashed prices for their crude to attract buyers amid record-high freight rates.
China imported 19.7 million tons of crude oil from the Persian Gulf producers, excluding Iran, in October, a 42.4% jump from the previous month, per calculations by the South China Morning Post based on Chinese customs data released on Friday.
October was the fourth consecutive month in which Chinese crude oil imports from the Gulf countries increased from the previous month, according to the data.
Gulf producers shipped almost half of total Chinese term supplies last month, at a level approaching the pre-war volumes, the estimates by the South China Morning Post showed.
The surge in Chinese imports from the Gulf coincided with the recovery of crude oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz.
Additionally, Gulf producers reduced the prices of their crude grades loading for Asia as Hormuz flows rebounded and pressured down Middle Eastern crude benchmarks.
Rising supply from the Middle East has weakened both the Dubai and Murban prices. At the end October, the prices of physical Middle East crude slumped as flows from the region recovered and reached pre-war levels on some days.
Lower prices for December are expected to continue attracting buying interest in China, especially amid the slide in international crude oil prices.
Saudi oil giant Aramco earlier this month slashed the price for its flagship Arab Light crude for Asia for loading in December by $2 per barrel, to a discount of $6.50 per barrel to the Oman/Dubai average. This is the steepest discount for Saudi crude to the Middle East’s benchmark since May 2020 during the COVID pandemic.

Nvidia shares were on track to post a seven-day losing streak if losses hold till market close on Friday.
The company's market capitalization has dropped about 41% from its early October peak.
Nvidia held the top spot among U.S. companies for much of the year before its recent decline in market value.
Nvidia's (NVDA) market capitalization fell behind Alphabet's (GOOG, GOOGL) in morning trade on Friday, making it the fourth most valuable U.S. company.
NVDA stock was down 4.6% in morning trading, extending a seven-day losing streak and hitting a fresh 16-month low, while GOOGL stock rose around 2.5%. Alphabet's market value was $3.44 trillion at the time of writing, against $3.41 trillion for Nvidia, a gap of about $30 billion.
Nvidia's market value peaked near $5.7 trillion in early October, and is now about 41% below that level.
U.S. equities were mixed in morning trade on Friday. The SPDR S&P 500 ETF (SPY) was down 0.76%, the SPDR Dow Jones Industrial Average ETF (DIA) gained 0.36%, while the Nasdaq-100 tracking Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ) plummeted over 2%. Micron Technology (MU) declined 9.5%, while Broadcom (AVGO) and Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) fell more than 7%.

Apple (AAPL) remained the most valuable U.S. company, with a market capitalization of about $5.08 trillion, according to Koyfin. Microsoft (MSFT) ranked second at $3.73 trillion, followed by Alphabet and Nvidia.
Amazon (AMZN) ranked fifth, with a market value of approximately $2.80 trillion, around $615 billion below Nvidia.

articles.title_orig: Ex-Super Micro exec married to Nvidia’s former sales chief says she took CEO job days before smuggling scandal broke
articles.title_zh: Ex-Super Micro exec married to Nvidia’s former sales chief says she took CEO job days before smuggling scandal broke
articles.content_orig:
A little-known figure in the palace intrigue involving Nvidia’s Jensen Huang and possible chip smuggling is rapidly gaining attention. Ying Cenly Chen, a former senior executive at Super Micro Computer , is alleged to have managed a significant portion of the company’s purchases of Nvidia chips during the period when Supermicro’s hardware was allegedly diverted to China, according to a lawsuit. Her new company, ChronoScale, where Chen serves as CEO, has business ties to both Supermicro and Nvidia.
Chen matters because of her position at Supermicro and because of when she left. A shareholder lawsuit claims that Chen, 50, controlled Supermicro’s supply of Nvidia chips and could not have been unaware of the company’s alleged illicit sales. She exited Supermicro within weeks of an indictment that named Supermicro co-founder, Yih-Shyan “Wally” Liaw in the smuggling scheme. She is also married to Ajay “Jay” Puri, Nvidia’s longtime sales chief, Chen confirmed to Fortune . Puri worked for the chipmaker for two decades before announcing his retirement in June.
That means Chen could hold some answers to the question now looming large above Nvidia, which is whether Huang, who resigned as CEO on Nov. 11, knew or turned a blind eye as its chips were potentially diverted to China. And it puts a spotlight on her role at ChronoScale, which develops datacenters that rely heavily on Nvidia chips.
Chen disputes the lawsuit’s account. In emails to Fortune , she said controlling customer allocations of Nvidia chips “was not part of my job responsibility” when she worked at Supermicro. Supermicro also denied that she controlled how its supply of Nvidia GPUs were distributed.
Chen also said she agreed to join ChronoScale before the Supermicro smuggling scandal broke. She told Fortune she accepted the offer on March 10 via DocuSign , nine days before the Liaw indictment was unsealed on March 19. She said the “offer documentation was completed on April 24” and her last day at Supermicro was April 30. That timing would mean Chen remained as chief growth officer at Supermicro for seven weeks after she said she accepted the ChronoScale job, and for six weeks after the indictment.
Liaw, the Supermicro cofounder, was arrested and indicted with two others in a sweeping $2.5 billion smuggling case in March. Liaw has pleaded not guilty; one of his codefendants, Ting-Wei “Willy” Sun, has pleaded guilty. On a May 5 earnings call , days after Chen’s departure, Supermicro CEO Charles Liang told analysts that “no one” at the company other than the three who had been indicted were involved in the alleged scheme. That declaration, which stunned some observers, came while the Supermicro board was still engaged in an ongoing investigation directors launched following Liaw’s arrest. Under typical circumstances, Liang as CEO and co-founder who knew Liaw for three decades, wouldn’t have been closely involved in an independent board-led investigation, particularly one that was ongoing at the time.
Neither Liang nor Supermicro have been named as targets in the alleged scheme, and Supermicro has said it is itself a victim and is cooperating with authorities. ChronoScale has also not been named by regulators as the target of any investigation. Puri and Nvidia declined to comment. A Supermicro spokesperson denied that Chen controlled how Nvidia GPUs were distributed to customers and said that after 18 years at Supermicro, Chen “voluntarily resigned in early 2026 to take the CEO role at ChronoScale.”
It wasn’t until August that the Supermicro board’s investigation officially concluded with a finding that the investigation team “did not find any evidence that any current member of senior management had knowledge” about the alleged scheme. By that time, Chen had landed as CEO of ChronoScale, an AI cloud company based in Silicon Valley formed on May 5, 2026, when data-center developer Applied Digital merged its GPU cloud subsidiary, Applied Digital Cloud, into Ekso Bionics Holdings, a Nasdaq-listed maker of robotic exoskeletons. The combined company renamed itself ChronoScale and Applied Digital owns about 96% of it.
Now, a shareholder complaint filed in October has cast a cloud over Chen herself. In a complaint filed Oct. 9 in federal court in San Francisco, former Supermicro employees who are not named allege that Chen controlled Supermicro’s supply of Nvidia chips and that she left because of the U.S. government’s smuggling investigation. Chen is not a defendant in the lawsuit, she has not been charged or accused of wrongdoing by any government agency, and the allegations are unproven.
The lawsuit is a securities class action brought by investors who say Supermicro, Liang and other executives misled them about company sales and export compliance while servers were being allegedly diverted illegally to China, and that they lost money when the March indictment by federal prosecutors in Manhattan sent the stock tanking.
Chen worked at Supermicro from March 2008 to April 2026 and was most recently its chief growth officer and a senior vice president, according to ChronoScale’s filings. According to Chronoscale’s website, she graduated with a Bachelor’s Degree in Science from Fudan University, a public university in Shanghai. The shareholder complaint describes her as a force inside Supermicro who “reported directly to” Liang and led a sales team that it says accounted for “approximately 80% of the company’s total sales.”
One former employee quoted in the lawsuit, described as a Supermicro sales director from July 2023 to July 2025, said Chen “had a very close relationship with Nvidia and managed the company’s acquisition of GPU chips from Nvidia.” Because the supply was limited and in such demand, the former employee said Nvidia “would allocate a certain number to Super Micro, and Chen decided how to distribute them among Super Micro’s customers.” Chen met routinely with Liang “to obtain Liang’s approval of how the chips would be allocated,” according to the complaint.
Supermicro disputes this allegation. “Cenly Chen did not control how Nvidia GPUs were distributed to customers,” the spokesperson said.
A second former employee in the lawsuit, described as a sales director who worked at Supermicro until 2024, said Chen “handled all allocations of Nvidia chips to Super Micro” and had taken over responsibility for the sales team that covered China. The person said “there was no way Cenly Chen lacked knowledge of the company’s illicit sales.”
The complaint also offers an account of why Chen left. The first former employee claimed that Chen’s emails had created a potentially problematic paper trail: “It was widely known within the company that Chen had to leave because she had sent emails requesting that Nvidia release chips with serial numbers associated with the GPUs illegally diverted to customers in China.” Citing the former employee, the complaint also states she “resigned so that the company could claim that no current employees were involved in the scheme for which Liaw was arrested.”
Chen disputes the account.
“I do not believe this email exists, as I would never knowingly do such a thing and I don’t believe I ever did,” Chen told Fortune . Both former employees had left Supermicro before Chen did, according to the complaint’s own description of their tenures, and it does not say how they learned the circumstances of her departure.
ChronoScale was created on May 5, when Applied Digital’s cloud business merged into Ekso Bionics Holdings, a public company. Chen’s hiring was not disclosed in securities filings before then. The offer letter ChronoScale filed with the SEC is dated May 5 and shows Chen’s acceptance dated April 24.
On April 3, more than three weeks after Chen says she accepted the job, Ekso mailed its shareholders an information statement describing the planned merger. It listed “the directors and executive officers of ChronoScale following the Business Combination” and named neither Chen

articles.title_orig: Ex-GM CEO on Mary Barra succession planning: 'It's going to be tough'
articles.title_zh: Ex-GM CEO on Mary Barra succession planning: 'It's going to be tough'
articles.content_orig:
Former General Motors CEO and Chairman Dan Akerson doesn't mince words when asked about the challenges the automaker faces in finding a successor for GM CEO Mary Barra : "It's going to be tough."
He should know. The 78-year-old businessman and U.S. Navy veteran helped with his own succession planning and recommended to GM's board in 2013 that Barra replace him as CEO. She has held the top job since Jan. 15, 2014.
Akerson said Barra will be hard to replace, citing her success and prominence as the first female CEO of any major automaker and the ongoing challenges facing the automotive industry, such as artificial intelligence , vehicle digitalization, and the rise of China and autonomous vehicles.
"It's going to be very, very dynamic," Akerson told CNBC during a phone interview. "It's going to be a big change."
Akerson declined to discuss potential internal candidates such as GM Chief Product Officer Sterling Anderson , CFO Paul Jacobson or President Mark Reuss, but he said the eventual successor needs to be dynamic and, if from the outside, "adaptable."
His comments to CNBC follow a Wall Street Journal report on Tuesday that GM is working with an executive search firm to identify possible outside candidates to succeed Barra, in addition to internal prospects. GM declined to comment on the report or Barra's succession.
Akerson, who came to GM as an outsider from The Carlyle Group in 2010, said selecting an outside candidate might be risky if there are already executives within the organization who have similar leadership and technical expertise.
"Is there anybody in the organization that has that background that you know better day to day over a period of time? You may be taking a risk by bringing in an outsider," he said.
The prospect of an outsider leading GM would be unusual in the auto industry, where major automakers have generally promoted internal CEO candidates, apart from periods of exceptional disruption such as the Great Recession.
Stellantis , BMW , Toyota Motor , Nissan Motor and Hyundai Motor have all appointed internal executives to their CEO positions in recent years.
Barra has said several times that her successor and her longevity in the role would be determined by the board.
A notable influence is likely Hewlett Packard veteran Patricia Russo, GM's longest-serving board member who has been on the board since 2009 and leads its CEO succession planning as independent lead director.
GM's CEO succession planning is done "at least annually," according to the company's yearly proxy filing. That process includes Barra providing the board "with recommendations for, and evaluations of, potential CEO successors and discusses developmental plans for these successors," according to the filing.
That is followed by board members engaging "with CEO candidates and senior management talent at Board and committee meetings and other forums to enable directors to personally assess candidates."
When Akerson was preparing to retire, Barra was among a pool of four candidates — two longtime GM employees and two relative newcomers — who were finalists for CEO in 2013, he said.
Akerson said he put the finalists through an extended evaluation, asking how they viewed GM's strengths and weaknesses, how they would organize the company, and their willingness to work together, potentially with other CEO candidates who didn't get the job.
Akerson said the final decision to appoint Barra was done at a day-and-a-half-long board meeting in Washington. The candidate field was narrowed to Barra and former GM executive Dan Ammann , an ex-Wall Street banker who was GM's CFO before leaving the automaker's Cruise unit, reportedly over a disagreement in strategy with Barra, in 2021.
"Mary's very deserving of all the accolades she's received," Akerson said. "She's done a terrific job."
Barra has been leading the automaker for nearly 13 years, which makes her the longest-serving CEO of the automaker since Alfred Sloan retired after a 23-year career as CEO in 1946.
Akerson said he believes that, like he did, Barra will have major influence in picking her successor. He described that dynamic as integral to continuing her legacy leading the automaker.
"This is important. I think if she doesn't pick the right person, in four or five years from now and things are back in the trough, that will tarnish her history. But I think she'll pick the right one," he said.

articles.title_orig: ‘The deal is done’: EU, UK agree to reset relations 10 years after Brexit
articles.title_zh: ‘The deal is done’: EU, UK agree to reset relations 10 years after Brexit
articles.content_orig:
The European Union has struck a deal on three policy areas with the United Kingdom in a move seen as the start of a reset of relations a decade after the Brexit vote.
After a summit in Brussels on Friday, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s office said negotiations have concluded and a reset ⁠deal has been sealed.
“This is a good day for Britain. This is a good day for Europe, and people across Europe and across the United Kingdom will get real benefit,” Burnham had told EU chiefs Ursula von der Leyen and Antonio Costa at the start of the talks.
Downing Street said ‌both sides agreed timelines for implementing a youth mobility scheme, a sanitary and phytosanitary agreement, ⁠and a link ⁠between their emissions trading systems. Details are due ⁠to be published ⁠in a ⁠joint statement.
A UK government spokesperson told Al Jazeera: “The deal is done. Negotiations have concluded. Now both sides will work towards implementation.
“As with all international agreements, there is a legal process in each respective country which will now take place,” the spokesperson added. “And talks will continue on some areas.”
Burnham said the deals could add 0.5 percent to Britain’s economy.
The arrangement to reduce controls on the movement of animals, plants and related products between the UK and EU is worth an estimated 5.1 billion pounds ($6.7bn) to the British economy.
The agreement linking emissions trading systems will exempt British and EU goods, such as steel, from each other’s border carbon levies.
The youth mobility scheme will allow 100,000 young Europeans to live and work in the UK for up to three years, and vice versa.
Despite the agreements, months or years of negotiations lie ahead for a deeper reset in relations to take effect.
Burnham has previously told the British public all options should be on the table for future relations, including rejoining the now-27-nation EU.
However, he has stressed that reversing Brexit is just one possible outcome and far from imminent.
That possibility and the agreements sealed so far will incur anger from the significant section of the British public that remains eurosceptic.
Nigel Farage, leader of the populist right-wing Reform UK party, called Burnham “naive” following the news of the agreements.
The EU has used this moment to “strong-arm the British prime minister”, he claimed. “It’s the same old game, and he’s fallen for it out of sheer inexperience,” Farage wrote on social media.

articles.title_orig: SpaceX’s subsidiary Cursor tells lawmakers it's considering phasing out Chinese AI models
articles.title_zh: SpaceX’s subsidiary Cursor tells lawmakers it's considering phasing out Chinese AI models
articles.content_orig:
SpaceX's artificial-intelligence coding platform, Cursor, is considering moving away from using of Chinese AI models due to "geopolitical risk," CNBC has learned.
Cursor, which SpaceX acquired at an implied $60 billion equity value in August, had built its coding model Composer 2 on top of Chinese lab Moonshot AI's Kimi K2.5.
It's among the U.S. firms that have adopted Chinese models, whose usage has spiked across the globe this year, worrying lawmakers in Washington . The battle for AI supremacy between the U.S. and China has reached new heights in 2026 as Chinese models have improved.
But now Cursor plans to "explore phasing out PRC [People's Republic of China]-developed open-weight models because of geopolitical risk," according to a report produced by the House Committee on Homeland Security and the House Select Committee on China, shared exclusively with CNBC ahead of its publication on Friday.
The report, which follows a months-long investigation into the adoption of Chinese AI models into the American tech stack, said Cursor "informed the Committees" of those plans. Airbnb and DoorDash also engaged with the investigation about their use of Chinese AI models.
SpaceX announced it entered into a formal agreement to buy Cursor in June; the deal was completed in August. SpaceX is developing the Grok family of models, which Cursor has been involved in training.
Cursor, SpaceX and DoorDash did not respond to a CNBC request for comment. Airbnb declined to comment. The U.S. Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The report found that cost, customization and near-frontier performance of Chinese AI models were driving adoption, with the U.S. lacking a competitive open-weight alternative at "price and performance the market demands."
"Beijing is now seeking to turn those technological gains into global market share and long-term dependence," the report says. China's embassy in the U.K. did not respond to a request for comment. China's Foreign Ministry did not immediately respond.
It also sets out recommendations to address the issues it has identified.
Those include launching a "national American open-weight initiative" that combines public computing power, shared evaluation infrastructure and "lawful access" to American frontier models for training.
The report also says an order, made public in October, that banned DeepSeek from federal civilian agency systems, should be built on, by prohibiting the use of "PRC-developed AI models" in federal information systems and in performance of federal contracts.
Separately, Washington is also concerned about Chinese companies accessing Nvidia chips remotely , via overseas data centers, and gaining ground by using " distillation ," where new models use older, more established ones to help train them.
The U.S. Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, or BIS, announced on Monday an interim final rule designed to prevent Chinese companies' remote access to AI chips.

articles.title_orig: Russian missile hits Poland as Ukraine's allies hold military exercise, says Tusk
articles.title_zh: Russian missile hits Poland as Ukraine's allies hold military exercise, says Tusk
articles.content_orig:
Poland says a Russian cruise missile was among three objects that violated its airspace early on Friday, with Prime Minister Donald Tusk saying it did not appear to be an accident when Western military exercises were taking place in the region.
Nobody was hurt and no damage has been reported, but Warsaw described the incident as a "provocation" from Moscow.
Russia has made no comment about the violations, which took place during one of its biggest aerial attacks on Ukraine since the start of the full-scale invasion in 2022.
Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said the Kh-101 missile hit a rural area at Nowy Lipowiec in southeastern Poland about 50km (31 miles) from the Ukrainian border.
The cruise missile, designed for precision targets, crashed at about 06:30 (5:30GMT) and Natalie Szponar, a local resident, said she was getting her children ready for school when she heard a "whistle and a dull impact".
The moment of impact was caught by a camera on a farm, and officials later made clear there was no risk to residents.
Another suspected missile went down near Rudnik nad Sanem to the west of Nowy Lipowiec, and a jet-powered drone crashed to the south near Mołodycz, said Kosiniak-Kamysz.
He called the incursion into Polish airspace a "provocation" from Russia and said he would be asking Nato for additional support.
Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte condemned "grave violations of Polish airspace" and said Nato jets had been scrambled in response. "This incident is clearly dangerous - a consequence of Russia's ongoing war against Ukraine," said Rutte, who was due to visit Warsaw on Saturday.
A UK- and France-led exercise called Koalicja 2026 is currently taking place in southeastern Poland involving 11 countries that are part of the West's Coalition of the Willing group in preparation for a potential peace deal in Ukraine.
"It is no coincidence that these objects landed near the site where military manoeuvres by a 'coalition of the willing' supported by Polish troops are taking place in Nowa Dęba," Tusk told reporters on Friday.
UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting, who was visiting Poland on Friday, said: "The impact of Russia's illegal war is being felt across Ukraine and increasingly in neighbouring countries." Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Friday's incident was "utterly unacceptable".
European Council President António Costa expressed his "strong solidarity" with the Polish people and said Russia had to come to the negotiating table to bring the war to the end.
The violations of Polish airspace came a day after 40 countries took part in a Coalition of the Willing summit in Berlin, where the allies pledged continued support for Kyiv, and Chancellor Friedrich Merz said peace talks with Russia should take place soon on neutral territory.
At least eight people were killed on Friday as Russian missiles and drones targeted three of Kyiv's bridges across the River Dnipro and a station in Lviv, days after Russia's Vladimir Putin threatened "painful" retaliation for repeated strikes on Russia's bridge across the Kerch Strait to occupied Crimea.
This is not the first time the war in Ukraine has spilled over into Poland. In July a cruise missile also landed in Poland, leaving a 10m-wide (33ft) crater. That incident also took place during an attack on the western Ukrainian city of Lviv.
Casualties in Poland have been rare, while Ukraine suffers deadly attacks on a daily basis. However, two Polish farmers were killed by a missile in November 2022, which was believed to have been a Ukrainian air-defence missile responding to a Russian attack.
Moldovan officials said on Friday that their airspace had also been violated on Friday, when a drone crossed briefly into its territory during Russia's attacks on Ukraine.
The Moldovan defence ministry has recorded 118 such violations since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022.

articles.title_zh: U.S. Has Floated NATO Membership for Ukraine in Recent Meetings
articles.content_orig:
Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
Donald Trump ’s top foreign envoys have suggested that Ukraine could still join the Nato military alliance in closed-door talks over the past few months, according to a shocking new report.
The idea of granting Ukraine membership to the bloc has long been considered dead in the water , a red line for a Russia that has opposed even the idea of deploying Nato peacekeepers in a post-war settlement.
But sources familiar with the matter told the Wall Street Journal that Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner has suggested that Kyiv could still join if it bends to Moscow ’s central demand for it to give up territory.
They said he had recently taken the idea right to Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky and other European officials in an effort to break the deadlock in peace talks.
The idea apparently emerged in August, some six months after a round of talks in Geneva ended without any clear breakthroughs.
It since came up at a meeting with both sides in the UAE, although it was unclear from the report what the Kremlin had made of it.
Ukraine maintains that it cannot and will not give up control of its eastern lands, which are mineral rich and host its defensive line of ‘fortress cities’ - as well as thousands of Ukrainian citizens.
But Nato membership could go some way to ensuring Ukraine gets its desired security guarantees against a future invasion.
The US, Russia and the UK offered security assurances when Ukraine gave up its nuclear weapons in 1994, but those failed to stop Vladimir Putin annexing Crimea in 2014 and launching a full-scale invasion in 2022.
And Trump has since cast doubt on whether he would even help a Nato ally in the event of an attack, saying last year he would not defend countries that failed to meet his “requirements” on defence spending.
In 2024, before his second term, he drew criticism for saying he would “encourage” Russia to attack any Nato member that fails to pay its bills.
An attack on Nato without the US - the bloc’s largest contributor - would leave Europe and Canada a weakened force against any potential adversary.
The growing rift between Washington and Europe since Trump’s return to office was felt this week as he met Putin on the sidelines of the Apec summit in Shenzhen , China.
Trump greeted the Russian leader by asking “Who is he? He’s my friend” before the two settled into discussions on the Ukraine war.
It was later reported that Trump reportedly had urged Europe to stop funding Ukraine, just hours after the warm bilateral with Putin.
Trump was said to have called into a meeting with the so-called Coalition of the Willing in Germany, attended by UK prime minister Andy Burnham and Ukraine’s president Volodymyr Zelensky, among others.
He raised concerns about billions in aid provided to Ukraine from Europe, according to European officials in Politico and Telegraph reports , stressing countries could save money if the war ended.
An unnamed US official later told Politico it was “not accurate” to say Trump told the leaders to end funding to Kyiv, but rather repeated his desire to bring the conflict to an end.

articles.title_zh: Poland Probes Possible Russian Airspace Breach as Ukrainian Regions Come Under Attack, Killed, Injured Reported
articles.content_orig:
Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
Nato scrambled jets on Friday after Poland said its airspace had been violated several times during a Russian attack on Ukraine.
Military aircraft were operating in Polish airspace while ground-based air defences were made ready , the Operational Command of the Polish Armed Forces said in a statement.
“These actions are preventive in nature and are aimed at securing and protecting Polish airspace, especially in areas adjacent to those under threat,” it added.
Poland earlier reported that three objects crossed over from Russia, likely including a KH-101 cruise missile, another missile and a drone.
Defence minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz condemned what he called a “provocation” from Moscow and said he would ask Nato for additional support on its eastern flank.
He assessed that it was unlikely to be a coincidence, occurring as Poland was set to hold military exercises of the 'Coalition of the Willing' of Ukraine's allies on Friday.
Russia’s foreign ministry says it will take ‘necessary measures’ after Estonia said it was closing its border with Russia.
The Baltic country's government said on Friday it would close its road border crossings with Russia on security grounds from December 1 and will decide after six months whether to extend the suspension.
Estonia on Sunday accused Russian security services of staging an attempted arson attack on an Estonian defence company, in what it said was the second such incident this year.
Estonia's northern neighbour Finland shut its Russia border crossings in 2023, and has kept them closed since then, while southern Baltic nations Latvia and Lithuania maintain open crossings.
Polish prime minister Donald Tusk said on Friday that the incursions into Polish airspace do not look like an accident but an “intentional provocation” from Russia.
"We know that what landed on Polish soil came from Russia,” he claimed in a press conference.
“Therefore — and this is not just my own assessment, but also that of our foreign partners, including those within NATO — it does not look like an accident. It appears that we are dealing with an intentional provocation.”
This week repeated Ukrainian strikes have seriously damaged the 19km (12-mile) Crimean Bridge, which straddles the Kerch Strait that links the Black and Azov seas.
The span is vital to sustaining Russia’s military operations, and the £3bn bridge is a potent reminder of Russia’s illegal annexation of the Crimean Peninsula, making it a prime target for Ukraine.
Train traffic stopped after the latest overnight strike into Thursday while authorities assessed the damage, but it resumed in the afternoon, according to Russian state news agency RIA Novosti.
The Ukrainian strikes seemed calculated to embarrass Putin as he met in China with Xi and Trump, as well as to undermine Russia's argument that its victory is inevitable.
In China, Putin insisted the bridge is a civilian asset, adding that he had ordered it closed to carrying military hardware or ammunition.
Putin also said that the road side of the bridge had been “seriously damaged” but vowed to rebuild it. The rail section, which runs parallel to the road, is believed to be stronger in order to bear the greater weight of cargo transport.
Ukraine’s defense ministry said the successful operation to target the bridge meant Russia would need to reroute fuel and ammunition supplies over land, where “our drones are waiting for the cargo.”
The US president should be embarrassed to be rubbing shoulders in this ‘fraternity of autocrats’ with a Russian leader wanted for war crimes by the ICC – but has shown he will stop at nothing for a seat with the ‘big men’ at the table, says Sam Kiley
In China, Trump called Putin “my friend.” The American president’s relationship with Zelensky has soured recently, although the question of US support for Ukraine could be raised by Democrats who will take control of Congress in January after their wins in the midterm elections.
European leaders have tried to isolate Putin diplomatically and have heavily sanctioned the Russian economy as they fear being sidelined by Trump’s direct talks with Putin.
Kushner said that, in his talks with Putin and Xi, Trump “sent a very strong message to both of them on the desire for peace and would like to engage both of them very aggressively to get there.”
He deferred to Trump on giving any details of the “private discussions,” but added: “I believe he also came away believing that peace is achievable and we need to all work together to try and achieve it.”
Putin said in Shenzhen that the Kremlin is not against European participation in talks, but “we need to understand with what Europe will come to these negotiations.” The Kremlin has proposed to European officials through diplomatic channels to come to Moscow “to determine their position,” Putin said, without elaborating. No date has been set.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov declined to say which European officials had been invited or whether Moscow had received a response, Russian state news agency Tass reported.
Polish authorities were investigating reports that at least two unknown objects had come down near the border with Ukraine after the army said Polish airspace might have been violated during Russian strikes on Ukraine.
Authorities in Nato-member Poland said it was too early to say what the objects were. A Ukrainian air force spokesperson said it was likely that a Russian missile had crossed into Poland.
The Russian embassy in Warsaw did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment.
Drones have repeatedly strayed into the airspace of countries on Nato’s eastern flank since Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022, fuelling tension ⁠with the military alliance and stoking fears that the war could spread.
"We confirm the crash of an unidentified object in the village of Nowy Lipowiec," the district prosecutor's office in Lublin wrote on X. "Reports regarding potential additional objects in the region are currently being verified by the relevant services."
Footage shared on ‌social media from what appeared to be a security camera at a property in the nearby village of Chmielek showed an explosion in the distance.
Polish infrastructure minister Dariusz Klimczak said on X that a traffic controller had heard a loud bang near railway premises in Rudnik nad Sanem, about 50km west of Nowy Lipowiec. He said no visible damage to the railway had been found but that an inspection vehicle had been dispatched.

articles.title_orig: Kushner says Russia OK with ‘NATO-like’ security pact for Ukraine: Is it?
articles.title_zh: Kushner says Russia OK with ‘NATO-like’ security pact for Ukraine: Is it?
articles.content_orig:
The United States has pitched a new plan to secure post-war Ukraine when its almost five-year war with Russia finally comes to an end.
At a meeting on Thursday with European leaders in Germany’s capital, Berlin, US President Donald Trump’s envoy and son-in-law Jared Kushner said he believes Russia is “comfortable” with NATO-like security guarantees for post-war Ukraine.
Kushner’s comments came just hours after an unprecedented summit involving Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen, China. At that meeting, Putin promised to retaliate against Ukraine’s attacks on Russia.
Following the Berlin summit, French President Emmanuel Macron said Ukraine’s membership of NATO should be considered again, prompting Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Sergei Ryabkov to push back.
Ryabokov said any form of “quasi membership” for Kyiv of the Western ‌military alliance was totally unacceptable for Moscow, Russian state media reported.
Ukraine applied to become a member of NATO in September 2022, seeking to fortify its borders with Russia.
But the Kremlin has repeatedly stated that Ukraine becoming a member of NATO would trigger “a harsh response” from Russia.
So could NATO-like security guarantees really work for Kyiv in light of Russia’s opposition?
European countries have been angered by the European Union being largely sidelined in the stop-start US negotiations with Russia and Ukraine since Trump returned to the White House in January 2025.
Trump’s summit with Putin and Xi on Thursday has added to apprehension about whether the US president is serious about ending Russia’s war on Ukraine, particularly after his criticism of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and his apparent recent overtures to Putin by relaxing sanctions on Russian oil.
But at a meeting of the “coalition of the willing”, a nearly 40-nation alliance of Ukraine’s European allies, in Berlin this week, Kushner and fellow US envoy Steve Witkoff tried to reassure European leaders, telling them Trump had held discussions in Shenzhen on ending the war on Ukraine.
“Trump wants to make a deal with Europe by his side,” Kushner said.
“We do believe that Russia having Europe at the table will be essential for ending the war,” he added.
Kushner also said Russia is “comfortable” with the idea of security guarantees for post-war Ukraine modelled on NATO’s Article 5, which says an attack on one member of the alliance is treated as an attack on all.
“I think we’ve gotten the Russians comfortable with that concept where any security guarantee for Ukraine would be based on Article 5,” he said, adding that Trump was “open” to the idea but “obviously, it has to be in America’s interest” and part of “a broader security package”.
Kushner said Trump also called in to the Berlin talks after his meeting with Putin and the latest round of peace talks in Abu Dhabi last week had produced no major breakthrough.
Described as the “cornerstone” of the military alliance, NATO’s collective defence principle, contained in Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty , was developed in 1949 to create a mutual protective pact to counter risks posed by the Soviet Union at the onset of the Cold War.
According to NATO, committing to Article 5 means that each member of the alliance knows that if one of them is the “victim of an armed attack, each and every other member of the alliance will consider this act of violence as an armed attack against all members”.
That means that each NATO member is obligated to “take the actions it deems necessary to assist the ally attacked”.
When Article 5 is invoked, NATO allies are free to provide whatever form of aid and assistance is deemed “necessary to respond to the situation”.
However, it is not an automatic process. The article must be invoked and then agreed upon by NATO members and can take time to implement. First, there must be a meeting of the North Atlantic Council to assess whether the attack meets Article 5 criteria. Then there must be a unanimous political decision and declaration to invoke the article. This can be slowed down by deliberations, intelligence gathering and legal reviews.
After that, determining what is necessary to respond to a given situation is the individual obligation of each NATO ally and may not necessarily include military action. As NATO states: “It is therefore left to the judgement of each individual member country to determine how it will contribute.”
Each country consults with all other alliance members in terms of response and with the ultimate aim “to restore and maintain the security” of alliance members.
Article 5 has been invoked only once, after the September 11, 2001, attacks on the US by al-Qaeda.
The triggering of Article 5 saw “NATO engage actively in the fight against terrorism, launch its first operations outside the Euro-Atlantic area and begin a far-reaching transformation of its capabilities”, according to the alliance.
“By invoking Article 5, NATO members showed their solidarity toward the United States and condemned, in the strongest possible way, the terrorist attacks against the United States.”
Ukraine applied to become a NATO member seven months after Russia’s full-scale invasion began. Since then, Zelenskyy, his officials and Ukrainians around the world have been lobbying NATO nations to speed up Kyiv’s accession process.
But NATO members remain divided about offering Ukraine alliance membership during an ongoing war despite a broad consensus to signal strong support for Kyiv.
NATO members bordering Russia, such as Lithuania and Poland, have been most enthusiastic about backing Ukraine’s ambitions. Several other nations in the alliance have also been supportive of an expedited process for Kyiv to join despite concerns about corruption in Ukraine and while seeking an end to the war with Russia as a condition for the country to become a NATO member.
Under Trump, the US has been far less receptive to Ukraine’s calls for NATO membership. Indeed, Trump has publicly told Ukraine to give up its hopes of joining the alliance.
Yet last week, Kushner and Witkoff suggested that Kyiv could join the alliance in exchange for relinquishing eastern Ukraine’s Donbas region to Russia.
At the Berlin meeting on Thursday, French President Emmanuel Macron revisited the topic of Ukraine’s NATO membership. “Faced with the maximalist nature of the Russian position, I believe we need to reopen the question of Ukraine’s accession to NATO,” Macron said.
Also at the meeting, Kushner pitched NATO’s Article 5-like security guarantees for Ukraine without specifying how they would work.
This year, Zelenskyy stressed that for Ukraine, guarantees of security first need to come from the US. In October, the Ukrainian president and Witkoff discussed US security guarantees for Kyiv similar to Article 5.
But on Thursday, Zelenskyy told reporters that at the Berlin meeting, there was no common understanding of what Article 5-style security guarantees for Kyiv would entail.
He questioned whether giving Ukraine such security guarantees would mean that US and European troops would be based on Ukrainian land because that was his understanding of Article 5.
“For me, the most important thing is how countries will react on aggression,” he said.
Harry Nedelcu, partner and senior director of geopolitics at the Rasmussen Global consultancy, who previously served on the NATO secretary-general’s policy planning staff, said there is inconsistency in US strategy.
“On one hand, they are proposing NATO membership to Ukraine in exchange for Kyiv entirely withdrawing its troops from the Donbas, and now they are saying Ukraine could get NATO-like security guarantees. It is clear Washington wants to show some kind of progress and get a peace deal done, also perhaps in light of the situation in Iran,” he told Al Jazeera.
