articles.title_orig: California investigates Nvidia over whether chip exports ended up in China
articles.title_zh: California investigates Nvidia over whether chip exports ended up in China
articles.content_orig:
State attorney says scandal ‘raises bright red flags’ and aims to find out if company misled investors
California has served an investigative subpoena on Nvidia after a scandal that prompted the departure of co-founder and longtime chief executive Jensen Huang.
Rob Bonta, the US state’s attorney general, issued the subpoena as part of an investigation into whether exports of the California-based company’s advanced semiconductor chips ended up in China, contravening US restrictions.
“The conduct of Nvidia and its former chief executive raises bright red flags, including about the ways in which the company may have misled investors,” said Bonta.
“Nvidia is in a messy, transnational situation but the underlying principle of our corporate securities law is clear: companies cannot mislead their investors.”
The subpoena, issued on Thursday, followed Huang’s resignation a week ago after it emerged he had multiple affairs, including one with Alice Huang, a suspected Chinese spy.
Alice Huang, who is not related, is associated with Singapore-based Megaspeed, which has bought nearly $5bn (£3.8bn) of Nvidia chips and hardware in recent years, and is being investigated for possibly diverting advanced restricted chips to China .
Megaspeed has said it is a “legitimate and lawful” business, and that Huang left the company late last year.
Bonta said the investigation would also look at whether the former Nvidia chief’s actions resulted in confidential information being passed to China.
“My office is investigating whether Nvidia or Jensen Huang’s actions resulted in China obtaining advanced chips or confidential information,” he said. “And if Nvidia misled investors and the public about this risk, in violation of the law.”
Nvidia’s shares are down by a fifth since Huang admitted the extramarital affair, hitting a one-year low at the close of trading on Thursday, and wiping almost $1tn off its market value.
Earlier this week, Harvey Jones, Nvidia’s chair, said the company had no intention of reinstating Huang after the former CEO said he would be “honoured” to return. Elon Musk and a host of tech bosses had campaigned for Nvidia to bring him back .
Huang is due to testify before several congressional committees over the potential breach of national security on 1 December.
after newsletter promotion
Shares in rival chipmaker AMD closed down almost 8% on Thursday after the publication of reports connected to short seller Hunterbrook warning about its links to China and the “circular financing” of customers.
The company, which has been targeted amid the Nvidia scandal, is looking at a further fall of more than 5% in pre-market trading.
Hunterbrook Media published allegations on the use of AMD’s software by a Chinese server maker blacklisted by the US. Sister publication, The Bear Cave newsletter, alleged that AMD’s use of datacentre lease guarantees and backstops for unsold cloud computing capacity could leave it exposed to a pullback in AI spending.
AMD said the reports’ claims “misrepresent AMD’s business practices and relationships”.
“AMD complies with applicable US export control laws and regulations and maintains rigorous processes to ensure compliance across our global operations,” the company said. “We remain focused on serving our customers and upholding the highest standards of integrity.”
AMD’s share price has more than doubled so far this year, giving the company a market capitalisation of more than $800m.

articles.title_orig: Xi Jinping says a ‘full turnaround’ has been achieved in Australia-China relations, praising Anthony Albanese
articles.title_zh: Xi Jinping says a ‘full turnaround’ has been achieved in Australia-China relations, praising Anthony Albanese
articles.content_orig:
US president appeared to doze off while Chinese leader made speech, but White House insisted he was awake
Donald Trump was, again, accused of falling asleep during a televised event, this time during the speech of the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in China.
The US president appeared to close his eyes for roughly 10 seconds on Thursday. As his eyes closed, Trump’s head tilted downward, and his hands remained clasped in front of him.
Several prominent Trump critics on social media alleged that the US president was asleep, including Republicans Against Trump , California governor Gavin Newsom’s press office and conservative lawyer George Conway .
White House officials denied the allegations, claiming the 80-year-old US president was looking down at papers in front of him.
“Fake News! President Trump was looking at papers in front of him while the speaker made remarks. You can clearly see his eyes move back and forth,” Steven Cheung, the White House director of communications, wrote on X in response to a Newsweek article.
“This is why the people despise media so much. They constantly lie,” Cheung added.
Trump often faces accusations of falling asleep during televised events such as Oval Office press conferences, cabinet meetings and sporting events.
Occasionally, while listening to other people speak, the US president will close his eyes for several seconds, appearing as though he is falling asleep . Despite footage of the instances going viral, the White House and Trump allies have insisted the US president does not fall asleep during meetings.
Administration officials have excused Trump’s apparent drowsiness as blinking or an example of the president listening intently. They consistently claim Trump “doesn’t sleep”.
Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state, testified to lawmakers earlier this year that he had “never seen” Trump fall asleep.
“On the contrary, the guy doesn’t sleep, which is a big problem because he calls me at two in the morning,” Rubio said in June.
Last year, JD Vance said that Trump hardly ever sleeps, even while traveling overnight.
“If we go on a 20-hour trip somewhere, he doesn’t sleep the entire time. And of course, if he’s not sleeping, if he’s working, he expects everybody else to be working too,” Vance told Fox News .
Trump became the oldest US president ever inaugurated when he was sworn in nearly two years ago. Despite his age, Trump often claims he is in near-perfect health , often bragging about his “perfect” cognitive test results and insisting he has a lot of energy.

articles.title_orig: As Trump courts Xi and Putin, middle powers make their own moves
articles.title_zh: As Trump courts Xi and Putin, middle powers make their own moves
articles.content_orig:
From an airy government villa in the hills of southern China on Thursday emerged an image, perhaps, for our times: the leaders of China, Russia and the US standing shoulder-to-shoulder, proclaiming themselves the stewards of world peace.
For Trump, the moment was a well-timed photo-op – a diplomatic flex for a president who revels in such spectacle and whose party is reeling from a major loss in the US midterm elections.
But for Xi and Putin, the meeting is more likely to go down as a vindication of their vision that the world is undergoing a fundamental rebalancing of power – in their favor.
In opening remarks before the roughly 90-minute meeting between them, Trump said he was honored to sit next to the two and framed the trio – the world’s three largest nuclear powers – as uniquely placed to work together for a “safer future.”
“No problems were ever solved under the old school, refusing to talk about them,” said Trump. “Together, we are choosing a different course.”

articles.title_orig: US AI chip curbs hit China tech stocks, spur self-sufficiency push
articles.title_zh: US AI chip curbs hit China tech stocks, spur self-sufficiency push
articles.content_orig:
Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
Chinese technology firms are bracing for impacts on their ambitious artificial intelligence plans as the U.S. tightens restrictions on China 's access to the world's cutting-edge chips.
Chinese tech giant Alibaba , which on Thursday announced another quarter of strong revenue growth for its global AI cloud and compute services, warned that the new U.S. rules could affect some of its global data center expansion plans. It said it was still assessing the repercussions.
The Trump administration this week issued new rules in the wake of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation, following the news that he’d had an extramarital affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy.
The rules now restrict remote computing access through data centers in third countries, the latest U.S. move to curtail China’s abilities to use advanced Nvidia chips to train its increasingly capable AI models.
Alibaba's AI revenues are surging as demand grows
As the technology race between the two superpowers intensifies, existing U.S. export restrictions already barred China from getting the world’s most powerful chips.
But some Chinese companies have been able to bypass those restrictions by renting remote computing access to train AI models, pushing the U.S. to close what some policymakers called a loophole.
As global AI usage grows, Alibaba has been expanding its capabilities across chips, cloud infrastructure and AI models. It launched its flagship Qwen4-Max AI model earlier this week. In September, Alibaba's CEO called its new Zhenwu V900 chip the “most powerful” AI chip in China, while it announced massive data center investment plans in China and abroad.
Alibaba Cloud’s AI-related revenue currently comes significantly from China and there’s still a lot of “untapped demand” from Chinese enterprises, said Jacob Cooke of the Beijing-based consultancy WPIC Marketing + Technologies.
For the latest July-September quarter, Alibaba reported a 53% year-on-year revenue surge for its AI cloud and compute services to nearly 61 billion yuan ($9 billion). Total revenue for the quarter rose 10% from the year before to almost 272 billion yuan ($41 billion), slightly better than what analysts had expected.
While the company has a strong cash buffer, capital expenditures jumped 60% during the quarter to 50.5 billion yuan ($7.6 billion) thanks to its increased spending on AI infrastructure buildout.
Tencent says US chip curb ‘sets everyone back in China’
Chinese tech giant Tencent on Wednesday said the new U.S. rule on chip access “sets everyone back in China.”
“Everyone is actually having less compute, advanced compute, to work with, no matter when you actually started leasing or building capacities outside of China,” Tencent President Martin Lau said on an earnings call. Training timelines for Tencent’s next versions of its AI models would probably be impacted, he said.
“Chinese AI firms are still heavily dependent on the most frontier Nvidia chips," said James Chai, a researcher at the ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute in Singapore, with new U.S. rules on remote access cutting off a huge portion of Chinese firms’ access to compute.
A study released in October by the Institute for Progress, a U.S. think tank, estimated that remote access to AI chips through overseas data centers could account for roughly one-third of China’s AI compute by the end of 2027.
Nvidia, meanwhile, said it is now “no longer shipping” chips including the H200, one of its more powerful chips, though not the most advanced, although the Trump administration greenlighted some sales to China, reflecting how Nvidia has toughened its stance on China following Huang’s ouster.
Analysts expect the U.S. will step up its chip export control policies against China after Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, a former senior executive of Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed, raised U.S. national security concerns. Earlier reporting by The New York Times suggested that U.S. officials suspected Alice Huang was a Chinese spy recruited in part to potentially influence Nvidia to make its most advanced chips more available to Chinese companies.
Beijing has rejected claims that Alice Huang was a Chinese spy, and has called the new U.S. rules blocking Chinese companies' remote access to computing power overseas “economic coercion.”
Analysts and industry leaders in China say the U.S.’s tightening of chip export control measures would ultimately accelerate China’s push to make its domestic chip industry self-sufficient.
“Over the longer run, we believe all Chinese players would actually have to rely on domestic supply chains and domestic chips, which we actually see the industry is actually progressing very fast,” said Tencent's Lau.

articles.title_orig: Hours after Trump reportedly says ‘tired’ Putin is ready for a deal, Ukraine hit with massive strikes
articles.title_zh: Hours after Trump reportedly says ‘tired’ Putin is ready for a deal, Ukraine hit with massive strikes
articles.content_orig:
Moscow launched a deadly missile and drone attack on Ukraine overnight into Friday, just hours after Russian President Vladimir Putin met his US and Chinese counterparts for historic trilateral talks in which the three powers billed themselves as a force for peace in the world.
Trump spoke to European leaders after the call, reportedly describing Putin as “tired” and ready for peace. But Kyiv said Russia fired at least 110 missiles overnight - an unusually large number even amid Russia’s frequent aerial assaults.
Eight people have been killed and at least 28 injured during the massive attack which has so far lasted more than eight hours, according to Ukrainian authorities.
Some 400 drones, including 120 jet-powered drones which are essentially compact cruise missiles, were also part of the attack.
The Polish government said on Friday that fighter jets were scrambled and Patriot air defense systems activated early on Friday after Poland’s airspace was violated during the attack, with “objects” flying in and falling inside the country’s territory.
The deadly assault came hours after Putin left China following a day of meetings in Shenzhen with US President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping.
The talks failed to produce any breakthrough on Moscow’s more than four-year war in Ukraine, and appeared to be used by Putin as an opportunity to repeat his maximalist demands and false narratives about the conflict in front of a global audience.
The Russian leader hailed the summit with Xi and Trump as historic and told reporters the discussions took place in a “relaxed and very intimate atmosphere.”
In his opening remarks, Putin said Russia, China and the US have “shared interests” in settling the Ukraine war.
No official declaration or a readout were released after the talks, but Trump did speak afterwards to the so-called Coalition of the Willing, a group of Ukraine’s key allies which was convening with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in Berlin.
According to a senior European official with knowledge of the call’s contents, the president’s main message was that “Putin is tired, wants to end this, ready for a deal.”
The official said Trump’s suggestion was “to reach out and grasp at the opportunity.”
He said the Europeans were “constructive in response but want proof.”
Poland’s Prime Minister Donald Tusk, who was part of the call, said that Trump sounded “fairly optimistic.”
“Although I have to say (his words) were received very cautiously in the room, when it comes to Putin’s and Moscow’s intentions regarding peace talks.”
“But I don’t hide the fact that I’ve heard this very often from President Trump. His belief in Putin’s goodwill seems unshakable, even though so far there are no facts to support it, he said, adding that it “would be good, if it really turned out that Russia was genuinely ready to engage in peace talks.”
Kushner said Trump had conveyed “a very strong message to both of them [Xi and Putin] on the desire for peace and would like to engage both of them very aggressively to get there.”
Russia’s defense ministry said in a post to Telegram it launched a “massive strike using high-precision weapons from land, sea, and air,” as well as drones, targeting Ukrainian military and energy facilities, port infrastructure in the Odesa region, and transport infrastructure in Kyiv.
But Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky said “a bsolutely all the targets were ordinary civilian infrastructure – things that literally sustain people’s lives.”
“This was one of the largest attacks. The strike tactics were particularly vicious this time: several groups of missiles were launched, with pauses of 20 to 30 minutes between them to make it harder to put out fires, clear rubble, and carry out repairs,” Zelensky said.
Zelensky said that 27 of the missiles
Earlier, Ukraine said Moscow’s targets included a hospital in Kharkiv and residential buildings in the Dnipropetrovsk, Lviv, Vinnytsia, Sumy, and Chernihiv regions.
Three of Kyiv’s bridges were damaged in the overnight strikes, according to mayor Vitaly Klitschko, halting transport links connecting the two sides of the capital.
“All emergency services have done and will continue to do everything possible to mitigate the consequences of the attack as quickly as possible,” Klitschko said, adding that people should avoid traveling if possible.
The deadly attack came after Putin vowed revenge for Ukraine’s recent attacks on prized project, the strategic multibillion-dollar bridge linking Russia with the occupied Crimea.
“There will be no negotiations,” he said. “I believe our response, as I have just said, will be far more painful than what the Kyiv regime did to the bridge.”
The attacks have also knocked down power in several regions across Ukraine, just as temperatures are beginning to drop to bellow zero.
Several districts in Kyiv were without power due to the attack, according to energy company DTEK. Emergency power outages have also been implemented in the Lviv, Zakarpattia, and Ivano-Frankivsk regions, according to Ukrenergo, the country’s state-owned electricity operator, which called the situation in the power grid “extremely critical.”
CNN’s Nick Paton Walsh and Victoria Butenko contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: China revels in Xi Jinping’s ‘Yalta 2.0’ moment
articles.title_zh: China revels in Xi Jinping’s ‘Yalta 2.0’ moment
articles.content_orig:
President Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin sat down together in Shenzhen, China, on Thursday in a rare face-to-face encounter for the leaders of three of the world's most powerful countries, but there appeared to be little concrete to show for the meeting in terms of resolving any of the crises facing the world.
The leaders offered a joint statement after their roughly hour-and-a-half-long meeting. Mr. Trump immediately left for his return flight to the U.S. without speaking to journalists on the ground. On the flight home, the president said on social media he will hold a press conference at noon on Friday to discuss the trip.
The presidents discussed Russia's ongoing war in Ukraine , which Mr. Trump has wanted to bring to a negotiated end. But the only significant statement on the conflict came after the meeting from Putin, who ruled out any direct negotiations with Ukraine, citing a major strike earlier this week by Ukrainian forces on a key bridge in Russian-held Crimea.
Putin's senior aide Yuri Ushakov told reporters after the meeting that the atmosphere had been good, and the Kremlin quickly released what it called a joint statement from all three leaders characterizing the talks. The White House later provided the same statement.
The three men "exchanged views in detail on the current international situation and reaffirmed their commitment to maintaining strategic stability and international security," the readout said, adding that as permanent members of the United Nations Security Council, they had "reaffirmed their commitment to reforming the UN so that it can more effectively respond to global challenges and fulfill its fundamental mission in the area of international peace and security."
They also committed to increasing gas and oil production "for the benefit of all countries," agreed on the "fundamental importance" of "the principle of state consent and respect for the immunities of state officials," and said the " International Criminal Court and other similar bodies should not abuse their powers."
Finally, the leaders "reaffirmed that there can be no winners in a nuclear war, and that it should never be unleashed."
The White House indicated that Mr. Trump might speak with reporters on Air Force One during the flight back to the U.S.
The Kremlin shared a short video on social media, via Russian state media, showing Xi accompanying Putin as they walked out of the meeting to Putin's waiting motorcade. Before they exit the building, Putin is seen shaking Xi's hand, thanking him for hosting the gathering and telling him, according to Russian state media, that nobody had expected it to go so well.
Before the meeting, Mr. Trump met separately with Putin on the sidelines of the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, and then with Xi.
"We've had a great relationship for many years," Mr. Trump said, standing alongside his Russian counterpart. "I think a lot of wonderful things can come out of this, or at least start."
As Mr. Trump approached Putin for a handshake, he said, "Who is that?" before laughing and saying, "He's my friend."
Democratic Sen. Tim Kaine, who sits on the Committee on Foreign Relations, said the image of Mr. Trump standing with Xi and Putin was concerning.
"Some of the pictures troubled me, seeing the president stand with Putin and Xi, rather than seeing the president stand with the leaders of the global democracies," Kaine said. "When I saw them, it turned my stomach a bit, and particularly President Trump's declaration that Vladimir Putin was a friend. Vladimir Putin is not a friend, and so you know he was either being insincere or he is deeply deluded if he thinks Vladimir Putin is a friend."
In a phone call with NBC reporter Gabe Gutierrez, Mr. Trump called the meeting a 12 on a scale of zero to 10.
Russia's TASS news agency said the war in Ukraine was the main topic discussed by the two leaders, and that Putin left the meeting in "an excellent mood."
After the trilateral talks Thursday, Putin told reporters that Ukraine and Europe were "not yet ready" to make the compromises necessary to resolve the war, according to Russian media.
"We will not negotiate after the attacks on the Crimean bridge," he declared, referring to this week's Ukrainian strike on the highly symbolic Kerch Bridge, which links Russia with Ukraine's Russian-occupied Crimean Peninsula.
Putin said Kyiv and Europe would eventually come to understand that it is better to make compromises than to face "realities."
Ukraine and its European partners have long feared that the White House appears willing to offer Putin too much — including the prospect of major energy deals — with no significant concessions from Russia  in return, while putting pressure on Kyiv to make major territorial concessions without any concrete security guarantees.
Mr. Trump then met for about an hour with Xi ahead of the three-way meeting. As the Trump-Xi session began, Xi told Mr. Trump relations between China and the United States were "stable and improved."
Mr. Trump told reporters he had spoken with Xi for two hours on Wednesday, with trade and tariffs being the main topics. He also said he would be asking China to "do some more" for American farmers, because China has an "insatiable appetite."
Mr. Trump said previously that he planned to talk about denuclearization with his fellow leaders. Russia and the United States are by far the world's largest holders of nuclear weapons , with stockpiles estimated at well over 5,000 warheads, while China is believed to be a distant third, with about 600 weapons.
Putin has made denuclearization a key talking point for decades, but both he and Mr. Trump have allowed previous treaties intended to limit nuclear proliferation to lapse in recent years. China, which has been building up its nuclear program , ruled out taking part in any denuclearization talks with the U.S. and Russia as recently as last year .
China's state-run Xinhua news agency quoted Xi , however, as saying ahead of the trilateral meeting on Thursday that nuclear weapons were a "sword of Damocles hanging over humanity," and calling for them to be "completely banned and completely destroyed, leading to a world free of nuclear weapons."
The Kremlin said in its readout of the three-way meeting that it would "continue dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing the proliferation of nuclear weapons" with China and the U.S.
A range of other global challenges lingered in the background of the trilateral meeting, including the war in Iran and tension over trade and artificial intelligence .
The summit took place in the capital of the Chinese tech industry, a sector that has drawn intense scrutiny in recent weeks amid worries that advanced U.S. computer chips are surreptitiously reaching China. The scandal was sparked by allegations that now-former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with a businesswoman and suspected Chinese intelligence asset, Alice Huang , whose company is accused of diverting Nvidia's coveted AI chips to China. Beijing has dismissed claims that Alice Huang is a Chinese spy as "groundless speculation" and "nothing more than an attempt to smear China."
Mr. Trump — an ally of Jensen Huang's — had previously told reporters he may bring up the businesswoman during his meetings in China, though he said, "I don't know that she is a spy." Her firm, Megaspeed , is under Justice Department investigation. It has denied wrongdoing.
Shortly after the concerns about Jensen Huang surfaced, the Trump administration issued a new rule aimed at curbing China and other countries' ability to remotely access advanced AI chips. China and the U.S. have also discussed broader AI policy issues in recent months, including setting up a communication channel to share information when AI systems go haywire.
Mr. Trump brought up AI during a speech at the APEC forum earlier in the day, vowing to block any "globalist regulation" of artificial int

articles.title_zh: White House pool have phones taken away on return from China as speculation mounts over unscheduled stop
articles.content_orig:

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
White House reporters traveling aboard Air Force One had their phones temporarily confiscated before President Donald Trump’s plane took off after his trilateral summit with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin, raising the specter of an unscheduled detour on his way back to Washington D.C.
U.S. officials collected reporters’ devices as the president’s plane prepared to leave Shenzhen, China, Thursday evening.
“At 6:45 pm consider this your wheels up,” the White House pool report read. “Our phones are being taken away for now for security reasons.”
No one on the trip has provided more information. The White House did not immediately respond to a request for more information.
It is highly unusual for reporters’ phones to be sequestered outside of situations when the president is traveling to a war zone, such as when Trump flew to Al Asad Air Base in Iraq at Christmas in 2018, and to Bagram Air Field in Afghanistan for Thanksgiving in 2019.
Fox News correspondent Jacqui Heinrich, the current president of the White House Correspondents’ Association, pointed out on X that the pool’s phones were not taken when Trump left Beijing after his state visit in May.
The move was later explained as a cybersecurity measure, as the phones used by journalists in China were placed in a metal-lined Faraday bag to prevent them from emitting any signals while the aircraft was aloft.
Most of the devices that were collected were so-called burner phones used only for the travel to China, as journalists had previously stored their regular devices in similar bags aboard Air Force One for use during the Philippines leg of the trip and while en route to Washington.
Separately, a flight restriction that had been imposed over Alaska around the time Air Force One had been scheduled to refuel there was lifted Thursday, raising questions as to the plane’s destination.
The most obvious candidate for a detour was North Korea. Trump spent the days before the summit musing that Kim Jong Un might join him when he met with China ’s Xi and Russia ’s Putin on the sidelines of the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation summit.
On Wednesday, Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters in Manila that the president was “prepared” to meet the North Korean leader.
“It may not happen, but he’s prepared to do it,” Rubio said.
However on a call with reporters before the trip, senior U.S. officials said there were “no plans at all for engagement with North Korea.”
Trump relished the pageantry and attention that were lavished on his first two meetings with Kim, though neither sit-down resulted in the denuclearization deals he had promised to reach with the brutal autocrat.
He also met Kim for a third time during a visit to the Korean Demilitarized Zone and briefly became the first American president to set foot in North Korea.
The intrigue surrounding the president’s departure from China followed Trump’s participation in the first-ever meeting between an American president and the autocrats who have led the other two major nuclear powers for a combined 41 years.
Trump gave Putin a warm reception when he met with him for a bilateral meeting immediately preceding the three-way sit-down.
The U.S. president pointed, smiled and called out “Who is that? He’s my friend!” as he walked into a room with his Russian counterpart. The scene was captured by TV cameras that had been permitted in, even as journalists were barred from attending to prevent the leaders from being asked any uncomfortable questions, though a Russian official attributed the move to space constraints.
Trump said of Putin: “We’ve had a great relationship for many years. We know each other for a long time, and I think a lot of wonderful things can come out of this, or at least start. But I think they’ll come out of this.”
The Kremlin said after the meeting that the pair had discussed the ongoing war in Ukraine , and that Putin left in an “excellent” mood.
The White House offered no official readout of the sit-down, which lasted approximately 40 minutes.
Following the trilateral meeting, the Russian, Chinese and American governments released a four-point “peace declaration” reaffirming that a nuclear war should never be fought and vowing to engage in dialogue on reducing nuclear risks.
The three leaders also pledged to advance reforms of the United Nations, to increase supplies of refined petroleum products for all countries and to uphold the immunity enjoyed by state officials in international courts.
The International Criminal Court in The Hague has issued arrest warrants for Putin and five other Russian officials. The Trump administration has been working to delegitimize and defund the ICC out of fear that Trump and his associates could be subject to war crimes charges over America’s campaign of airstrikes against alleged drug smugglers or an airstrike against an Iranian school that left over 100 children dead.

articles.title_orig: Asian Equities Tumble as AI Stock Selloff Deepens
articles.title_zh: Asian Equities Tumble as AI Stock Selloff Deepens
articles.content_orig:
Asian markets on track for their worst week since 2020, with European and US stocks also way down
Business live – latest updates
Global stock markets have slumped as Anthropic’s record-breaking IPO failed to stem a sell-off in AI-linked companies.
Asian stock markets were on track for their worst week since 2020, as shares in big chip companies fell on Friday. In Taiwan, stocks dropped 6.7% to hit their lowest point since mid-April, with the chip maker TSMC down about 6%.
In Japan, the Nikkei index fell 5%, while South Korea’s tech-heavy Kospi index lost 5.5%. Shares in the tech investor SoftBank had their worst day in more than two years, down 14.5% in Tokyo, amid worries around its aggressive bets on AI.
European stock markets were heading for their worst week since March, with the pan-European Stoxx 600 dropping 1.3% in the first 90 minutes.
The sell-off followed losses on Wall Street on Thursday, where the main indices all fell by more than 2% on a day dominated by Anthropic’s IPO .
Anthropic’s shares jumped by 17% on Thursday, after briefly surging by almost 40% when trading in the frontier AI firm began. But they were heading for losses on Friday, down 6% at $91.30, falling back towards the IPO price of $83.
Anthropic’s flotation has failed to ease worries around the AI trade, as investors increasingly question whether companies can deliver the returns necessary to justify the billions of dollars being poured into the AI build out.
Daniela Hathorn, a senior market analyst at Capital.com, said: “The IPO demonstrated that demand for AI exposure remains strong, but it has not been enough to overcome concerns about elevated valuations, profitability and the sustainability of investment spending.
“The broader market mood has shifted from buying the dip towards questioning whether the correction has further to run. The weakness in equal-weighted indices suggests that selling pressure is no longer confined to a handful of technology giants, while Europe’s recent outperformance has also faded.”

Britain’s FTSE 100 share index hit a five-month low on Friday morning. It has dropped by 4.8% this week, and is heading for its biggest weekly fall since the start of the Iran war.

articles.title_orig: Tears of joy, prayers for return home: Rohingya react to genocide ruling
articles.title_zh: Tears of joy, prayers for return home: Rohingya react to genocide ruling
articles.content_orig:
Trump’s state department says it is examining the ICJ judgment while stressing the need to avoid ‘politicisation’ of the body
The US has reacted with caution to the world’s highest court ruling that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority, while the EU more effusively framed the decision as a “landmark” judgment.
The historic ruling from the international court of justice (ICJ) – which has never previously found a state responsible for genocide – could set a precedent for future genocide claims, notably a case against Israel .
The US state department said on Thursday Washington was examining the judgment while stressing the need to avoid “politicisation” of the ICJ.
Donald Trump’s administration has taken a dim view of international law, in particular vowing to dismantle the international criminal court (ICC), which it regards as a renegade globalist institution. The ICJ and ICC are separate entities and the administration has yet to question the legitimacy of the ICJ.
The state department reiterated US support for the people of Myanmar and said it shared “grave concerns over the continued abuses of human rights against Rohingya Muslims and members of other minority groups”. It noted the US is the largest single humanitarian donor to the Rohingya humanitarian crisis response.
In Brussels, the EU said Myanmar must fully implement the ICJ’s ruling “without delay” and that “compliance with ICJ’s decisions is not optional, it is an obligation under international law”.
“The European Union holds the ICJ in the highest regard and remains steadfast in its support for its critical role in the peaceful resolution of disputes and the upholding of the rule of law at international level,” an EU spokesperson said in a statement .
“The Rohingya people have endured immense suffering, including displacement and violence, and their plight must not be forgotten. This landmark ruling underscores the imperative of justice for victims and the necessity of upholding international law.”
The UN secretary general, António Guterres, called the ruling “a demonstration of international justice and a reaffirmation that impunity for such horrific acts must not stand”. Shortly after the ruling was read, the UK foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, said his government was expelling Myanmar’s defence attache from the UK and “calling urgently for a UN security council session to discuss the judgment”.
Australia’s foreign minister, Penny Wong, called for those behind the Myanmar military’s grave human rights abuses to face justice.
In August 2017, Myanmar’s military launched what it called a clearance campaign in Rakhine state in response to an attack by a Rohingya insurgent group. The campaign led to accusations that security forces committed mass rapes and killings and burned thousands of homes.
The court said evidence showed Myanmar forces killed about 10,000 Rohingya.
Under the 1948 convention, to establish that genocide occurred, the court had to find that there was an intent to destroy the Rohingya “in whole or in part”.
About 1.2 million Rohingya refugees now live in Bangladesh, primarily in crowded camps across Cox’s Bazar district, where they endure harsh conditions marked by fire hazards, infectious diseases, monsoon landslides, inadequate sanitation and strict work restrictions.
Judges at the court based in The Hague have also been asked to rule on other allegations of genocide.
South Africa has accused Israel of breaching the genocide convention during its offensive in Gaza, a claim Israel vehemently denies. That case, which the US has pushed back on, is years from completion. An interim ICJ judgment in 2024 ordered Israel to ensure its forces do not commit acts of genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.
Ukraine also has a case pending against Russia . Shortly after Moscow’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, Kyiv accused Russia of fabricating genocide claims against Ukraine to justify the attack.

articles.title_orig: Ten years on, is the UK preparing to undo Brexit?
articles.title_zh: Ten years on, is the UK preparing to undo Brexit?
articles.content_orig:
Leaders from the United Kingdom and European Union will meet for a landmark summit on Friday as British Prime Minister Andy Burnham pushes for a closer relationship with the bloc a decade after the Brexit vote.
The package of agreements Britain hopes to secure would create new opportunities for young people to live, study and travel on the continent, link emissions trading and remove trade barriers on food products.
Britain’s center-left Labour government inherited Brexit from its predecessors, the Conservative Party, and has long spoken of “resetting” ties with Brussels.
But in the four months since he became prime minister, Burnham has staked out a more bullish position on Europe, appearing willing to revisit the politically charged Brexit debate and take on the right-wing parties that fiercely oppose reversing 2016’s referendum result and reestablishing closer ties with Europe.
“The hard Brexit we were given is not good enough,” Burnham said in his first major foreign policy speech on Monday, referencing the 2020 deal under which the country left the EU.
Ten years on, Britain counts the cost of Brexit
Last month, he even said he’d like to see Britain rejoin the bloc in his lifetime but ruled that out in this parliament, alongside crossing his party’s “red lines” from their 2024 manifesto of returning to the single market or customs union, or restoring freedom of movement.
Nonetheless, he committed to beginning talks with the EU “about options for our long-term relationship” after Friday’s summit without providing further details or timeline.
Economists broadly agree that leaving the EU stymied the UK’s economic growth potential – with estimates ranging from 2% to as much as 8% of foregone output. So as the government scrabbles for levers to kickstart economic growth, the EU, as Britain’s biggest trading partner and neighbor, has become part of the conversation.
Following Labour’s election in 2024 under Burnham’s predecessor Keir Starmer, it promised to “make Brexit work.” Starmer’s strategy was to reboot the UK-EU relationship by negotiating limited deals and aligning some regulations to ease trade frictions. But Starmer’s technocratic, cautious approach – on Europe and other policy areas – led in large part to his party ousting him this summer. The more confident, media-savvy Burnham emerged in his place.
Friday’s summit is largely a product of Starmer’s approach, originally scheduled for earlier this year but delayed when his premiership imploded.
Nick Thomas-Symonds, a member of parliament who served as Europe minister under Starmer, told CNN the deal was “90% there” when Burnham’s team took over.
Issues like aligning tuition fees for EU students studying at UK universities with those of their British counterparts, a final position on UK participation in the EU’s “Made in Europe” initiative – which threatens to squeeze UK businesses out of European supply chains – and the numbers permitted under a youth mobility scheme were still undecided, he said. It’s unclear if Friday’s talks will move the needle in these areas.
Burnham’s rhetoric on Europe has been more forceful, but his actual approach hasn’t changed “an iota” from Starmer’s, said Anand Menon, a professor at King’s College London and director of the think-tank UK in a Changing Europe.
“The only difference is how we talk about the future, and Burnham saying we might consider rejoining,” he told CNN. “The more people talk about rejoining, the more obviously complicated an undertaking it becomes. I don’t know where Burnham goes on this.”
Further changes in the UK-EU relationship are unlikely, Menon added, unless the government compromises on its “red lines.”
His assessment echoes the EU’s former Brexit negotiator Michel Barnier, who warned earlier this month that the UK cannot “cherry pick” certain elements of the single market.
For his part, Thomas-Symonds pointed to more cooperation on immigration, stronger military ties and aligning regulations in other sectors as ways to deepen ties with the EU without breaking party promises. “Obviously, these bigger points are ones that we’re looking at in the next manifesto,” he said.
Burnham’s ambitious rhetoric has shifted the political conversation. Two campaign groups – both with ties to the original “Vote Leave” campaign – either launched or rebranded this week with the express purpose of opposing any attempts to rejoin the EU.
Conservative opposition leader Kemi Badenoch, meanwhile, accused Burnham of having “not learnt the lessons of the past,” arguing that “the problems this country faces today have nothing to do with being in or out of the EU.” Brexit architect Nigel Farage, who leads the hard-right Reform UK party, said that Burnham “has no mandate” to negotiate closer ties with Brussels.
David Cameron and Boris Johnson, two former Conservative prime ministers whose premierships were defined by Britain’s divorce from the EU, have likewise cautioned Burnham against reopening old wounds.
Notwithstanding the Euroskeptic right flank, who are unlikely ever to vote for Labour, the politics of promising to rejoin the EU might actually be favorable for Burnham, noted Morgan Jones, deputy director of Persuasion UK, an organization that researches public opinion.
Polling suggests that if “there were an option to rejoin on 2016 terms tomorrow, it would be resoundingly popular,” she told CNN, saying that it also appeals to the different voters Labour would need to win a parliamentary majority.
But the same cannot be said of the process of actually doing so, she added. “We found that people were put off by the prospect of budget contributions or any threat of joining the Euro and also simply by the process itself – there is significant voter exhaustion on this topic,” she said, citing research Persuasion conducted with a pro-EU think tank.
So far, the “reset” has yielded few tangible outcomes aside from an agreement for Britain to rejoin the Erasmus student exchange program next year, at a much higher cost than it paid previously.
The UK government “really needs” the three deals on the table at this summit, Menon said, because if they don’t secure them, “it’s going to look ridiculous.”
Britain to rejoin EU’s Erasmus student exchange program in Brexit reversal
Burnham says these agreements could add up to 0.4% of GDP to the British economy and remove bureaucratic hurdles for food exporters. But Europe Minister Hamish Falconer conceded to the BBC that their implementation would compel the UK to accept EU regulations on products without being able to shape them.
It echoes the old trade-off – sovereignty versus frictionless trade – which underpinned the fractious yearslong Brexit debate, the legacy of which hangs over whatever Burnham’s government decides to do next and Europe’s own moves.
Indeed, the bloc’s foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said last week that the EU had suffered “a lot of trauma” from Britain’s departure before warning that any future negotiations “will not be that easy.”

Burnham’s rhetoric on Europe has been more forceful, but his actual approach hasn’t changed “an iota” from Starmer’s, said Anand Menon, a professor at King’s College London and director of the think-tank UK in a Changing Europe.
“The only difference is how we talk about the future, and Burnham saying we might consider rejoining,” he told CNN. “The more people talk about rejoining, the more obviously complicated an undertaking it becomes. I don’t know where Burnham goes on this.”
Further changes in the UK-EU relationship are unlikely, Menon added, unless the government compromises on its “red lines.”
His assessment echoes the EU’s former Brexit negotiator Michel Barnier, who warned earlier this month that the UK cannot “cherry pick” certain elements of the single market.
For his part, Thomas-Symonds pointed to more cooperation on immigration, stronger military ties and aligning regulations in other sectors as ways to deepen ties with the EU without breaking party promises. “Obviously, these bigger points are ones that we’re looking at in the next manifesto,” he said.
Burnham’s ambitious rhetoric has shifted the political conversation. Two campaign groups – both with ties to the original “Vote Leave” campaign – either launched or rebranded this week with the express purpose of opposing any attempts to rejoin the EU.
Conservative opposition leader Kemi Badenoch, meanwhile, accused Burnham of having “not learnt the lessons of the past,” arguing that “the problems this country faces today have nothing to do with being in or out of the EU.” Brexit architect Nigel Farage, who leads the hard-right Reform UK party, said that Burnham “has no mandate” to negotiate closer ties with Brussels.
David Cameron and Boris Johnson, two former Conservative prime ministers whose premierships were defined by Britain’s divorce from the EU, have likewise cautioned Burnham against reopening old wounds.
Notwithstanding the Euroskeptic right flank, who are unlikely ever to vote for Labour, the politics of promising to rejoin the EU might actually be favorable for Burnham, noted Morgan Jones, deputy director of Persuasion UK, an organization that researches public opinion.
Polling suggests that if “there were an option to rejoin on 2016 terms tomorrow, it would be resoundingly popular,” she told CNN, saying that it also appeals to the different voters Labour would need to win a parliamentary majority.
But the same cannot be said of the process of actually doing so, she added. “We found that people were put off by the prospect of budget contributions or any threat of joining the Euro and also simply by the process itself – there is significant voter exhaustion on this topic,” she said, citing research Persuasion conducted with a pro-EU think tank.
So far, the “reset” has yielded few tangible outcomes aside from an agreement for Britain to rejoin the Erasmus student exchange program next year, at a much higher cost than it paid previously.
The UK government “really needs” the three deals on the table at this summit, Menon said, because if they don’t secure them, “it’s going to look ridiculous.”
Britain to rejoin EU’s Erasmus student exchange program in Brexit reversal
Burnham says these agreements could add up to 0.4% of GDP to the British economy and remove bureaucratic hurdles for food exporters. But Europe Minister Hamish Falconer conceded to the BBC that their implementation would compel the UK to accept EU regulations on products without being able to shape them.
It echoes the old trade-off – sovereignty versus frictionless trade – which underpinned the fractious yearslong Brexit debate, the legacy of which hangs over whatever Burnham’s government decides to do next and Europe’s own moves.
Indeed, the bloc’s foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said last week that the EU had suffered “a lot of trauma” from Britain’s departure before warning that any future negotiations “will not be that easy.”

articles.title_orig: Riyadh’s tallest skyscraper hit in Houthi strike on Saudi wealth fund HQ
articles.title_zh: Riyadh’s tallest skyscraper hit in Houthi strike on Saudi wealth fund HQ
articles.content_orig:
RIYADH, Saudi Arabia — Riyadh’s tallest skyscraper, headquarters of the Saudi sovereign wealth fund , was struck on Thursday in a Houthi attack in the latest blow to the kingdom in its war with the Iran-backed Yemeni group.
Saudi Arabia’s civil defense said a Houthi attack on a tower in Riyadh’s financial center caused material damage to several floors of the building and nearby buildings, but no injuries were reported , state news agency SPA said. The statement did not identify the tower, but an accompanying photograph published by SPA showed the PIF Tower.
The Houthis said they had targeted Riyadh’s financial center twice on Thursday, first at dawn and again in the evening.
They also said they had attacked King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, Khamis Mushait airbase in southern Saudi Arabia and SADAF Petrochemical Company in Jubail in the kingdom’s Eastern Province. There was no immediate Saudi confirmation of these attacks.
The kingdom’s foreign ministry said it reserved the right to take “all necessary measures” to defend its sovereignty and protect its citizens and national assets following the Houthi attack.
The strike blew out windows across seven to eight floors of the PIF Tower, bending parts of its metal facade . It was the second time in less than two weeks that a Houthi attack damaged a landmark in Riyadh’s financial district, with state oil company Aramco’s building hit in a November 8 attack.
The King Abdullah Financial District was closed to visitors following the attack.
Three sources familiar with the matter said the building had been struck by an incoming Houthi missile . The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis said it had “dealt with a missile threat” launched towards Riyadh and that debris had fallen.
PIF, which stands for the Public Investment Fund, acknowledged receiving a Reuters request for comment. The Houthis issued no immediate statement on the strike.
The Houthis have been firing at Saudi airports and oil infrastructure since Yemen’s frozen civil war reignited in July amid the US-Iran war. On the ground in Yemen, the group has seized swathes of territory from the Saudi-backed government, forcing it to stage a major retreat at the weekend.
Residents of the Saudi capital were awoken by a loud boom in the early hours of Thursday.
Saudi Arabia’s civil defense issued several warnings of potential danger in Riyadh throughout Thursday, including after the attack, before announcing that the threat had passed.
The Houthi-run Saba news agency reported that Saudi aircraft had carried out airstrikes on the Houthi-controlled Yemeni capital Sanaa early on Thursday, without providing further details.
Saudi authorities did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the strikes.
The conflict has dealt a blow to Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman’s plans to develop and diversify the economy of Saudi Arabia, the world’s biggest oil exporter and a US ally.
The prince met US Central Command chief Admiral Brad Cooper in Riyadh on Wednesday, Cooper’s third publicly reported visit to Saudi Arabia since the Yemen conflict resumed.
Reuters reported on Wednesday that Saudi officials now foresee the campaign stretching on for up to six months , according to two Western officials briefed by the Saudis on the kingdom’s plans. A third ​source familiar with the Saudi plans confirmed the accounts.
The sources said the Saudis, who replaced the commander of their coalition fighting in Yemen this week, want to see their allies make gains on the ground before they enter any negotiations with the Houthis.
Meanwhile, the situation in Yemen has appeared to favour the Houthis, who have seized Yemen’s entire Red Sea coast including the strategically vital Bab el-Mandeb Strait at its mouth, and have surrounded the city of Taiz in highlands overlooking the government’s temporary capital Aden.
In the wider war, which began in February when the United States and Israel attacked Iran , there has been no sign of a breakthrough in negotiations mediated by Qatar.
Meanwhile, there has been an uptick in hostilities in the Gulf in recent days, with Iran firing at US allies Bahrain and Kuwait and US airstrikes hitting Iran’s Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday.
Saudi Arabia first entered the Yemen conflict in 2015 at the head of an Arab coalition to try to restore Yemen’s government to power ​after the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa and much of the country. They fought to a bloody stalemate and in 2022 reached a ceasefire that lasted until summer this year.

articles.title_orig: Cyberattack may have exposed Chase Bank and Mastercard customer data
articles.title_zh: Cyberattack may have exposed Chase Bank and Mastercard customer data
articles.content_orig:
Payment services were unaffected, the companies said.
JPMorganChase said Thursday morning that "third parties who provide services" to the banking giant "were the target of a cyberattack."
"Based on our investigation so far, we believe the attackers accessed certain marketing data held by those vendors, which may include some customer names and email addresses," the statement continued.
"There is no disruption to our services," according to the statement.
JPMorganChase, the largest U.S. bank, did not disclose when the cyberattack occurred or name the third-party companies that were targeted.
"Where appropriate, we will contact affected customers directly and offer support, including complimentary credit monitoring," the company said in its statement.
JPMorganChase said on Monday that it experienced technical issues that triggered online delays across several major U.S. banks and blamed the outage on a "software bug." The company said Thursday that it found "no connection to service disruptions some customers experienced earlier this week" regarding the third-party provider data breach.
Mastercard also reported on Thursday that one of its third-party providers was hacked, while Visa said earlier this week that it was aware that one of its third-party providers experienced a data breach.
"They are associated with an incident involving a third-party service provider in Asia Pacific," Visa said in its statement. "Visa’s systems were not involved and were not impacted. No payments data such as card numbers were affected."
"We were recently informed of an incident at a third-party provider that resulted in the exposure of [a] limited amount of email addresses – non-payments information – from a small subset of cardholders enrolled in a specific benefit program," Mastercard said in its statement Thursday.
"There is no impact to the Mastercard payment network or the ability for people to use their cards," Mastercard further said. "At this time, the exposure has been contained, and our teams are working with the provider to support the impacted cardholders as needed."
There have been several recent tech outages across the nation that affected air travel, email and hotel reservations, and even slowed classified internal communications at the National Security Agency.
Top Trump administration officials continued this week to insist that there is no evidence that those outages were the result of cyberattacks.

articles.title_orig: UK conducting offensive cyber ops against Russia, China, Iran and North Korea, top commander reveals
articles.title_zh: UK conducting offensive cyber ops against Russia, China, Iran and North Korea, top commander reveals
articles.content_orig:
Xi, Putin and Trump outline priorities that include UN reform, boosting oil supplies and ‘protection of diplomatic immunity’
China, Russia and the US say they have agreed a peace statement after an unprecedented trilateral summit, but the declaration made no mention of the wars in Ukraine and Iran caused by two of the participants.
The declaration on Thursday also outlined a set of priorities that included changing the UN, boosting oil supplies and what it said was the protection of diplomatic immunity.
The statement affirmed that “a nuclear war cannot be won and must not be fought”, but stopped short of suggesting the beginnings of a framework for denuclearisation.
The meeting between Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump has dominated the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit this week, with China, the host, promising it would be “groundbreaking”.
“We are really making history,” Trump told Xi and Putin at the start of the meeting. “No peace was ever forged by declining opportunities for engagement.”
Putin told a press conference later that the three men had had a “free discussion” and now had a “mutual understanding”.
Some had hopes that the talks, which lasted about one hour and 20 minutes, could be used to discuss reductions in arms between the world’s three largest nuclear powers. Beijing has previously rebuffed Trump’s advances to join such talks, pointing to the larger US and Russian stockpiles. On Thursday, though, Xi called for nuclear weapons to “be completely prohibited and thoroughly destroyed over time to make the world free of [them]”.
The language of the declaration around nuclear war is the same as that previously issued by the five permanent members of the UN security council, which includes France and the UK.
“The real test will be whether the three countries follow through on their stated commitment to discuss nuclear risk reduction and preventing nuclear proliferation,” said Patricia Kim, an expert on Chinese foreign policy at the Brookings Institution, a US thinktank. Even the suggestion that China would engage was significant, said Yun Sun, a senior fellow at the Stimson Center.
Analysts had said that the meeting’s primary significance was in its optics. “Overall, very little of substance seems to have been accomplished … This summit appears to have been all about the symbolism and prestige value,” said Prof William Hurst, from the University of Cambridge’s Centre for Geopolitics. Putin pushed back at the suggestion the summit had just been a photo-op. “It is a serious collaborative work,” he said.
In the declaration, the men “committed themselves to maintaining strategic stability and international security”.
First among their concerns was “promoting UN reform so that it may respond more effectively to global challenges”. Sun said this was a favourite topic of China’s and showed that Beijing was “flexing its diplomatic muscles”. She said: “It is able to set the agenda and the deliverables according to its priorities … and make other great powers accept them.”
The declaration also agreed that “the international criminal court [ICC] and other similar institutions must not abuse their jurisdiction”. Putin is subject to an ICC arrest warrant and so the clause added to the perception that he has done well from the summit. Since the 2022 invasion of Ukraine, the Russian president has been treated as an international pariah by Kyiv’s allies and he has not been to an Apec summit in years.
Hurst said: “This was no Yalta moment, but it was certainly a solid public demonstration of Russia’s (and Putin’s) continuing relevance and power. It’s yet another example of Putin playing a poor hand to maximum effect.”
Xi, his status as a global power broker now assured, began the morning by addressing Apec leaders, reiterating the themes of trade openness and innovation he has emphasised throughout the summit. However, Apec affairs appeared to take a back seat for most of the day, with business dominating the discussions. For all the camaraderie on display, relations are complex. Russia is under US sanctions over the Ukraine war, while China and the US spent much of the last year engaged in an escalating tit-for-tat trade war before Trump and Xi called a truce .
Trump and Putin earlier held a separate meeting – their first since August 2025 – where the US president called his Russian counterpart his “friend”.
European allies meeting in Berlin to show their support for Ukraine expressed indignation at the cosy optics. “Mr Putin is not our friend and ⁠will never be,” the Polish prime minister, Donald Tusk, said in a rejoinder to Trump. The Danish prime minister, Mette Frederiksen, said she found it “very incomprehensible” that a US ​president would want to sit down with Putin.
The peace declaration in Shenzhen said the three countries planned “to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products for the benefit of all nations”. That was important, said Shan Guo from Hutong Research, a Shanghai-based advisory firm, but “now let’s see if the US will lift sanctions”.
Trump and Xi then held their third bilateral of this year. Xi said the US-China relationship was “generally stable and positive”, according to state media. But he cautioned Washington over Taiwan, saying the US “must keep doing the right thing to avoid major setbacks in US-China relations”.
Another watched-for topic lacking detailed findings was that of AI. Xi said the two countries should “enhance communication and coordination to guard against security risks … and ensure that AI remains under human control at all times”.
Ultimately, the lack of breakthroughs might suit China, which has no appetite to move beyond the role of convener, said Kim. “Beijing has little interest in taking on the diplomatic risks of brokering an actual peace agreement in Ukraine or resolving the conflict with Iran. That would entangle China in conflicts it would rather avoid,” she said.

articles.title_orig: Anthropic IPO 'exactly what the markets need,' but analysts warn of volatility
articles.title_zh: Anthropic IPO 'exactly what the markets need,' but analysts warn of volatility
articles.content_orig:
Anthropic's blockbuster IPO on Thursday gave markets a much-needed boost after weeks of weakness, though analysts warned that the stock could remain volatile in the coming weeks.
Share of the Claude maker opened at $111.50 and closed at $97.17 per share, 17% above the IPO price. The offering raised $81.3 billion through the sale of 980 million shares — surpassing SpaceX's June listing to become the largest IPO on record .
Nomura strategist Charlie McElligott described investors as "foaming at the mouth" for the offering, with allocations "impossibly low," underscoring the strength of demand.
"Anthropic's IPO is exactly what the markets need to revive overall sentiment," said Rebecca Walser, chief investment officer at Walser Wealth Management, adding that markets have been "depressed with all of the negativity in the AI complex over the past several weeks."
Still, U.S. equities fell sharply on Thursday, with the tech heavy Nasdaq Composite dropped 2.25% to end at 23,879.20, S&P 500 down 2.02% and the Dow Jones Industrial Average down 2.19%.
Artificial intelligence and technology stocks initially rose thanks to the IPO, but the gains faded as "profit-taking spread across AI-related stocks," said James Ooi, chief market strategist at Tiger Brokers.
While the initial pop was not surprising for such a highly anticipated listing, investors should avoid "chasing the IPO," Walser said.
She expects the stock to come under pressure in the coming weeks as former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang testifies before the U.S. Senate , potentially reviving concerns around the AI sector.
"The shares remain highly volatile," said Morningstar senior equity analyst Malik Ahmed Khan.
Walser said that any weakness around the time of Huang's testimony could offer an entry point for investors interested in Anthropic, adding that she remains bullish on the OpenAI rival over the long term.
"For investors, it's going to become a blue-chip stock like Google," Ross Gerber, president and CEO of Gerber Kawasaki Wealth & Investment Management told CNBC's "Squawk Box Asia."
He added that U.S. technology valuations are at ridiculously low levels relative to the "crazy amazing innovation" coming out of California.
Morningstar's Khan struck a more cautious tone, warning investors against getting swept up in the enthusiasm around Anthropic, advising them instead to step back and "carefully" assess the company as a long-term business.
That will depend on Anthropic's ability to scale enterprise adoption, continue improving its models and turn those capabilities into economically useful products and services in the AI ecosystem, he said.
"We remain confident that the firm will be able to execute on all three fronts," Khan added, setting a $92 fair value estimate for the stock.
Walser stated that Anthropic is "extremely important for the overall AI story" as the first non-Chinese large language model developer to go public.
Its listing gives public-market investors their first direct test of how a major standalone AI model developer will be valued and perform outside the chip sector. Meanwhile, rival OpenAI could follow with an IPO sometime in 2027.
"This IPO is the show me moment for the AI story," Walser said, as much of the stock market's AI narrative has so far centered on chipmakers.

Fox News host Jesse Watters was aghast, amazed and a little out of pocket upon witnessing the hyper-realistic graphics featured in the newly released "Grand Theft Auto VI."
During Thursday's edition of "The Five," Watters and his co-hosts reacted to footage from the long-awaited game's extended look.

After watching the clip for the first time, Watters said he thought it was real life and that the games he grew up playing were nothing compared to "GTA VI."
"It's like I saw a clip of this the other day. And I thought it was real. Remember the guy with, like, the jacked — he's like walking through — I thought I was looking at 'The Bachelor' promo. I was like, 'Wow, this is crazy.' This is real. Can you have *** in this?" Watters said.
However, Watters seemed somewhat disappointed when his co-host, Emily Compagno, informed him that players couldn't solicit *** workers like they could in previous installments of the franchise.
"What? This game went woke?" Watters said.

"Some people are complaining about that, yes," Compagno replied.
"GTA VI" developer Rockstar Games told ShackNews that it excluded the ability to hire *** workers to focus more on the game's crime drama/romance narrative between the main protagonists, Jason Duval and Lucia Caminos.
"Many aspects of previous titles are not present in GTA VI, but the elements we have we believe are all necessary and complementary to the feeling and motivations we wanted to emphasize as you play through Jason and Lucia's story," the game developer said.

articles.title_orig: World reacts to ICJ finding Myanmar guilty of genocide against Rohingya
articles.title_zh: World reacts to ICJ finding Myanmar guilty of genocide against Rohingya
articles.content_orig:
The International Court of Justice (ICJ) has ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against the predominantly Muslim Rohingya minority in 2017.
The landmark judgement in The Hague on Thursday is the first time a state has been held responsible for genocide at the ICJ.
The case filed by Gambia in 2019 has been closely watched by governments, lawyers, rights groups and Rohingya communities for its implications for how states are judged under the 1948 Genocide Convention.
The court said Myanmar has an obligation to compensate the Rohingya for the violations ‌it committed, with the terms to be determined at a later date.
Here’s how key parties and world leaders reacted to the landmark verdict:
The National Unity Government, which includes remnants of former leader Aung San Suu Kyi’s National League for Democracy party, said it respects the authority of the International Court of Justice and its judgement.
It pledged to consider the court’s findings and orders, reaffirming its commitment to accountability and preventing further atrocities.
A US official told Al Jazeera that the United States was studying the ICJ’s ruling to assess its implications, while stressing the importance of preventing the court from being politicised.
“The proper interpretation of the Genocide Convention is of paramount importance, as is preventing politicization of the ICJ. We are studying the decision to fully assess its implications,” the official said.
“We express our support for the people of Burma and share the grave concerns over the continued abuses of human rights against Rohingya Muslims and members of other minority groups.”
The Gambia, which brought the case against Myanmar in November 2019 with the support of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation, welcomed the ruling with “profound satisfaction”, calling it “a historic day for international justice”.
The government said the obligation to prevent and punish genocide is shared by all states party to the 1948 Genocide Convention and called on Myanmar to comply with the judgement “fully and without delay”.
Bangladesh has welcomed the ICJ’s ruling and urged Myanmar to implement it without delay, saying the decision could pave the way for the safe, voluntary and dignified return of Rohingya refugees.
In a statement reported by the state-run Bangladesh Sangbad Sangstha (BSS) news agency, the Foreign Ministry said Myanmar was legally bound to comply with the judgement and reaffirmed that repatriation remained the only viable solution to the Rohingya crisis.
In a post shared on X, the OIC commended the ICJ’s judgement, saying it offered “redress for victims and [upholds] the principle of no impunity”.
Antonio Guterres described the ruling as a “demonstration of international justice” and a reaffirmation that impunity for “such horrific acts must not stand”.
He noted that it marked the first time the court had found a state responsible for committing genocide and called on Myanmar to comply with its decision.
The UN refugee agency (UNHCR) said the ruling was an important step towards addressing the causes of Rohingya displacement and finding lasting solutions, including access to citizenship and the creation of conditions for their safe, voluntary and dignified return.
The agency said more than 1.3 million Rohingya refugees remained displaced across the region, most of them in Bangladesh, while more than 100,000 people remained internally displaced in Myanmar’s Rakhine State.
Volker Turk said the judgement “clearly concludes” that Myanmar is responsible for “one of the most egregious crimes known to humankind.”
In a post shared on X, he added that the Rohingya people’s “suffering is a stain” on humanity.
Ed Miliband said the United Kingdom ordered the expulsion of Myanmar’s defence attache and summoned the country’s charge d’affaires. He also called for an urgent UN Security Council session to discuss the ruling.
He said further measures would be announced in the coming days to ensure those responsible are held accountable.
Yanghee Lee called it a “deeply emotional day for all Rohingya people”, adding that “justice has been decided, but not yet delivered”.
Activist Nay San Lwin said justice for the Rohingya means the restoration of their citizenship, recognition of their identity and their safe and dignified return home.
He added that their struggle would continue until those demands are met.
A coalition of 219 Rohingya and other Myanmar civil society organisations welcomed the judgement and called on the international community to ensure its full implementation.
In a joint statement published by Justice For Myanmar, the groups demanded reparations, the restoration of Rohingya citizenship and the safe return of refugees. They also called for criminal accountability for Myanmar’s military leadership, including Min Aung Hlaing.
Activist Wai Wai Nu, executive director of Women’s Peace Network, said the ruling had shattered the military’s decades-long efforts to erase Rohingya identity, deny their existence and dismiss their suffering.
“By finding that Myanmar committed genocide, ordering a guarantee of non-repetition, and ordering restitution and compensation, the world’s highest court has permanently shattered that state-sponsored lie,” she said.
The human rights group said the ruling was a “historic and authoritative recognition of the atrocities committed against the Rohingya and a rare moment of justice for survivors, victims and their families”.
Maria Elena Vignoli welcomed the court’s decision, calling it a “long-awaited recognition of the suffering the Rohingya have endured from Myanmar’s military”.

articles.title_orig: Asian shares head for worst week since 2020 as AI rout deepens
articles.title_zh: Asian shares head for worst week since 2020 as AI rout deepens
articles.content_orig:
Shares of Japan's SoftBank Group plunged 16.16% on Friday, leading a broader sell-off in Asian technology stocks following the highly anticipated market debut of artificial intelligence startup Anthropic .
SoftBank is one of the biggest backers of OpenAI, Anthropic's rival, having invested a total of $64.6 billion in the ChatGPT maker.
The sharp decline underscores growing investor concerns over SoftBank's aggressive bets on artificial intelligence, particularly its exposure to OpenAI, as markets question whether massive investments in AI infrastructure will generate sufficient returns.
SoftBank's heavy exposure to OpenAI has made its shares particularly sensitive to shifts in sentiment toward the AI sector. The stock lost 30% in October and is down 31% so far this month.
If Friday's losses hold, it would be SoftBank's worst day in more than two years.
Japanese semiconductor stocks also tumbled, with Tokyo Electron falling 7.19%, Lasertec declining 6.75% and Renesas Electronics dropping 6.71%.
The sell-off extended to South Korea, where Nvidia suppliers SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics dropped 6% and 4.7%, respectively, pressuring the benchmark Kospi, which fell 4.6%.
Elsewhere in the region, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co , or TSMC, fell 4.76% in Taiwan.
Chinese tech giant Tencent declined 1.89%, while memory chipmaker CXMT fell 4.35% to a fresh record low, while Baidu dropped 4.42%. AI chipmaker Enflame , dubbed as one of China's " four little dragons " fell 3.93%.
The declines in Asia come after the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite fell more than 2% overnight following Anthropic's highly anticipated Wall Street debut.
